Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 30, verse 1:

﴿Alif Lam Mim﴾

The discussion of its like has preceded in many surahs, especially in Surah al-'Ankabut, and that this surah is one of three surahs that begin with the disjointed letters (huruf al-tahajji, the individual letters of the Arabic alphabet pronounced separately) that are not followed by anything referring to the Qur'an. It has also preceded at the beginning of Surah Maryam.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 30, verses 2–3 (part 1 of 2):

﴿The Romans have been defeated in the nearest land, but after their defeat they will overcome﴾ ﴿within a few years﴾ [al-Rum: 2–4]

His saying, ﴿The Romans have been defeated﴾, is a statement used, by way of kinayah (allusion), for its necessary implication: meaning, We know that the Romans were defeated, so let that not weaken you, nor let them boast over it against Our Messenger and Our allies, for We know that they will overcome those who defeated them after a few years, in such a way that defeat in a case like theirs is not counted as defeat.

Thus the purpose of the speech is the clause ﴿but after their defeat they will overcome, within a few years﴾, and what precedes it was a preface to it.

The verb is attributed to the passive form because the aim is to speak about the one defeated, not about the victor; and because it was known that those who defeated the Romans were the Persians.

Al-Rum (the Romans) is a name that became common in Arabic usage for a mixed people of Greeks and Slavs, and of the Romanians whose origin is from the Latins, the inhabitants of Italy, who migrated to the eastern edges of Europe. This people, called the Rum, was formed upon this mixture, and from it came a state that occupied a part of Europe and a part of Asia Minor, namely the lands of Anatolia. The Arabs applied the name al-Rum to the whole of this people, distinguishing them from the Latin Romans (al-Rumān). They also called the Rum "Banu al-Asfar" (the Sons of Yellow), as came in the hadith of Abu Sufyan concerning the letter of the Prophet ﷺ sent to Heraclius, the ruler of the Romans, who was in Homs in the land of Syria, when Abu Sufyan said to his companions: "The affair of Ibn Abi Kabshah has become great; indeed he fears him, the king of Banu al-Asfar."

The reason for the connection of the Roman nation with the Greek nation, and the formation of the Rum people from the two mixed elements, is that the Greeks had control over Sicily and some lands of Italy, and were thereby in contacts and back-and-forth wars with the Romans; the Roman kingdom gradually grew and expanded through conquests, and its authority spread to Africa and the regions of Asia Minor through the conquests of "Julius Caesar" to Egypt, North Africa and the lands of Greece, and through the successive conquests of the Caesars after him, so that it reached from Rome to Armenia and Iraq. Within it entered the lands of Greece, the cities of Rhodes, Sakis and Caria, and the Slavs who were on the river Danube. There joined it the Byzantines, attributed to the city of Byzantium located at the site of Istanbul on the Bosphorus, who were varieties of Greeks and Spartans, and who were people of great commerce at the beginning of the fourth century BC. Then they formed a union between themselves and the people of Rhodes and Sakis. Byzantium was among the kingdom of Alexander the Macedonian, and after his death, when his commanders divided the kingdom after him, Byzantium became an independent state, and then came under the authority of Rome, and the Caesars of the Romans ruled it, until Constantine became Caesar of Rome and alone held authority within the bounds of the year (332) CE, and he gathered the scattered kingdom. He made for the kingdom two capitals: a western capital, which is "Rome," and an eastern capital, which he laid out as a great city upon the remains of the city of Byzantium and named "Constantinople." His aspiration was directed to inhabiting it, so it attained a fame exceeding that of Rome. After his death in the year (337), the kingdom was divided among his sons. The eastern part, which is the land of the Rum and whose capital is Constantinople, went to his son "Constantius," and from that time the kingdom of Constantinople became the kingdom of the Rum, while the kingdom of "Rome" remained the kingdom of the Romans. The separation of the two kingdoms increased in the year (395) when "Theodosius" divided the lands of the Roman sultanate between his two sons, making them into two parts: an eastern kingdom and a western kingdom. The eastern kingdom became famous by the name of the land of the Rum, and its capital was "Constantinople." The Rum are known among the Franks as the Byzantines, attributed to "Byzantium," the name of an ancient Greek city situated on the shore of the Bosphorus, which is part of the site of the city that came into being after it, as has preceded above. It became a city of great commerce in the fifth century BC, and its harbour was called the Golden Horn. At the end of the fourth century BC it threw off the obedience of Athens. In the middle of the fourth century CE, Constantine was made ruler of the city of Constantinople.

This defeat mentioned in this verse is the defeat of the Romans in the war which took place between them and the Persians in the year (615) CE. That is because Khusraw son of Hormizd, king of the Persians, attacked the Romans in the lands of Syria and Palestine, which were among the lands under the rule of Heraclius, Caesar of the Romans. He besieged Antioch and then Damascus, and the great defeat of the Romans occurred at the outskirts of the land of Syria bordering the land of the Arabs, between Busra and Adhruat. That is what is meant in this verse by "the nearest land," i.e., the nearest of the lands of the Romans to the lands of the Arabs.

Thus the definite article in "al-ard" is for prior reference, i.e., the land of the Romans being spoken of, or the lam is a substitute for the genitive complement, i.e., "in the nearest of their land," or "the nearest land of God." The complement of "adna" was omitted because its implied meaning is evident: "from your land," i.e., the nearest of the lands of the Romans to the land of the Arabs, for the land of Syria was then subject to the Romans, and it is the nearest realm of the Romans to the lands of the Arabs.

This defeat was a great defeat for the Romans.

His saying, ﴿but after their defeat they will overcome, within a few years﴾, is a report of a promise, conjoined to the report that precedes it. The plural pronouns refer to the Romans.

Their defeat (ghalabihim) is a verbal noun annexed to its object. The object of "sayaghlibun" is omitted, since it is known that its implied sense is: "they will overcome those who defeated them," i.e., the Persians, since it is not supposed that the meaning is that they will overcome other people; for their victory over other peoples, although it raises their status and removes from them the disgrace of the Persians' victory over them, the story clarifies the intended meaning; and because the completion of the favour upon the Muslims is that the Romans should overcome the Persians, whose victory the polytheists rejoiced in and gloated over the Muslims because of, as has preceded.

The benefit of mentioning "after their defeat" is to alert to the magnitude of that defeat upon them, and that it is such that no victory for them is expected after it. Hence the polytheists rejoiced. Therefore the promise that they will overcome after that defeat within a not-long period is a challenge with which the Qur'an challenged the polytheists, and an indication that God decreed for them victory over the Persians in a manner beyond the ordinary: a miracle for His Prophet ﷺ and a dignity for the Muslims.

The word "bid'" with a kasra on the ba' is a metaphor for a small number that does not exceed ten. It has already been discussed in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So he remained in the prison a few years﴾ [Yusuf: 42] in Surah Yusuf. This is a term for their return of the advantage over the Persians.

The wisdom of leaving the number of years indefinite is that it is required by the state of speech of the Mighty, the Wise, that it be restricted to the intended matter in summary, and not descend into detail; for such detail would be regarded as superfluous by people of sound intellect; and so that the Muslims might have hope for a period nearer than what appeared, and in that there is relief for them.

This verse is among the miracles of the Qur'an that belong to the fourth aspect in the tenth introduction of the introductions to this exegesis.

At-Tirmidhi related, with sound and good chains, that the polytheists used to love that the people of Persia would prevail over the Romans, because they and the Persians were people of idols; and the Muslims used to love that the Romans would prevail over the people of Persia, because they were people of a Book like them. So when the verse ﴿Alif Lam Mim﴾ [al-Rum: 1] ﴿The Romans have been defeated﴾ was revealed, Persia was dominant over the Romans. They mentioned it to Abu Bakr, and Abu Bakr mentioned it to the Messenger of God ﷺ, and the Messenger of God said: "Indeed they will overcome," and this verse was revealed. Abu Bakr al-Siddiq went out shouting in the outskirts of Makkah: ﴿Alif Lam Mim﴾ ﴿The Romans have been defeated in the nearest land, but after their defeat they will overcome﴾ ﴿within a few years﴾. Some people of Quraysh said to Abu Bakr: "That is between us and you. Your companion claims that the Romans will overcome Persia within a few years; shall we not wager you on that?" He said: "Yes," and that was before the prohibition of wagering. They said to Abu Bakr: "How many years do you make the 'bid' — three to nine years? Name between us and you a middle term at which we will stop." So Abu Bakr named six years for them. Abu Bakr and the polytheists deposited a pledge and agreed on the wager. Six years passed before the Romans prevailed, so the polytheists took Abu Bakr's pledge. The Messenger of God ﷺ said to Abu Bakr: "Why did you not lower it, O Abu Bakr? Why did you not make it less than ten? For the bid is between three and nine." The Muslims criticised Abu Bakr for naming six years, and many people embraced Islam at that time."

The exegetes mentioned that the one who wagered with Abu Bakr was Ubayy ibn Khalaf, and that they made the stake five camels; and in another report, after they had set the term at six years, they changed it to nine years and increased the number of camels. When Abu Bakr wished to emigrate with the Prophet ﷺ, Ubayy ibn Khalaf clung to him and said: "Give me a guarantor for the stake, in case you are defeated." So Abu Bakr gave as guarantor his son 'Abd al-Rahman, who was at that time still a polytheist remaining in Makkah. When Ubayy ibn Khalaf wished to go out to Uhud, 'Abd al-Rahman demanded from him a guarantor, and he gave him one. Then Ubayy died in Makkah from a wound the Prophet ﷺ had inflicted on him. When the Romans prevailed after seven years, Abu Bakr took the stake from the heirs of Ubayy ibn Khalaf.

The Romans' overcoming of the Persians occurred in the year six, and the news reached the Muslims. In the hadith of al-Tirmidhi from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, he said: "When the day of Badr came, the Romans prevailed over Persia, and that pleased the believers." The well-known account is that this was on the day of Hudaybiyah. It has preceded at the beginning of the surah that the interval between the defeat of the Romans and the defeat of the Persians was seven years — with the sin before the nun — and that what occurred in some reports that it was nine is a copyist's error. The Romans' overcoming of the Persians was in the reign of Heraclius, Caesar of the Romans, and after it Heraclius came to the land of Syria, stayed at Homs, and met Abu Sufyan ibn Harb in a group of people of Makkah who had come as merchants to Syria.

Know that this report about the wager of Abu Bakr and Ubayy ibn Khalaf, and the Prophet's ﷺ approval of it, was used as evidence by Abu Hanifah for the permissibility of usurious contracts with the people of war. As for the majority, they hold that this is abrogated by the prohibition of gambling in absolute terms, which was not restricted to non-combatants. The verification of the matter is that the wager that took place between Abu Bakr and Ubayy ibn Khalaf took place under the original permissibility, since there was no sharia in Makkah at that time, so there is no evidence in it for the permissibility of wagering; and the prohibition of wagering afterwards is a new legislation and not abrogation at all.

﴿To God belongs the command, before and after﴾ [al-Rum: 4]

This is a parenthetical clause between the conjoined clauses. By "the command" is meant the command of decree and creation: that is, God decreed the first and second victories before they occurred, i.e., before the Romans' victory over the Persians, which is the period from the day the Persians overcame them, and after the Romans' victory over the Persians.

There are thus two annexing nouns whose annexed complements (*mudaf ilayhi*, the noun in the genitive that completes them) are omitted. Therefore *qablu* (قَبْلُ, "before") and *ba'du* (بَعْدُ, "after") are built on a *damma* (*mabni*, indeclinable, the vowel being fixed rather than a case ending), because the annexed complement has been omitted. Their meaning requires an implied annexed complement, so they resemble the particle (*harf*) in needing to be connected to something else. This indeclinable form is the most eloquent usage when the complement of *qablu* and *ba'du* is omitted and its presence is indicated by evidence in the speech. If the annexation is not intended, but the words refer to the past time and the future time, then they take case endings like other indefinite nouns (*nakirat*). An example is the verse of Abdullah ibn Ya'rub ibn Mu'awiya, or Yazid ibn al-Sa'q:

*So the drink became palatable to me, though before I had been*
*nearly choking on scalding water.*

That is, "and I had been in a time past, not intending a specific time."

*And from before, every mawla called out to his kinsman,*
*but the bonds did not sway the mawla toward him.*

with a kasra on the *lam* of *qabli*. He rejected al-Farra's claim that it was narrated with a kasra without tanwin. Al-Zajjaj means that what is obligatory is that it be narrated with a damma.

The fronting of the prepositional phrase in the words ﴿لِلَّهِ الأمْرُ﴾ [Ar-Rum: 4], "To God belongs the command," serves to refute the arrogance of the polytheists, whom the victory of the Persians over the Romans delighted, because they were worshippers of idols like themselves. This implies the belief that that victory came from the idols supporting their worshippers. So He explained to them the falsity of that, and that control belongs to God alone in both states, for the wisdom that we have explained above, as the concluding appendage (*tadhyil*, a closing statement that reinforces the meaning) indicates with the words ﴿يَنْصُرُ مَن يَشاءُ﴾ [Ar-Rum: 5], "He gives victory to whom He wills."

In this there is a great lesson in conduct (*adab*) for Muslims, so that they do not attribute events to causes other than their real causes, and do not invent causes that suit their desires, as the charlatans among the soothsayers (*kuhhan*) and their like used to do.

The Prophet (ﷺ) used to proclaim this meaning in his sermons. When the sun was eclipsed on the day Ibrahim, the son of the Prophet (ﷺ), died, people said: "The sun was eclipsed for the death of Ibrahim." So the Prophet (ﷺ) delivered a sermon and said in it: "Indeed the sun and the moon are two of the signs of God; they do not eclipse for the death of anyone or for his life."

It is part of the craft of deception (*dajal*) that the practitioners of deception seize upon events that coincide with certain circumstances and claim that they happened because of them, even though those events benefit some people and harm others. For this reason the support through the victory of the Romans was promised in this verse beforehand, so that all people would know that it was a challenge announced before its occurrence, not a claim made after its occurrence. For this reason, after the promises, He said, ﴿ويَوْمَئِذٍ يَفْرَحُ المُؤْمِنُونَ بِنَصْرِ اللَّهِ﴾ [Ar-Rum: 4], "And on that day the believers will rejoice in God's victory."

**Commentary of Ibn ʿĀshūr (al-Taḥrīr wa al-Tanwīr) on Sūrah 30, verses 6–7:**

﴿The promise of Allah. Allah does not fail His promise, but most of the people do not know.﴾ ﴿They know an outward appearance of the worldly life, but they are heedless of the Hereafter.﴾

"Waʿda Allāh" is in the accusative as an absolute object (al-mafʿūl al-muṭlaq). This is an absolute object emphasizing the meaning of a sentence before it, one that has the same sense as it. The grammarians call it a "verbal noun emphasizing itself" (maṣdaran muʾakkidan li-nafsihi), an unusual designation, meaning by "itself" its sense and not its wording. A similar example is in al-Kashshāf, and they illustrate it with the phrase "laka ʿalayya alfun ʿurfan" ("You have from me a thousand, by acknowledgment"), because ʿurfan means "acknowledgment." It emphasizes the content of the sentence "laka ʿalayya alf." Likewise, "waʿda Allāh" emphasizes the content of the sentence "wa-hum min baʿdi ghalabihim sayaghlibūn fī biḍʿi sinīn" ("and they, after their defeat, will overcome in a few years") [al-Rūm: 3].

Attributing the promise to Allah hints that it is certain to be fulfilled, because the promise of the Truthful, the Able, the Self-Sufficient has no reason for being broken.

The sentence "lā yukhlifu Allāhu waʿdahu" ("Allah does not fail His promise") explains what is meant by the phrase "waʿda Allāh." Since that phrase indicated, by allusion, that the promise is certain, this sentence states it explicitly. Because it stands in the position of explanation, it is separated and not joined by a conjunction. The purpose of first stating in general and then in detail is to establish the ruling and reinforce it. Moreover, the sentence "lā yukhlifu Allāhu waʿdahu" brings dismay to the polytheists through this emphasis. He called it a "promise" with regard to the state of the believers, which is the more important consideration here. It is also a warning to the polytheists that their partisans will be forsaken, and that those who boast of resembling their religion will be disgraced.

The place of the exceptive contrast in "wa-lākinna akthara al-nāsi lā yaʿlamūn" ("but most of the people do not know") is what the general statement requires. Its detail is that this is a matter beyond doubt, that it is the promise of Allah, who is true to His promise and able to grant victory to the defeated and make them victorious. So He points out that the polytheists' wagering on its not occurring arose from the deficiency of their minds. They deemed it impossible that the Romans, after their weakness, should gain power over the Persians, who had defeated them in a short period of a few years. They did not know that what Allah has decreed is greater.

Therefore, "akthar al-nās" (most of the people) primarily refers to the polytheists, because they heard the promise and wagered that it would not come to pass.

It also includes everyone who regarded a Roman victory over the Persians within such a period as impossible: men of state and men of war among the Persians, who were elated by their victories; people of other nations; and the Romans themselves. Therefore he expressed this multitude with "akthar al-nās," in the comparative form.

The definite article in "al-nās" is for comprehensiveness (lil-istighrāq).

The object of "yaʿlamūn" is omitted, indicated by His saying "sayaghlibūn fī biḍʿi sinīn" [al-Rūm: 3]. The sense is: "they do not know this near and wondrous victory." It is also permissible that the verb be treated as intransitive, meaning that they are placed in the position of those who have no knowledge at all. Because they did not attain the understanding of subtle matters or grasp rational proofs, what knowledge they had was like its absence, since they did not reach the perfection attained by those firmly grounded in knowledge, the people of reflection. Thus there is hyperbole in declaring them ignorant, which is what the context requires.

Since among the causes of their denial of the promise of the Romans' victory over the Persians after a few years was that they regarded it as impossible, and since their reckoning it so was a confusion of ordinary improbability with impossibility, while they overlooked the rare destinies that Allah the Exalted decrees and for which He prepares causes they do not reckon with, so that things come about according to His decree and not according to what people estimate. A sensible person should consider all possibilities and examine them by testing and evaluation. Allah turned this against them by following His statement that they lack knowledge with the truth of the Qur'anic promise, by describing the whole state of their knowledge: the utmost of their thinking is confined to the outward appearances of the worldly life, which do not require rational reflection, namely perceptible things, tested experiences and signs. They do not know the inner meanings of evidence, which require the exercise of thought and reflection.

The most likely reading is that "min" in "min al-ḥayāt al-dunyā" is partitive (tabʿīḍiyyah), meaning: they know the outward aspects of what is in this world, and do not know its subtleties, which are the true sciences, all of which are found in this world. In this sense the world is the field of the Hereafter.

The discourse implies a censure of their condition, and the target of the censure is the sentence "wa-hum ʿani al-ākhirati hum ghāfilūn" ("and they are heedless of the Hereafter"). As for knowing the worldly life, that is not blameworthy, since the believers also knew the outward aspect of the worldly life. What is blameworthy is that the polytheists know what is outwardly apparent of worldly affairs, but do not know that beyond the world of matter there is another world, the unseen world. In declaring them ignorant of the unseen world, he limited their ignorance to their ignorance of the existence of the Hereafter, in a remarkable restriction through which he moved from the subject of the promise of the Romans' victory to a more important subject, which is the proof of resurrection. This restriction implies the unseen world, since resurrection necessarily entails it. It serves as an example of their ignorance of the unseen world and a censure of it, in that it led them into the peril of neglecting hope in the Hereafter and neglecting preparation for what such hope requires. This is the position of His saying "wa-hum ʿani al-ākhirati hum ghāfilūn." Thus the sentence "yaʿlamūna ẓāhiran min al-ḥayāt al-dunyā" is a substitute (badal) for the sentence "lā yaʿlamūn," a substitution of inclusion (badal ishtimāl), in view of what follows it, namely "wa-hum ʿani al-ākhirati hum ghāfilūn," because their knowledge implies the negation of knowledge of the hidden matters of the Hereafter, even though they know the outward aspects of the worldly life.

The sentence "wa-hum ʿani al-ākhirati hum ghāfilūn" may be taken as coordinated (ʿaṭf) with the sentence "yaʿlamūna ẓāhiran min al-ḥayāt al-dunyā," so that they are reported as knowing some things and not knowing others. You may also take the sentence "wa-hum ʿani al-ākhirah" and so on as being in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), with the "wāw" being the "wāw" of circumstance.

Their ignorance of the Hereafter is expressed as heedlessness, as a metonymy for the evident proofs of the existence of the Hereafter, had they looked at the indications that establish the existence of a Hereafter. Their ignorance of this was thus like heedlessness, since it is such that it would be revealed if they had cared to reflect. So "ghāfilūn" is used figuratively, as a subordinate metaphor (istiʿārah tabaʿiyyah).

The first "hum" is in the position of a subject, and the second "hum" is a pronoun of separation (ḍamīr faṣl). The nominal sentence indicates their firm entrenchment in heedlessness of the Hereafter and their persistence in that heedlessness. The separating pronoun serves to convey exclusivity with regard to them, meaning: they alone are heedless of the Hereafter, not the believers.

Among the rhetorical beauties is the combination of "lā yaʿlamūn" and "yaʿlamūn," in which there is antithesis (ṭibāq) with respect to what the two words signify, not with respect to their objects. Close to it is His saying, exalted is He: "wa-laqad ʿalimū lamani ishtarāhu mā lahu fī al-ākhirati min khalāq" ("And they certainly knew that whoever purchased it would have no share in the Hereafter") [al-Baqarah: 102], and "wa-labi'sa mā sharaw bihi anfusahum law kānū yaʿlamūn" ("And wretched is that for which they sold themselves, if they only knew") [al-Baqarah: 102].

It is conjoined (*ʿaṭf*, coordination) to the clause ﴿And they are heedless of the Hereafter﴾ [al-Rum: 7], because they denied the Hereafter. This proof was brought to them to show that the Hereafter is among the requirements of wisdom.

The pronoun in *yatafakkarū* ("they reflect") refers to the heedless people who are unaware of the Hereafter, at the head of whom are the polytheists of Makkah. The interrogative is one of wonder (*taʿjībī*) at their heedlessness and their failure to reflect. The implied sense is: "They are heedless, and it is astonishing that they do not reflect." The reason for this shift is that the discourse about the signs of God's power returned to the Romans after their defeat, and there were two causes for this:

The first: their habit of confining their thoughts to wandering among familiar things, without considering the realm of what is possible. This is one of the causes of their denial of resurrection, which is the greatest of the things they denied for this reason.

The second: their rebellion against denying the Messenger (ﷺ) after they had witnessed his miracle. So the discourse moved to refuting their opinions concerning these two causes.

*Tafakkur* (reflection) means exercising the mind (*fikr*), that is, the rational faculty, in order to benefit from it. It is contemplation of rational evidence. It was discussed earlier at the words of God, Exalted be He: ﴿Say: Are the blind and the seeing equal? Will you not then reflect?﴾ [al-Anʿam: 50], in Surat al-Anʿam.

*Anfus* is the plural of *nafs*. *Nafs* is applied to the whole essence (*dhāt*), and it is also applied to the inner self of a person. From the latter is the words of God, Exalted be He, quoting ʿIsā, peace be upon him: ﴿You know what is in my self﴾ [al-Maʾidah: 116].

Like the saying of ʿUmar on the day of al-Saqifah: "There had occurred to my mind (*zawwat fī nafsī*) a statement," meaning in my intellect and my inner self.

The preposition *fī* in His words ﴿in themselves﴾ may be for true, conventional inclusion (*ẓarfiyya ḥaqīqiyya iʿtibāriyya*, the sense of a container), in which case it is a complement of the verbal noun of *yatafakkarū*, meaning: a reflection settled within themselves. The position of this adverbial phrase relative to what precedes it is that of a descriptive qualifier of the reflection. Since reflection occurs only within the self, ﴿in themselves﴾ is mentioned to strengthen the imagery of reflection. It is like a clarifying qualifier that fixes the meaning of reflection in the hearer's mind, as in His words: ﴿nor do you write it with your right hand﴾ [al-ʿAnkabut: 48], and His words: ﴿nor a bird that flies with its two wings﴾ [al-Anʿam: 38]. On this reading, the clause ﴿what God created of the heavens and the earth﴾ and so on explains the clause *yatafakkarū*, since its content is what they are to reflect upon, as in His words: ﴿Have they not reflected that there is no madness in their companion?﴾ [al-Aʿraf: 184].

It may also be that *fī* is for figurative inclusion (*ẓarfiyya majāziyya*), connected to the verb *yatafakkarū* in the manner of an object complement, meaning: they should ponder and contemplate concerning themselves. "Selves" here means the essences, and this is in the sense of His words: ﴿And in yourselves; will you not see?﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 21]. The proper method of reasoning, which leads to knowledge of God's oneness and the certainty of resurrection, is to begin by reflecting on the conditions of the creation of man. God, Exalted be He, said: ﴿Did you think that We created you in vain, and that you would not be returned to Us?﴾ [al-Muʾminun: 115]. This is like His words: ﴿Have they not looked into the dominion of the heavens and the earth?﴾ [al-Aʿraf: 185], meaning: into the indication of the dominion of the heavens and the earth. On this interpretation the clause ﴿what God created of the heavens and the earth﴾ and so on is a substitute of inclusion (*badal ishtimāl*) for "in themselves," since the discourse involves an elision of a noun in construct. Its implied sense is: "in the indication of their selves." The indication of their selves includes the indication of the creation of the heavens and the earth and what is between them with truth, because "their selves" comprise the creation that is in the earth and point to what is in the earth. Likewise, the general notion of what is in the earth points to the creation of their selves.

On both possibilities, the verb *yatafakkarū* is suspended from acting upon two objects because of the negation that follows it. The meaning of the creation of the heavens and the earth and what is between them with truth is that their creation is accompanied by truth.

The truth here is that which is fitting to be the wisdom and the cause for the creation of the heavens and the earth. The truth (*ḥaqq*) of every kind and species is what it is fitting for it to achieve of perfection in its properties, and that it is worthy of this, as a father says to his son who is dutiful to him: "You are truly my son." Do you not see that they made the definiteness of an indefinite noun, by the article of the genus, indicate the sense of perfection in expressions such as "You are the beloved," because a generic noun in the context of address indicates its perfection in its attributes? The truth of each kind is known only through the attributes by which it has its capacity. Whoever considers the capacities that God, Exalted be He, placed in the kinds of created beings will find that every kind was created with specific limits, which when it reaches them it does not accept more. Thus the horse, the cow, and the dog, which existed in past ages and up to the time of Adam, are no different from their later counterparts; they do not exceed the limits they had. This is shown by the experiences of people living alongside these generations, by the reports of people who lived before them about the generations contemporary with them, and by the analogy of what existed before the times of history with the generations that became extinct before them. The exception is the human species, for God created it with a capacity for increase in unlimited perfections, according to the conditions of the renewal of generations in perfection and advancement, and He made it the sovereign over this world and the one who disposes of the kinds of created beings in its world, as He said: ﴿He it is who created for you all that is in the earth﴾ [al-Baqarah: 29]. This is by what He placed in it of intellect.

Observation has also shown that the individuals of the human species differ in their perfection in what suits them, with a difference of far-reaching extremes, as al-Buhturi said:

*I have not seen the men differ so much in excellence*
*that a thousand is counted as one against one.*

Thus experience through observation shows this, just as reports about the past and the analogy of what came before history with what came after it all indicate this meaning. Because of this difference, the Creator imposed upon man laws so that he might reach the summit of perfection that is fitting for him in his time, taking into account the circumstances of his time that surround him, and so that he might avoid corrupting himself and corrupting his fellow members of the species. Yet what was given to the human species of branches of intellect allowed it to act according to its will and desire, and to seek what is right or not to seek it. When its Creator imposed upon it the obligation to follow the laws of His legislation, it committed and avoided, so at times it attained the stations of its perfection, and at other times it fell short of them with varying degrees of shortfall. Therefore, it was part of wisdom that it not be left to continue unchecked on the steps of deficiency and corruption. This is done either by empowering a compelling force over it that uproots the corrupter and preserves the reformer, or by training it to do good until it moves toward goodness by its praiseworthy choice. However, another divine wisdom required the continuance of the world's habitation and that it not be uprooted. Because of this, the use of the uprooting force was rendered inoperative, so the use of its training toward goodness became necessary. God combined the two wisdoms by making a reward for the righteous according to the measure of their righteousness and a punishment for the corrupters according to the measure of their deeds. All of this takes place in a world other than this world. This was communicated to them through the tongues of His messengers and prophets, to remove the stain and to alert them to the wisdom. So one group feared and hoped, and acted or refrained, while another group turned away and kept away, and committed and earned. It was among the rights of the effects of these wisdoms that the righteous not be deprived of his reward, and that the corrupter not escape by what he did, so that the right of the people of perfection and of those below them in ranks might become evident. Therefore God made the continuance of the individuals of the species in this world limited by specified terms, and made a specified term for the continuance of this entire world. When all the terms come to an end, the Day of Recompense for deeds comes, and the people of deficiency are distinguished from the people of perfection.

Thus the appointment of terms for the continuance of created beings is among the truth with which they were created in accompaniment. For this reason it was singled out for mention, out of concern for its matter, to alert to its place, and to show that it is the aim of their existence. So He conjoined it to the truth, out of concern for it, just as He conjoined its opposite to falsehood, in His words: ﴿Did you think that We created you in vain, and that you would not be returned to Us?﴾ [al-Muʾminun: 115]. Thus He said: ﴿Have they not reflected within themselves that God did not create the heavens and the earth and what is between them except with truth and for a specified term?﴾

It has already passed in Surat al-Anʿam, His words: ﴿And He it is who created the heavens and the earth with truth, and the day He says "Be," and it is; His word is the truth﴾ [al-Anʿam: 73], and so on.

The benefit of mentioning the heavens here is that the conditions of the heavens, with their sun, stars, and angels, are among the truth with which they were created in accompaniment. As for what lies beyond that of their conditions, whose connection to this world we do not know, we leave its matter to God and measure the unseen by the seen, so we are certain that it was not created except with truth in the same way.

Thus the evidences of the truth of resurrection and recompense are manifest in the minute details of the creation of created beings. For this reason He followed it with His words: ﴿Indeed, many of the people are disbelievers in the meeting with their Lord﴾. This is like His words, Exalted be He: ﴿Did you think that We created you in vain, and that you would not be returned to Us?﴾ [al-Muʾminun: 115].

*Al-musammā* means the determined, the appointed. The term "naming" (*tasmiya*) was applied to determination, and this was discussed earlier at His words, Exalted be He: ﴿and We cause to remain in the wombs what We will for an appointed term﴾ [al-Hajj: 5], in Surat al-Hajj, and at His words, Exalted be He: ﴿Had there not been an appointed term, the punishment would have come upon them﴾ [al-ʿAnkabut: 53], in Surat al-ʿAnkabut.

The clause ﴿Indeed, many of the people are disbelievers in the meeting with their Lord﴾ is a concluding summation (*tadhyīl*, a closing statement that reinforces the preceding argument).

Its emphasis with *inna* ("indeed") is to treat the hearer as one who doubts that there exists anyone who denies the meeting with God after this proof that has passed, let alone that the disbelievers in it would be many. What is meant by "many" here is the polytheists of Makkah and the rest of the polytheistic Arabs who deny resurrection, and those like them among the naturalists (*dahriyyūn*). He did not express it here as "most of the people," because those who affirm resurrection are numerous, such as the People of the Book, the Sabians, the Magians, and the Copts.

[Page 53]

(Ibn 'Ashur's commentary on Surah Al-Rum, verse 9)

﴿Have they not travelled through the earth and observed how was the end of those before them?﴾ This is a conjunction (ʿatf) onto the clause ﴿Have they not reflected within themselves?﴾ [Al-Rum: 8]. It is similar to the clause it is conjoined to, which is connected to what is implied by His words ﴿But most people do not know﴾ [Al-Rum: 6]. Among the causes of their lack of knowledge is their denial of the Messenger (ﷺ), who informed them of the Resurrection. When the evidence of the wisdom of the Resurrection and of recompense in truth was presented to them, He followed their warning with an admonition about the ends of the nations who denied their messengers, because the intended point is the outcome of their denial of the messengers of Allah. This is His words ﴿Their messengers came to them with clear proofs, but Allah would not wrong them﴾, and so on.

The command to travel through the earth has already occurred in His words ﴿Say: Travel through the earth, then observe how was the end of the deniers﴾ [Al-An'am: 11] in Surah Al-An'am, and in His words ﴿Say: Travel through the earth and observe how He originated creation﴾ [Al-'Ankabut: 20] in Surah Al-'Ankabut.

The interrogative in ﴿Have they not travelled﴾ is confirmatory (taqriri). The confirmation has been expressed in negative form for the reason we mentioned in His words ﴿Did they not see that it does not speak to them?﴾ [Al-A'raf: 148], His words ﴿Did there not come to you messengers from among you?﴾ [Al-A'raf: 35] in Al-A'raf, and His words ﴿Is there not in Hell an abode for the disbelievers?﴾ [Al-'Ankabut: 68] at the end of Al-'Ankabut.

Al-ard (the earth) is the name for the sphere on which people live.

[p. 57]

Al-nazar (observation) here is visual observation, because the Quraysh used to pass by the dwellings of Thamud and the people of Lut on their journeys to Syria, and by the dwellings of 'Ad on their journeys to Yemen.

The mode of the outcome (kayfiyyat al-'aqibah) is the condition of their final state: the ruin of their lands and the cutting off of their descendants. It thus reinforces the indication of reflection in His words ﴿Have they not reflected within themselves?﴾ [Al-Rum: 8], and so on, by the indication of the senses in His words ﴿and observe how was the end of those before them﴾.

Kayfa is an interrogative that suspends the verb (yanzurū) from its object. It is as if it were said: "and observe," and then it is resumed and said: "how was the end of those before them."

Al-'aqibah (the outcome) is the final matter, whether good or bad, unlike al-'uqba, which is specifically for good, except in a context of mushakalah (rhetorical correspondence, using a word in a form that matches a preceding one). The term al-'aqibah has already been mentioned in His words ﴿And the good outcome is for the righteous﴾ [Al-A'raf: 128] in Al-A'raf.

His words ﴿Observe how was the end of those before them﴾ combine a threat against their denial of the Prophet (ﷺ) and a declaration of their ignorance for their rejection of what is possible, since they were certain that the Persians could not be defeated after their victory.

These are the remains of great nations that once dominated the earth, but their dominion disappeared and their lands became empty because of the domination of other nations over them.

By "those before them" is meant 'Ad, Thamud, the people of Lut, and those like them, whose remains the Arabs witnessed. The meaning is that they were, before the Quraysh, in the same condition of polytheism and of denying the messengers sent to them, as is indicated by His words that follow: ﴿They were stronger than them in power﴾, and so on.

* * *

﴿They were stronger than them in power, and they stirred up the earth and cultivated it more than these have cultivated it, and their messengers came to them with clear proofs. Allah would not wrong them, but they were wronging themselves.﴾

All of those were stronger than the Quraysh and had greater longevity on the earth. All of them were visited by messengers, and all of them ended in annihilation. The Quraysh cannot acknowledge any of this.

[p. 58]

The clause ﴿They were stronger than them in power﴾ is an explanation (bayan) of the clause ﴿how was the end of those before them﴾.

Al-shiddah (strength) is physical hardness of the body. It is frequently used metaphorically for the intensity of one of the qualities of a thing, comparing the completeness and perfection of the attribute to hardness in resisting change. This has already occurred in His words ﴿and possessors of great might﴾ [Al-Naml: 33] in Surah Al-Naml.

Al-quwwah (power) is a state by which its possessor resists whatever would bring about his collapse. Among its forms are the strength of the body and the strength of wood. Quwwah is also used metaphorically for that by which hostile attack is repelled and a condition is kept upright. It is thus a collection of attributes by which a thing remains in its most perfect state, as in His words ﴿We are possessors of strength﴾ [Al-Naml: 33]. The power of a nation is the collection of what repels attacks on its existence and preserves the goodness of its conditions: war equipment, wealth, children, and wives. The condition of the polytheists of the Quraysh does not approach the conditions of those nations in power. It suffices to mention 'Ad, who were the proverbial example of power in all their affairs. The Arabs describe something great of its kind as "'adiyy," attributing it to 'Ad.

The verb athārū (they stirred up) is coordinated (ʿatf) onto kānū (they were). It is a verb derived from al-ithārah, with a kasrah on the hamzah, which is the moving of the parts of a thing. Al-ithārah is the lifting of a thing that was at rest and its overturning after it has settled. God the Exalted said: ﴿Allah is He who sends the winds, and they raise clouds﴾ [Al-Rum: 48], meaning that they drive it and push it from one place to another.

Al-ithārah is here applied to the overturning of the earth's soil by bringing what was underneath to the surface, which is ploughing. God the Exalted said: ﴿not trained to plough the earth﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 71]. Al-Nabighah said, describing wild cattle when they dig up the dirt:

They stir up the pebbles until they touch their coolness, when the sun has spat out its saliva upon their breasts.

It is also possible that athārū here is a figurative representation (tamthil) of the condition of the intensity of their control over the earth and their domination over others, by the image of one who stirs up something still and agitates it. From this, the word thawrah (revolution) is used for leaving the community. This possibility is more suitable to the intended meaning, which is describing the nations by strength and capacity, than the possibility that ithārah means ploughing the land, since ploughing falls under cultivation. The pronoun in athārū refers to what the pronoun in kānū ashadd was referring to.

The meaning of cultivating the earth ('imarat al-ard) is making it populated and not empty, through building, planting, and sowing.

[p. 59]

It is said: "a flourishing estate" (ḍay'ah 'āmirah), meaning one filled with what estates are filled with. The opposite is said: "a neglected estate" (ḍay'ah ghāmirah). Because the Quraysh did not have stirring of the earth in either sense, since they lived in a valley without cultivation, the phrase "more than they have stirred it" was not said regarding this aspect.

The two masculine plural pronouns in His words ﴿and cultivated it more than these have cultivated it﴾ refer, the first to what the pronoun in athārū referred to, and the second to what the pronoun in ﴿travelled through the earth﴾ referred to.

The distribution of the two pronouns is known from context, like the distribution of the demonstratives in His words ﴿This is of his faction and this is of his enemy﴾ [Al-Qasas: 15] in Surah Al-Qasas, and like the two pronouns in the words of 'Abbas ibn Mirdas, recounting the fighting of Hawazin on the day of Hunayn:

We returned, and had we not, their host would have encircled the Muslims and seized what they had gathered.

Its detailed explanation has already occurred at His words ﴿So let them rejoice in that; it is better than what they accumulate﴾ [Yunus: 58] in Surah Yunus. The meaning is: those before them cultivated the earth more than these did. The Quraysh indeed had cultivation of the earth through a little planting, building, and digging of channels, but this is minuscule before the cultivation of the earlier nations such as 'Ad and Thamud.

The phrase ﴿So Allah would not wrong them﴾ is grammatically connected (tafri') to His words ﴿and their messengers came to them with clear proofs﴾. It is a wonderful brevity through ellipsis (ijaz hadhf), because the coming of messengers with clear proofs implies acceptance and denial. When He then states as a consequence that they wronged themselves, it is known that they denied the messengers and that Allah requited them for their denial of His messengers by punishing them. Had such punishment been for no offence, it would have resembled injustice. So from the combination of the negation of Allah's wronging them and the affirmation of their wronging themselves, one knows that they denied the messengers, opposed them, and that there befell them what is known from seeing their dwellings and hearing reports about them.

The istidrak (corrective contrast) arises from what the negation of Allah wronging them requires: that they were treated with a harsh treatment which, had they not deserved it, would have been treatment of injustice.

The wronging of themselves is expressed in the present tense to indicate the continuation and repetition of their wronging, and that Allah gave them respite, so they did not desist until He seized them with what that outcome indicates. The indication is His words (kānū), that is, "they were".

[p. 59 continued]

The placement of (anfusahum), which is the object of (yazlimūn), before its verb is for emphasis on themselves, in that they imposed their wrongdoing upon themselves, since it is a wrong that is a cause for wonder. There is also, in this placement, consideration of the fasilah (verse-final rhyme). The placement of the object here is not for restriction (hasr), because the restriction is already achieved from the two clauses of negation and affirmation.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 30, verse 10:

﴿Then the end of those who did evil, the worst of ends, was that they denied the signs of Allah and used to mock them.﴾ (10)

"Thumma" (then) here indicates a graded sequence (al-tarakhi al-rutbi), because this end is greater in rank of evil than the punishment of this world. Accordingly, this statement may be a conclusion (tadhyil) to the account of what befell the earlier nations, from His saying ﴿How was the end of those before them?﴾ [al-Rum: 9].

The meaning is: then the end of everyone who did the worst evil is like theirs. This is an allusive warning (ta'rid bi'l-tahdid) directed at the polytheists of the Arabs, like His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Allah has destroyed them, and there are similar fates for the disbelievers﴾ [Muhammad: 10]. So what is meant by ﴿those who did evil﴾ is every evildoer of the kind of that evil, which is shirk.

It is also possible that it is a warning to the polytheists of the Arabs spoken of in His saying ﴿but most people do not know﴾ [al-Rum: 6], so that they are the ones meant by ﴿those who did evil﴾. Here the explicit noun stands in place of the pronoun, contrary to what the context would require, for the purpose of indicating the causal link through the relative clause; that is, the cause of their worst end is their evil-doing. The underlying wording is: then their end was the worst.

This is a warning after an admonition and an explicit statement after an analogy, for Allah admonished those who denied the Messenger ﷺ with the ends of the nations that denied their messengers, so that they would be wary of a similar end by way of analogical reasoning (qiyas al-tamthil). Then He followed that admonition with a warning that a similar end would be theirs. He placed the past verb "kana" in the position of the present, to alert to the certainty of its occurrence, like ﴿The command of Allah has come﴾ [al-Nahl: 1], completing the warning.

Al-'aqibah (the end) is the final state that follows a state before it. It has occurred earlier in His saying ﴿Then look how was the end of the deniers﴾ [al-An'am: 11] in Surat al-An'am, and in His saying ﴿and the good end is for the righteous﴾ [Taha: 132] in Surat Taha.

Page 60
﴿Those who did evil﴾ are the disbelievers of Quraysh. What is meant by ﴿the signs of Allah﴾ is the Qur'an and the miracles of the Messenger ﷺ.

Al-su'a (the worst) is the feminine of al-asw' (the worst), meaning the state that is excessive in being characterized by evil, and it is the greatest of evil, just as al-husna (the best) is the feminine of al-ahsan (the best) in His saying ﴿For those who did good is the best﴾ [Yunus: 26].

The definiteness of al-su'a is the definiteness of the genus, since there is no particular known end here.

It may be that ﴿those who did evil﴾ refers to the nations who stirred up the earth and cultivated it, so that it is an explicit noun in place of a pronoun, in order to make a judgment against them that they did evil and deserved the worst, which is Hell.

The verb "kana," in what it has of alerting to the certainty of occurrence, stands as it is.

Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Abu Ja'far and Ya'qub read ('aqibatu) in the nominative, following the original order between the subject and predicate of "kana." The rest read it in the accusative, taking it as the predicate of "kana" placed before its subject, which is a common usage.

The separation between "kana" and its nominative by the predicate justified dropping the feminine ta' from the verb "kana."

﴿An kadhdhabu﴾ is an explanation for why their end was the worst, with the lam omitted before "an." The signs of Allah are the Qur'an and the miracles.

The ba' in ﴿bi-ha yastahzi'un﴾ is for transitivity, and fronting the prepositional phrase serves to emphasize the matter of the signs and to accommodate the rhyme (fasila).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 30, verse 11:

﴿Allah originates creation, then repeats it; then to Him you will be returned.﴾ This is a fresh, independent resumption (isti'naf ibtida'i), and it marks the beginning of what this surah is built upon: spelling out the proofs that Allah alone holds sway over people, by bringing them into existence and bringing their existence to an end, by providing for them and by the various stages of their lives. The aim is to nullify the idea that their associates have any share in such control. These are clear proofs of the Oneness (wahdaniyya) that they were blind to.

Since the opening of the surah was revealed on the occasion of the idolaters rejoicing at the victory of the Persians over the Romans, Allah cut short their boasting over the Muslims by informing them that the final outcome of victory belongs to the Romans over the Persians, a lasting victory. Because the source of dispute between the idolaters and the believers was each party's inclination toward those closer to them in religion, that event became an occasion for extended argumentation in this surah to refute the religion of polytheism.

These proofs are set out in four resumptions of similar style, each beginning with the Name of Majesty (ism al-jalala), followed by predications about realities that they cannot possibly deny, for they can only either acknowledge some of them or be unable to overturn their evidence. The first resumption begins with the words ﴿Allah originates creation, then repeats it﴾; the second with ﴿Allah is the One who created you, then provided for you﴾ [al-Rum: 40]; the third with ﴿Allah is the One who sends the winds﴾ [al-Rum: 48]; and the fourth with ﴿Allah is the One who created you from weakness﴾ [al-Rum: 54].

As for His words ﴿Allah originates creation, then repeats it﴾, this is an argument from something they cannot but acknowledge, namely the origination of creation, since they do not dispute that Allah alone is the Creator of creation. For this reason Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Or have they set up for Allah partners who created as He created, so that the creation seemed alike to them?﴾ [al-Ra'd: 16], and so on.

As for His words ﴿then repeats it﴾, this is an interpolation (idmaj), for once the origination of creation is granted to Him, granting Him its repetition is all the more fitting and appropriate. What makes the placement of this resumption fitting is that it follows the mention of past nations and present nations, some of which succeeded others. Since this is an example of the return of individuals after their annihilation, and since the outcome of those who denied the messengers in this world was mentioned, it was appropriate, in the context of drawing a lesson, to present to them the argument for the possibility of resurrection, so that the mention of the recompense that follows it would fall in a position of persuading them.

The placement of the Name of Allah before the verbal predicate is merely for emphasis (lil-taqawwi). Here "thumma" (then) indicates a gradation in rank (al-taraakhi al-rutbi), as is its usage in conjoining sentences, because returning to Allah is greater in importance than the repetition of creation, since it is the purpose both of repetition and of the origination of creation.

Accordingly, the address in (turja'un) ("you will be returned") is to the idolaters, by way of the shift (iltifat) from the third person to the second person.

Page 62

The majority (al-Jumhur) read (turja'un) with the ta' of address. Abu 'Amr, Abu Bakr from 'Asim, and Rawh from Ya'qub read it with the ya' of the third person, in keeping with the preceding verb.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 30, verses 12–13:

﴿On the Day the Hour comes to pass, the guilty will be dumbfounded.﴾ ﴿And they will have no intercessors among their associates, and they will disavow their associates.﴾

This is a conjunction (ʿaṭf) with the clause ﴿Then to Him you will be returned﴾ [al-Rum: 11], serving to clarify the state of the polytheists at the time of that return, as if it were said: "Then to Him you will be returned, and on that day the guilty will be dumbfounded." It also has a further connection with the clause ﴿Then the end of those who did evil will be the worst [outcome]﴾ [al-Rum: 10]. The apparent form would have been to say "and on that day the guilty will be dumbfounded," or "and on that day you will be dumbfounded," meaning "and on the day you are returned to Him, the guilty will be dumbfounded." Instead, he departed from the implied clause that the noun "day" (yawm) is attached to, which is indicated by ﴿to Him you will be returned﴾ [al-Rum: 11], by mentioning another clause that has the same meaning, in order to make the return clearer: that it is the return of people to Him on the day the Hour comes to pass. This is therefore an elaboration (iṭnab) for the sake of clarification and an increase in the awe that is implied by attributing the standing (qiyam) to the Hour, with its suddenness and terror. This intent is supported by the repetition of this temporal expression in the verse after it, with this same elaboration.

The term "the Hour" (al-sāʿa) has become common usage for the time of the gathering (ḥashr) and reckoning (ḥisāb). Its original meaning is a measure of time, and it is specified by an annexation or by definiteness.

Iblās (al-iblās) is stillness accompanied by bewilderment. It is said: "ablasa," when a person does not find a way out of a hardship he is in. It was previously discussed at His saying, exalted is He, ﴿then they will be dumbfounded therein﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 77], in Surat al-Mu'minun.

The guilty (al-mujrimun) are the polytheists, and they are the ones to whom the pronouns of the third person and the pronouns of the second person were applied, by the indication of His saying ﴿and they will have no intercessors among their associates﴾.

The use of the noun in place of the pronoun is to attach the attribute of criminality (ijram) to them. The apparent form would have been to say "you will be dumbfounded," in the second person, or with the third-person ya'. They are described with criminality to belittle the religion of polytheism and to show that it contains a great crime.

One of the causes of dumbfounding, and the greatest of them at that time, has been mentioned, namely that they will not find intercessors from

their gods whom they associated with Him, and whom they used to think were intercessors with God. So when they look and turn their gaze around and find no intercessors, they will be disappointed, despairing and dumbfounded. They have other causes of disappointment which the purpose of the passage does not concern itself with mentioning. As for the punishment that befalls them, that is a state of despair, not a state of dumbfounding.

"Min" (in ﴿min shurakā'ihim﴾) is partitive (tab'iḍiyya), and the speech is not of the category of tajrīd (abstraction/detachment).

The negation of the verb "yakun" with "lam," which converts the present tense into the past, indicates the certain occurrence of this negation, similar to His saying ﴿The command of God has come﴾ [al-Nahl: 1].

The matching of the plural pronoun with the plural form "shurakā'" is of the category of distribution (tawzī'), meaning that none of the guilty will have a single intercessor, let alone a number of intercessors.

Likewise His saying ﴿and they used to disavow their associates﴾, because the intended meaning is that they will disavow them on the Day the Hour comes to pass, like His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Then on the Day of Resurrection, some of you will disown others and curse one another﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 25].

In the Mushaf it is written (shufa'u') with a wāw after the ʿayn and an alif after the wāw. By combining the wāw and the alif, they intended to draw attention to the fact that the hamza is pronounced with a ḍamma, so that it is known that shufaʿāʾ is the subject of kāna, and that its subject is not the phrase ﴿min shurakā'ihim﴾, through a supposition that "min" is a noun meaning "some," or that it is extra in the negation. They therefore kept the wāw to make the ḍamma of the hamza explicit, and kept the alif because the alif is the written form of the hamza.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 30, verses 12–13:

﴿On the Day the Hour comes to pass, the guilty will be dumbfounded.﴾ ﴿And they will have no intercessors among their associates, and they will disavow their associates.﴾

This is a conjunction (ʿaṭf) with the clause ﴿Then to Him you will be returned﴾ [al-Rum: 11], serving to clarify the state of the polytheists at the time of that return, as if it were said: "Then to Him you will be returned, and on that day the guilty will be dumbfounded." It also has a further connection with the clause ﴿Then the end of those who did evil will be the worst [outcome]﴾ [al-Rum: 10]. Iblās (al-iblās) is stillness accompanied by bewilderment. It is said: "ablasa," when a person does not find a way out of a hardship he is in. It was previously discussed at His saying, exalted is He, ﴿then they will be dumbfounded therein﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 77], in Surat al-Mu'minun.

The guilty (al-mujrimun) are the polytheists, and they are the ones to whom the pronouns of the third person and the pronouns of the second person were applied, by the indication of His saying ﴿and they will have no intercessors among their associates﴾.

The apparent form would have been to say "you will be dumbfounded," in the second person, or with the third-person ya'. They are described with criminality to belittle the religion of polytheism and to show that it contains a great crime.

One of the causes of dumbfounding, and the greatest of them at that time, has been mentioned, namely that they will not find intercessors from

their gods whom they associated with Him, and whom they used to think were intercessors with God. So when they look and turn their gaze around and find no intercessors, they will be disappointed, despairing and dumbfounded. They have other causes of disappointment which the purpose of the passage does not concern itself with mentioning. As for the punishment that befalls them, that is a state of despair, not a state of dumbfounding.

"Min" (in ﴿min shurakā'ihim﴾) is partitive (tab'iḍiyya), and the speech is not of the category of tajrīd (abstraction/detachment).

The negation of the verb "yakun" with "lam," which converts the present tense into the past, indicates the certain occurrence of this negation, similar to His saying ﴿The command of God has come﴾ [al-Nahl: 1].

The matching of the plural pronoun with the plural form "shurakā'" is of the category of distribution (tawzī'), meaning that none of the guilty will have a single intercessor, let alone a number of intercessors.

Likewise His saying ﴿and they used to disavow their associates﴾, because the intended meaning is that they will disavow them on the Day the Hour comes to pass, like His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Then on the Day of Resurrection, some of you will disown others and curse one another﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 25].

In the Mushaf it is written (shufa'u') with a wāw after the ʿayn and an alif after the wāw. By combining the wāw and the alif, they intended to draw attention to the fact that the hamza is pronounced with a ḍamma, so that it is known that shufaʿāʾ is the subject of kāna, and that its subject is not the phrase ﴿min shurakā'ihim﴾, through a supposition that "min" is a noun meaning "some," or that it is extra in the negation. Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 30, verses 14–16:

﴿On the Day the Hour is established, that Day they will be divided.﴾ ﴿As for those who believed and did righteous deeds, they will be in a meadow, made joyful.﴾ ﴿And as for those who disbelieved and denied Our signs and the meeting of the Hereafter, those will be in punishment, brought forth.﴾

The phrase ﴿On the Day the Hour is established﴾ is repeated to increase the awe of the matter whose explanation has just preceded. He repeated "that Day" (yawma'idhin) to emphasize the reality of its being a time-frame.

Since the despair (iblas) of the polytheists was mentioned, which suggests their expectation of evil and punishment, He followed it with a detailed account of the states of people on that Day, along with a statement of the outcome of the despair of the disbelieving group.

The pronoun in (﴿they will be divided﴾) refers to something known from the context, indicated by the mention of the criminals, so it is understood that another group is their opposite, because the mention of the criminals' despair on that Day implies that others are not like that, in general terms.

Tafarruq (division): the splitting of a gathering and the scattering of the parts of a whole. It is used here as a metaphor (kinaya) for separation, because separation is customarily accompanied by distance.

The division is specified here by His saying ﴿As for those who believed and did righteous deeds﴾ to the end of the verse.

Rawda (meadow): any land with trees, water and flowers, whether in the desert or in gardens. Among the proverbs of the Arabs is "more beautiful than an egg in a meadow," meaning the egg of an ostrich.

The beauties of the meadow are gathered in the words of al-A'sha:

"Is there a meadow among the gardens of al-Hazn, lush and green, upon which a pouring, heavy rain has fallen,
Laughing at the sun with a shining star, wrapped in dense vegetation, bright-faced."

Yuhbarun (they will be made joyful): they will be gladdened, from al-hubur, which is intense joy. It is said: habbarahu, when he made him happy with a happiness that brightened his face and its effect appeared in it.

Muhdarun may be from ihdar, meaning making something present, i.e., they will not be absent from it, i.e., they will not leave it. This conveys confirmation by way of metaphor (kinaya), because when it is mentioned after His saying ﴿in punishment﴾, it is fitting that the purpose of describing them as "brought forth" not be merely that they are in punishment, lest it become mere emphasis on a meaning already contained in "in punishment," since establishing a new meaning is more effective than emphasis. It may also be that muhdarun means "brought to the punishment," as the usage of muhdar and similar words in the Qur'an is common in the sense of "punished." He, exalted is He, says: ﴿And the jinn have certainly known that they will be brought forth﴾ [al-Saffat: 158]. The demonstrative (ism al-isharah) is a notice that they are deserving of that punishment because of what was mentioned before the demonstrative, as in His saying ﴿Those are upon guidance from their Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah: 5].

In the orthographic script of the Mushaf, (wa-liqa'i) was written with a hamza on a ya', to indicate that the hamza is kasra (vowelled with i), and this is from the tawfiqi script (script fixed by transmission), whereas the analogical expectation would be that the hamza be written on the line after the alif.

﴿So glory be to God when you enter the evening and when you enter the morning﴾ ﴿And to Him belongs all praise in the heavens and the earth, and in the late afternoon and when you enter midday﴾

The *fa'* (the particle *fa*) requires that what follows be connected to what precedes it. It is either a *fa' fasiha* (an eloquent *fa'* that signals an implied condition), or a *fa' of ta'frif* (a *fa'* of consequence) following what came before. The beginning of the discourse was His saying: ﴿Do they not reflect within themselves? God did not create the heavens and the earth and what is between them except with truth﴾ [al-Rum: 8]. The pronoun refers to the majority of people in His saying: ﴿But most people do not know﴾ [al-Rum: 6], and by them are meant the disbelievers. Thus the *tafri'* (consequential connection) or the *if-sah* (clarification) arises from this. The intended meaning of "glory be to God" (*subhan Allah*) is therefore the creation of an act of declaring God exalted above what they attributed to Him of incapacity to bring people back to life after their death, and the creation of an act of praise of Him.

The address in "﴿you enter [the evening]﴾" and "﴿you enter [the morning]﴾" follows the address before it, in His saying: ﴿Then to Him you will be returned﴾ [al-Rum: 11]. It is directed to the polytheists by way of *iltifat* (the shift from third-person pronouns, beginning from His saying: ﴿Do they not reflect within themselves﴾ [al-Rum: 8], through to its end), as you have just learned. This is the most suitable reading in light of the use of the verbal noun *subhan* in its usual contexts in speech and in the Qur'an, such as His saying: ﴿Glory be to Him, exalted above what they associate﴾ [Yunus: 18]. It is the predominant usage of the verbal noun *subhan* in speech, if it is not the only correct one, as the sayings of the linguistic authorities imply. This differs from the usage in His saying: ﴿And glorify your Lord with His praise when you arise﴾ [al-Tur: 48], and in the line of al-A'sha in his *dal*-rhymed ode:

*And glorify [Him] at the times of evenings and mornings*

His saying "﴿when you enter the evening and when you enter the morning﴾" and "﴿and in the late afternoon and when you enter midday﴾" are adverbial phrases (*zuruf*) related to the sense of the verb contained in the act of declaring Him exalted. That is, the declaration of God's exaltation is created at these times, which are the divisions into which time is subdivided. The intended meaning is perpetuity, as when you say: "Glory be to God always." He expressed it in a lengthy manner (*itnab*) because this suits the context of praise.

Some exegetes allowed that *subhan* here is a verbal noun standing in place of an imperative verb of glorification, as if it were said: "So glorify God with glorification." On this reading falls what is narrated that Nafi' ibn al-Azraq asked Ibn 'Abbas: "Do you find the five prayers in the Qur'an?" He said: "Yes," and he recited His saying: ﴿So glory be to God when you enter the evening and when you enter the morning﴾ up to His saying ﴿and when you enter midday﴾.

[p. 66]

If what is narrated from him is sound, its interpretation is that *subhan* is a command that they should say "Glory be to God." This is a metonymy (*kinaya*) for prayer, because prayer includes the saying: "Glory be to my Lord, the Most High, and praise be to Him."

His saying "﴿when you enter the evening﴾" and to its end is an allusion to the times of the prayers, and this requires that the address be directed to the believers. The connection with what preceded is that when He promised them a good outcome, He taught them to give thanks for God's blessing by performing the prayer at the divisions of the day and night.

This consequential connection indicates that the glorification and praise that occur are the creation of praise of God, as a metonymy for thanks for the blessing. This is because undertaking the creation of praise right after the granting of a blessing, or after a promise of it, shows that the one praising was moved to praise in that situation only by the intention of repaying the blessing with what is within his capacity, as it has been reported: "If you cannot repay him, then pray for him."

The five prayers and their times are not the intended meaning of the verse, but it is woven in a fabric suitable for encompassing the five prayers and their times. This is one of the aspects of the *i'jaz* (inimitability) of the Qur'an, because although prayer contains glorification and is called *subha* (a string of glorification beads), it is not called "*subhan Allah*."

The noun *hin* (time) is annexed to the two clauses "﴿you enter [the evening]﴾" and "﴿you enter [the morning]﴾."

The verb of entering the evening was placed before the verb of entering the morning, either because the Arabic usage regards the nights as the starting point of the counting of days, as in His saying: ﴿Travel through them by night and by day, safe﴾ [Saba': 18], or because when the discourse came right after the mention of resurrection in His saying: ﴿God begins creation, then repeats it, then to Him you will be returned﴾ [al-Rum: 11], and mention of the Hour suited that the entering of the evening, which is the end of the day, be present in the mind, so its mention was placed first.

"*Ashiyyan*" (in the late afternoon) is coordinated (*'atf*) with "﴿when you enter the evening﴾."

His saying "﴿And to Him belongs all praise in the heavens and the earth﴾" is a parenthetical clause (*jumla mu'taridah*) placed between the adverbial phrases. It indicates that the glorification of God by the believers is not for God's benefit but for the benefit of those who glorify Him, because God is praised in the heavens and the earth, so He is independent of our praise.

The fronting of the prepositional phrase in "﴿And to Him belongs all praise﴾" serves to convey a restriction of ascription (*qasr idda'i*) of the genus of praise to God, Exalted, because His praise is the complete praise, in the manner of their saying: "So-and-so is the brave one," as has been discussed previously at the opening of Surat al-Fatihah. You may also take the fronting as being for emphasis on the divine name (*damir al-jalala*).

*Al-imsa'*: the arrival of evening. *Al-isbah*: the arrival of morning. This was discussed under His saying: ﴿Splitter of the dawn﴾ [al-An'am: 96] in Surat al-An'am. *Al-imsa'* is the approach of sunset until the night prayer (*'isha'*). *Al-sabah* is the beginning of the day, and *al-izhar* is the arrival of the time of midday prayer (*zuhr*), which is the middle of the day.

The verb form *if'al*, whose initial hamza signifies entering a place, has been used, as in *anjada* (he entered Najd), *atha-ma* (he entered sin), *ayman* (he went right) and *ash'ama* (he went left), for the arrival of times of evening, morning and midday, by analogy of that arrival to being in a place. So it is common to say *asbaha*, *adhha*, *amsa*, *a'tama* and *ashraqa*. He, Exalted, said: ﴿So they pursued them at sunrise﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 60].

*Al-'ashiyy* is what comes after the afternoon prayer (*'asr*). It was discussed previously at His saying: ﴿And do not drive away those who call upon their Lord in the morning and the evening﴾ [al-An'am: 52] in Surat al-An'am.
