Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 30, verse 19:

﴿He brings the living out of the dead, and He brings the dead out of the living, and He revives the earth after its death. And thus you will be brought out.﴾ This sentence is a substitute (badal) for the sentence ﴿Allah originates creation, then repeats it﴾ [al-Rum: 11]. It is also permissible that it be the cause (ʿillah) for the sentence ﴿So glory be to Allah when you enter the evening and when you enter the morning﴾ and what is conjoined to it, meaning: He deserves to be glorified and praised because of His disposal of creatures through wondrous origination and through reviving after death. From among His great acts, the act of giving life and causing death in animals and plants was chosen, because it is a means of reaching the intended purpose, which is establishing the resurrection, in response to the speech about what preceded it in His saying ﴿Allah originates creation, then repeats it, then to Him you will be returned﴾ [al-Rum: 11].

From this it is concluded that the command to glorify Him and praise Him is caused by two matters: fulfilling the due of His gratitude, indicated by the particle of consequence (fa' al-tafriʿ) in His saying (﴿So glory be to Allah﴾ [al-Rum: 17]), and fulfilling the due of exalting and magnifying Him. The intended matter is the bringing of the living out of the dead. As for the conjunction of ﴿and He brings the dead out of the living﴾, it is for guarding against restricting His power to some of its acts, and for showing the wondrous nature of His power, that it produces opposites.

In the verse there is tibaq (antithesis). This address to the believers is an indirect rebuttal of the polytheists.

Al-ikhraj (bringing out) is the separation of a thing contained from its container. One says: he brought it out of the house, and he brought his hand out of his pocket; here it is used to mean the creation of a thing from another thing.

The use of the present tense in yukhriju and yuhyi is to bring the wondrous state to mind, like His saying ﴿Allah is He who sends the winds﴾ [al-Rum: 48]. This bringing out and reviving is a great sign of His deserving magnification and of being singled out for worship, since He deposited this wondrous system in existent things, making in what has no life a power and properties that cause it to produce living, enduring, acting things, and placing in the earth's dust powers that bring forth crops and plants, living and growing.

The bringing of the living out of the dead appears in many conditions, among them: the formation of embryos from drops of fluid, and the formation of chicks from eggs. The bringing of the dead out of the living appears in the reverse, and it has been discussed in Surat Al 'Imran. In the verse there is an allusion that Allah brings out of extreme polytheists righteous believers, like the bringing out of Khalid ibn al-Walid from his father al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, and the bringing out of Hind bint 'Utba ibn Rabi'a from her father, one of the leaders of disbelief. She said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "No household of a tent was more beloved to me that they be humbled than the people of your tent; and today no household of a tent is more beloved to me that they be honored than the people of your tent." The Prophet (ﷺ) said to her: "And also," meaning: you will increase in love for us because of the light of Islam. And the bringing out of Umm Kulthum bint 'Uqba ibn Abi Mu'ayt from her father. "When Umm Kulthum bint 'Uqba spoke to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) concerning her conversion to Islam and her emigration to Medina, when her two brothers came seeking to return her to Mecca according to the terms of the truce, she said: O Messenger of Allah, I am a woman, and women's condition is weakness, so I fear they will tempt me in my religion, and I have no patience. The Prophet (ﷺ) recited ﴿He brings the living out of the dead﴾," and the verse of the test was revealed, so the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) did not return her to them, and she was the first of the women who emigrated to Medina after the Treaty of Hudaybiyya.

The comparison in His saying (﴿And thus you will be brought out﴾) refers to what is suitable for it among what was mentioned before it, which is what involves the creation of life for a thing after its death, based on what we have already stated, that His saying ﴿and He brings the dead out of the living﴾ is not intended as a proof but is a guard and a completion. It is also permissible that the comparison refers to the nearest thing mentioned, which is the reviving of the earth after its death, meaning: just as the plant is brought out of the earth after its death within it, so your bringing out from the earth will occur after you were dead within it, as He, exalted is He, said ﴿And Allah has caused you to grow from the earth as plants, then He returns you into it and brings you out a bringing out﴾ [Nuh: 17]. There is no basis for restricting the comparison to the second without the first.

The meaning: origination and repetition are equal, so resurrection after death is no more wondrous than the beginning of creation, but the polytheists made habit the judge in a place where reason should judge.

Nafi', Hafs and Hamza read (al-mayyit) with a doubled yaʾ (shaddah). The rest read it with a single yaʾ. The majority read (tukhrajun) with a dammah on the upper tāʾ. Hamza and al-Kisa'i read it with a fatḥah on it.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 30, verse 20:

﴿And among His signs is that He created you from dust; then, behold, you are human beings dispersing (across the earth).﴾ When the argument for the Resurrection contained signs of His sole power of disposal (tafarrud bi-l-tasarruf) and of His indication of Oneness (wahdaniyyah), he moved from that argument to signs of that great disposal, other than what contains the affirmation of the Resurrection, both to firm up the believers and to leave as an excuse (i'dhar) for those who associated others with Him in divinity. Six verses concerning Oneness have already preceded, and they began with the phrase "And among His signs" (wa-min ayatihi), to draw attention to the unity of their purpose. So this is the first verse, and it bears a resemblance to the argument for the Resurrection, because the creation of humankind from dust, and the instilling of life and dispersal among them, is a kind of bringing forth of the living from the dead. Therefore it came first in mention, for its suitability to what preceded it, and it was made a transition (takhallus) from the proofs of the Resurrection to the proofs of the magnitude of power. This verse concerns the creation of the essence of the human being and the shaping of his humanity.

It has already been explained how the creation from dust took place, at His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿And We created man from an extract of clay; then We made him a drop (of semen) in a firm place﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 12], in Surat al-Mu'minun.

The pronoun of object in "khalaqakum" refers to all people, and this is in the sense of His saying, Exalted is He, in Surat al-Hajj, ﴿Indeed, We created you from dust, then from a sperm-drop, then from a clinging clot﴾ [al-Hajj: 5], and so on.

This is an argument addressed to people through themselves, because they are more aware of themselves than of anything else. People know that the sperm-drops are the origin of creation, and if they reflect, they know that the sperm-drop is formed from nourishment, that nourishment is formed from the plants of the earth, and that the plants of the earth consist of earthen components which brought them forth.

Page 70
Thus they knew that they were created from dust, and by this it is correct to make the formation from dust a sign (ayah) for people, that is, a token of great power, despite its being a hidden matter.

Moreover, the argument may be built upon what is common among humankind, that the origin of the human being is dust, as all the religions have reported.

By this interpretation it is also valid that the meaning of "khalaqakum min turab" is that He created your origin, who is Adam; but the first of the aspects is the most apparent.

Dust is dead, with no life in it, and its nature is contrary to the nature of life, because dust is cold and dry, and that is the nature of death, while life requires heat and moisture. So from that cold dry thing there arises a living, perceiving creature. Life and perception are indicated by His saying, ﴿then, behold, you are human beings﴾, and movement and activity by His saying, "dispersing". Since the completion of humanity arises from the development of dust into plant, then into sperm-drop, then into the stages of formation over successive times, the sentence was conjoined with the particle of delay (thumma), which indicates the lapse of time together with the lapse of rank, which is the basic use of conjoining sentences with thumma.

The sentence was introduced with the particle of surprise (idha al-fuja'iyyah) because becoming human appears to people suddenly, with the placing of embryos or the emergence of chicks from eggs, while the stages between these, which the particle of delay requires, are hidden developments that are not witnessed. So the combination of the particle of delay and the particle of surprise was a reminder of that wondrous development. From the contrast between the particle of delay and the particle of surprise arose a kind of antithesis (shibh al-tibaq), though the referent of each of the two particles differs from the other's.

And "al-intishar" means appearing upon the earth and spreading apart among people in their affairs; He, Exalted is He, said, ﴿then disperse in the earth﴾.

[Page 71]

This is a second verse containing admonition and reminder about the general order of human beings, namely the system of pairing (al-izdiwaj) and the existence of the family and the foundation of procreation. It is a wondrous system that God has fixed in human nature (al-jibilla), and none deviates from it except aberrant individuals (al-shudhdhadh).

The verse contains several signs (ayat). Among them: God has made for humanity a law of procreation (namus al-tanasul, the natural law or system of reproduction); He made human reproduction occur through pairing, and did not make it like the reproduction of plants from themselves; He made the spouses of humans of their own kind and did not make them of another kind, because companionship (al-ta'annus) does not occur with a different kind; He placed in that pairing intimacy (uns) between the two spouses and did not make it a violent or destructive pairing like the mating of frogs; He placed between every two spouses affection (mawadda) and love (mahabba), so that the two who were mutually indifferent before marriage become loving after it; and He placed between them mercy (rahma), so that they, who had no tender feeling between them before marriage, become merciful toward one another after it, like the mercy of fatherhood and motherhood. Because of the greatness of what this proof contains and what follows it of blessings and proofs, He made this verse many signs in His words, ﴿Indeed in that are signs for a people who reflect﴾.

This verse concerns the creation of the essence of both kinds of human beings: the male kind and the female kind, and the deposit within their natures of the system of mutual attraction between them. This is among the relative essential attributes (al-dhatiyyat al-nisbiyya) between the two kinds.

In this verse there is also an implicit reminder of a blessing, indicated by His saying (for you) (lakum), meaning for your benefit.

The phrase ﴿for a people who reflect﴾ is connected to (signs) because of the meaning of indication (al-dalala) it contains. The signs were made for a people who reflect because reflection and contemplation upon those proofs is what clarifies their reality and increases the contemplator's insight into other benefits within them.

Those who reflect are the believers and the people of judgment among the polytheists who came to believe after the revelation of this verse.

The address in His words ﴿that He created for you﴾ is to the whole human species, males and females. The word zawj (spouse) is that by which one becomes a second for another; it is applied to a man's wife and a woman's husband. God has thus made for each individual a spouse.

The meaning of ﴿from yourselves﴾ is "from your own kind," so all spouses are of the human kind. As for the verse of Ta'abbata Sharran:

*And I married in my youth a ghoul, with a gazelle as her bride-price, and my dowry a wineskin of wine*

it is among their fabrications, and likewise what the sorcerers claim about marrying jinn women, and what the people of superstitions and tales claim about the existence of daughters in the sea and that some humans marry some of them.

Al-sukun (rest, tranquility) here is used figuratively for companionship and joy of the soul, because in that there is the removal of the agitation of loneliness and sorrow. The sukun which is the removal of bodily agitation is as they said: "he found peace in such-and-such" (ita'anna ila kadha) and "he was devoted to such-and-such" (inqata'a ila kadha).

The verb (li-taskunu) includes the meaning of "so that you may incline," so it is construed with the preposition (ila, to), although its proper construction would be with (inda, at) and similar adverbial expressions.

Al-mawadda is love (al-mahabba). Al-rahma is a quality that inspires good treatment.

God made this in many signs only in view of the fact that this creation includes many subtle details, some of which arise from others, which reflection and contemplation bring to light, so that many signs gather from them.

The lam in His words ﴿for a people who reflect﴾ has a meaning resembling possession (shibh al-tamlik), a meaning which the author of Mughni al-Labib established. It appears to be an intermediate between the meaning of possession and the meaning of causation. In the Mughni he exemplified it with His words, Exalted is He, ﴿He made for you from yourselves spouses﴾ [al-Nahl: 72]. Among the twentieth of the meanings of lam mentioned, Ibn Malik in his Kafiyya named it lam al-ta'diya (the lam of transitivity), and perhaps he means a specific transitivity, exemplified by His words, Exalted is He, ﴿so grant me from Yourself an heir﴾ [Maryam: 5].

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 30, verse 22:

﴿And among His signs is the creation of the heavens and the earth, and the diversity of your tongues and colours. Indeed in that are signs for those who know.﴾ This is the third verse, and it is the verse of the earthly order in the creation of the earth together with its inhabitants. The creation of the heavens and the earth is a great sign, witnessed in what they contain of the variations of celestial and terrestrial bodies, and in their conditions, which are either concomitant and mutually linked, like night and day and the seasons, or contrary, like height and descent.

Since the most noble thing upon the earth is the human species, what is in some of its conditions of signs has been coupled with what is in the creation of the earth of signs, and what was singled out from its conditions were the differing ones, because they are more instructive, since in them there is difference between things that are united in quiddity; and because these differing conditions of this one species we find the causes of their difference to be among the effects of the creation of the heavens and the earth. The difference of tongues is caused by settling in different, distant homelands; the difference of colours is caused by the difference of the inhabited regions of the earth and the difference in the angles at which the rays of the sun strike them. These are therefore among the effects of the creation of the heavens and the earth.

For this reason, it is apparent that the intended meaning is the sign of the difference of languages and colours, and that what preceded it of the creation of the heavens and the earth is a preparation for it and an allusion to the fact that the causes of difference are folded within the secrets of the creation of the heavens and the earth.

This verse has been concerned with accidental conditions in the human being that are constant for him; by this constancy they resemble absolute and then relative essential conditions. Therefore this verse was mentioned after the two preceding verses, according to the previous order.

The aspect of comparison between the creation of the heavens and the earth and the difference of human tongues and colours has become clear. Earlier in Surat Al 'Imran, His saying appeared: ﴿Indeed in the creation of the heavens and the earth and the alternation of night and day are signs for people of understanding﴾ [Al 'Imran: 190].

Al-alsina (ألْسِنَةُ, "tongues"): the plural of lisan, which is used for language, as in His saying ﴿And We did not send any messenger except with the language of his people﴾ [Ibrahim: 4] and His saying ﴿The tongue of the one they point to is foreign﴾ [al-Nahl: 103].

The difference of human languages is a great sign, for despite their unity in species, the difference of their languages is a sign indicating what God placed in the nature of humans of difference in thinking and variation in the manner of forming languages, and the change of their modes through dialects, reduction, omission and addition, such that original unified roots turn into many languages.

There is no doubt that language was one for humankind when they were in one place, and languages only differed with the dispersal of human tribes into distant dwellings, and change entered their languages gradually. Moreover, the expansion of languages with the expansion of the need to express things for which there had been no need to express has necessitated difference in the assignment of names to them, so languages differed thereby in their substance, just as they differed in what was agreed upon between them through differences of pronunciation dialects and differences of usage. Thus the difference of tongues has two causes. The locus of the lesson is difference together with the unity of the root of the species, as in His saying ﴿Watered with one water, yet We make some of them excel others in fruit﴾ [al-Ra'd: 4], and because of the secrets that difference in that entails.

In the eleventh chapter of the Book of Genesis there occurs what outwardly gives the impression that the difference of tongues happened at once after the Flood in the land of Babel, and that humankind dispersed after that. Apparently there is an inversion of order in the expression, and that the dispersal occurred before the confusion of tongues. That chapter has also given a reason which God is too exalted to be described by its implication.

It has also been said: by the difference of tongues is meant the difference of voices, such that the voices of people speaking one language are distinguished, so that we recognise the owner of a voice even if he is not seen.

As for the difference of human colours, it is also a sign, because humankind descends from one origin, namely Adam, who had one colour without doubt, perhaps whiteness mixed with redness. When his progeny multiplied, the different colours came into their skins. That difference is caused by several causes, the most important of which are the differing lands in heat and cold; among them is begetting from two parents of different colour, like one born of a black mother and a white father; among them are illnesses and diseases that affect the skin with colouring; and among them is the difference of foods. For this reason the difference of human colours is not evidence of a difference of species; rather it is one species. Humans have many colours, whose roots are whiteness and blackness. Abu 'Ali ibn Sina (Avicenna) indicated this in his urjuza on medicine with his saying:

By scorching heat that changed the bodies, until it clothed their whiteness in blackness.

And the Slavs acquired whiteness, until their skins became tender and soft.

The original colour was whiteness, because it does not need a cause, and because dissection proved that the colours of the human flesh beneath the skin layer are of one colour. From whiteness and blackness the colours of the tribes of humankind branched out: from them came the yellow colour, the dark colour and the red colour. Among the scholars, (Cuvier) made the roots of human colours three: white, black and yellow, which is the colour of the people of China. Others added red, which is the colour of the native inhabitants of the continent of America, called the Indians of America. Know that from the totality of the difference of languages and the difference of colours, human stocks have been distinguished, and their mixed lineages have been united.

They have now divided human stocks into three original races: the Caucasian white race, the Mongolian yellow race, and the Ethiopian black race; and they subdivided them into eight: white, black, Ethiopian, red, yellow, Semitic, Indian, and Malay, named after the lands of (Malaya).

He made that signs in His saying ﴿Indeed in that are signs for the worlds﴾, because of what has been known of the details of its proofs and causes, that is, signs for all people. This is the counterpart of His saying just before, ﴿Indeed in that are signs for a people who reflect﴾ [al-Rum: 21].

The lam in His saying (lil-'alamin) is the counterpart of what preceded in the verse before it. He made that signs for the worlds because it is established and known to them, enabling them to perceive its signs merely by a glance of the mind without deep contemplation.

The majority read (lil-'alamin) with a fatha on the lam. Hafs read it with a kasra on the lam, meaning for those of knowledge.

﴿And among His signs is your sleep by night and by day, and your seeking of His bounty. Indeed in that are signs for a people who listen.﴾ This is the fourth sign, and it inheres in accidents (a'rad, sing. 'arad) of people that none of their members is free of. However, these are detached, non-permanent accidents. Therefore it falls below the accidents on which the third sign was founded, and for this reason this sign was mentioned after it.

The state of sleep is a wondrous condition among the states of humans and animals. God placed in the arrangement of the nerves of his brain a mechanism by which he recovers the strength of his nervous system after exhaustion has overtaken him from exerting his mind and body. So a kind of near-death overtakes him, which numbs his perception but does not suspend the movements of his principal organs. Rather, it slows them until a sufficient amount of time has passed for the recovery of his strength. Then he awakens from his sleep and his life returns to him in full. This was discussed previously at the words of the Exalted, ﴿Neither drowsiness nor sleep seizes Him﴾ [al-Baqarah: 255], in Surat al-Baqarah.

Al-manam (sleep) is a mimi (m-prefixed) verbal noun of "al-nawm" (sleeping), or it is a noun of verbal noun (ism masdar).

His saying ﴿by night and by day﴾ is connected to ﴿your sleep﴾. The bi' here is for time, meaning "in" (fi). So people sleep at night, and some of them sleep during the day at the midday rest (al-qa'ilah), especially those engaged in strenuous labor who rest from it at midday, particularly in hot lands or in the hot season.

Al-ibtigha' from God's bounty means seeking sustenance through work, because God's bounty is sustenance. This was made a metonymy (kinayah) for rising up to work, since seeking entails rising from sleep. That is another sign, because it is the revival of strength after it had weakened and failed. Because seeking sustenance is a characteristic of daytime, it is stated here without being restricted to "night and day." You may also take the omission of such a restriction, like the one applied to your sleep, as relying on the indication of the preceding restriction, with the implied meaning: "and your seeking of His bounty in both." The author of al-Kashshaf took great pains and made the speech an instance of laff wa nashr (a rhetorical device of "wrapping and unfolding," in which several items are mentioned and then each is matched to its corresponding referent). However, in it there is a separation within the wrapping. His annotator al-Qazwini justified it by saying that the fronting serves to draw attention to the sign of night and day.

The indications of sleep and of seeking God's bounty have been made "for a people who listen" for two reasons:

First: these two are states that alternate over people, which they have become accustomed to, so few reflect on what they indicate of God's exquisite craftsmanship. Most people need someone to make them aware of this indication and guide them to it.

Second: what people hear about the states of sleep contains a stronger indication of the greatness of God's craftsmanship than what the sleeper himself perceives of his own sleep states. This is because the sleeper knows of his sleep only the readiness for it, and that when he awakens from his sleep he knows he was sleeping. As for the condition of the sleeper during his sleep, the degree of his responsiveness to one who wakes him, his perception of the sounds that occur near him, and the lights that spread over his sight, which either rouse him or do not, all of this is received by the sleeper only through report from those who are awake at the time of his sleep. Thus the path to knowledge of the details of the conditions of sleepers and their variations is hearing. A person may witness the state of another's sleep, but the lesson of his own particular sleep is stronger. So the path of hearing is the most general of paths to knowing the details of the states of sleep, and for this reason it was said "for a people who listen."

Also, sleep prevents awareness of what is heard first and foremost, before it prevents awareness of what is seen.

The attribute "who listen" is applied to the people to indicate that hearing is firmly established among them, to the point that it is as if it were one of the constituents of their people-hood, as was discussed previously at His saying ﴿for a people who use reason﴾ [al-Baqarah: 164], in Surat al-Baqarah.

The reason for making that into signs is what it contains of multiple indications, through the multiplicity of those who draw inferences, and the generation of the subtleties of that sign from one another, as was mentioned just before.

The meaning of the lam in His saying ﴿for a people who listen﴾ is as was discussed previously regarding its meaning at His saying ﴿Indeed in that are signs for a people who reflect﴾ [al-Rum: 21].

**[Page 78]**

﴿And among His signs is that He shows you the lightning, as a fear and a hope, and sends down water from the sky, and with it gives life to the earth after its death. Indeed in that are signs for a people who use their reason.﴾ This is the fifth sign. It concerns human beings but is not connected to them in the same way. The lightning is one of the signs of Allah's making, for it is among the creations of the luminous electrical forces in the clouds, and of making their effects visible. How many forces like these are dispersed in the upper worlds whose effects are never seen.

Among the divine wisdoms in the lightning being visible is that it stirs in souls a fear that Allah has sent it as a punishment, and a hope that He has willed it as a good for people, so that they hope for the descent of rain. For this reason He followed it with His words ﴿and sends down water from the sky﴾, since the descent of rain is what comes to mind when the lightning is mentioned.

His words ﴿min ayatihi﴾ ("among His signs") are a prepositional phrase (jar wa-majrur) which requires a verb of existence to be supplied (taqdir kawn) if it is a stable adverbial complement (zarf mustaqarr), or some other complement if it is a non-stable adverbial complement (zarf laghw). The position of this prepositional phrase in this verse follows the positions of similar phrases in the preceding and following verses that resemble it. This calls for treating what comes after the prepositional phrase as meaning a subject (mubtada') described by the prepositional phrase placed before it, by analogy with its counterparts. The meaning is: "And among His signs is His showing you the lightning," and so on. For this reason the grammarians (a'immat al-nahw) said: here it is permitted to make the present-tense verb carry the meaning of a verbal noun (masdar) without the presence of "an" (that) or its implied presence; that is, without putting the present-tense verb in the subjunctive by means of an implied "an." They cited as examples the verse of 'Urwa ibn al-Ward:

*"They said: 'What do you wish?' I said: 'Amusement until morning is more preferable, O one of traces.'"*

and the verse of Tarafa:

*"Unquestionably, O you who rebuke me, do I attend the battle?"*

They also cited the verse of the Almighty, ﴿Say: Do you order me to worship other than Allah, O you ignorant ones?﴾ [al-Zumar: 64], with "a'budu" in the nominative (raf') in the well-known readings, and the saying in the proverb: "Hearing about the little man is better than seeing him," and the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Every day on which the sun rises, charity is due for establishing justice between two people, and helping a man with his mount, lifting him onto it or lifting his baggage onto it, is charity, and removing harm from the road is charity." It was narrated by al-Bukhari and Muslim from Abu Hurayra.

Among the elegant features of usage is that these verses vary in expressing the meanings of the verbal noun with the various forms in which it occurs in usage: sometimes with the explicit form of the verbal noun, as in His words ﴿And among His signs is the creation of the heavens and the earth﴾ [al-Rum: 22] and His words ﴿and your seeking of His bounty﴾ [al-Rum: 23]; sometimes with the verbal noun formed from "an" (that) the verbal-noun particle joined to a past-tense verb, ﴿that He created for you mates from among yourselves﴾ [al-Rum: 21], and joined to a present-tense verb, ﴿And among His signs is that the heaven and the earth stand by His command﴾ [al-Rum: 25]; sometimes with the noun of the verbal noun (ism al-masdar), ﴿And among His signs is your sleep by night and by day﴾ [al-Rum: 23]; and once with the bare verb which is interpreted as a verbal noun, ﴿And among His signs is that He shows you the lightning﴾.

**[Page 79]**

You may make the prepositional phrase dependent on "yurikum" ("He shows you"), with "min" functioning as the min of origin (ibtida'iyyah) in a position of circumstantial qualification (hal) of "al-barq" (the lightning). In that case the clause "yurikumu al-barq" ("He shows you the lightning") is conjoined to the clause "And among His signs is your sleep by night and by day" [al-Rum: 23], and so on. The change of style is because the focus of this verse is to make people acknowledge it, since it is not connected to their own selves. Their share of it is therefore nothing but witnessing it and affirming that it is a clear sign. This affirmation is like His words ﴿Allah is He who raised the heavens without pillars that you can see﴾ [al-Ra'd: 2]. This also makes it possible for ﴿and sends down water from the sky﴾ to be conjoined to it, since it completes this verse.

His words ﴿khawfan wa-tama'an﴾ ("as a fear and a hope") are an object of purpose (maf'ul li-ajlihi) conjoined to what precedes it. The meaning is: a fear you fear and a hope you hope. The two verbal nouns are interpreted with the meaning of "will" (irada), that is, the will that you fear with fear and hope with hope. The discussion of the lightning has already been given in His words ﴿He is the One who shows you the lightning, as a fear and a hope﴾ [al-Ra'd: 12] in Surat al-Ra'd, where it was explained there that "khawfan" is an object of purpose and "tama'an" likewise, and the reasoning for that.

This verse is described as signs because it contains great subtleties in the creation of the forces that are the causes of lightning, the descent of rain, and the emergence of plants from the earth after it has dried and died. Benefiting from these signs is attached to those possessing the quality of reason, because sound reason, unmixed with the defect of obstinacy and arrogance, is sufficient to grasp the proofs and wisdoms in those things mentioned, in the manner established earlier in similar cases.

The use of "ya'qilun" ("who use their reason") in agreement with the word "qawm" ("people") is to allude to what was mentioned earlier in similar contexts.

The meaning of the lam in His words ﴿li-qawmin ya'qilun﴾ ("for a people who use their reason") is like the meaning of its counterpart in His words ﴿li-qawmin yatafakkarun﴾ ("for a people who reflect") [al-Rum: 21].

[Page 80]

**﴿And among His signs is that the heaven and the earth stand by His command. Then, when He calls you with a single call from the earth, behold, you will come forth.﴾** The verses ended with this sixth sign, which indicates the great power to preserve the order of the great created beings after their creation. The creation of the heavens and the earth is an independent sign that was mentioned earlier, and the preservation of their order over the course of centuries is another sign. The point of lesson in this verse lies in its first part: that the heaven and the earth stand in this perfectly ordered standing by the command of God alone, without any other.

The meaning of "standing" (qiyam) here is complete remaining, resembling the remaining of one who stands, neither lying down nor sitting, from the saying: "the market stood (qamat al-suq)" when buying and selling flourished in it. This is what is expressed in His words, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, God holds the heavens and the earth lest they cease [Fatir: 41]﴾ and His words ﴿and He holds back the sky from falling upon the earth except by His permission [al-Hajj: 65]﴾.

The matter attributed to God is His originating command (amr takwini), which is the whole of what God has established of the order of the upper and lower world. That order guards them from the occurrence of disruption, by bringing that order into existence.

"By His command" is connected to the verb "stand," and the "ba'" is causal (sababiyya).

"Thumma" (then) is a conjunction joining one sentence to another, and the purpose of the conjoined sentence is a precaution (ihtiraz) against what might be imagined from His words ﴿that the heaven and the earth stand by His command﴾, namely that the heavens and the earth exist eternally. The sentence thus conveys that this earthly order is subject to disruption when God wills the ending of the earthly world and the bringing of creation to the Gathering (hashr), as a confirmation against the polytheists by establishing resurrection.

So the content of the sentence ﴿when He calls you with a single call from the earth, behold, you will come forth﴾ is not part of the completion of this sixth verse, but is a supplement (takmila) and insertion (idmaj) addressed to those who deny resurrection.

Regarding the object of the prepositional phrase in His words (﴿from the earth﴾) there is disagreement. The view of the author of al-Kashshaf is that it is connected to "called you" (da'akum), because "da'akum" includes a subject and an object, and what is connected to the verb may be part of the circumstances of the subject or of the object according to the context. As you say: "I called so-and-so from the top of the mountain, and he came down to me," meaning I called him while he was on the top of the mountain. This usage is contrary to what is common, but the context indicates it, while avoiding that the prepositional phrase be connected to "you come forth," because what follows the particle of sudden occurrence (harf al-mufaja'a) does not govern what precedes it. Yet in this prohibition there is room for consideration. It cannot be connected to "a call" (da'wa), because the verbal noun (masdar) does not include a subject and an object. This view is sound, and its speaker's taste suffices as proof. I say: close to it is His words, exalted is He: ﴿Those are called from a distant place [Fussilat: 44]﴾.

"Min" here denotes the starting point of place, and the prepositional phrase is an adverbial complement (zarf lagha).

It is also possible that the prepositional phrase is a circumstantial (hal) from the pronoun of object in "da'akum," in which case it is a stable adverbial (zarf mustaqirr).

It is also possible that "from the earth" is connected to "you come forth" and is placed before it. This was mentioned in Mughni al-Labib, where it reports that Abu Hatim had related it from them in his book al-Waqf, and this is better and farther from artificial strain. On this basis, the fronting of the prepositional phrase is for emphasis, as a rebuke of their error, since they deemed it impossible that they should come forth from the earth after having been lost in it, in their saying as related by God, exalted is He: ﴿And they said: "When we are lost in the earth, shall we indeed be in a new creation?" [al-Sajda: 10]﴾ and their saying ﴿"When we are dust and our fathers, shall we indeed be brought forth?" [al-Naml: 67]﴾.

As for the question of fronting the governed element before the particle "idha" of sudden occurrence, if its impermissibility is granted, then the latitude regarding the prepositional phrase and adverbial complement is a matter of wide discussion. It is strange how the author of Mughni al-Labib closed the door of such latitude in this respect in the second section of the fifth chapter.

The particle of sudden occurrence is brought in His words ﴿when you come forth﴾ to convey the speed of their coming out toward the Gathering, like His words ﴿It will be but a single shout [al-Nazi'at: 13]﴾ ﴿and behold, they are on the surface [al-Nazi'at: 14]﴾.

The particle "idha" of sudden occurrence requires that what follows it be a subject (mubtada'). The predicate of the subject is brought as a verbal sentence (jumla fi'liyya) to convey the emphasis arising from the verb bearing the pronoun of the subject, so that it is as if its mention were repeated, as its author, the author of al-Miftah, indicated.

The present tense is brought in to evoke the wondrous image of that coming forth, like His words ﴿and behold, they are from the graves to their Lord, hastening [Ya Sin: 51]﴾.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 30, verse 26:

﴿To Him belongs whoever is in the heavens and the earth; all are devoutly obedient to Him.﴾ After mentioning Allah's establishing of the heavens and the earth, this verse follows with a reminder that all rational beings in the heavens and the earth are servants of Allah, the Exalted. It is thus among the complements of what the sentence "And among His signs is that the heaven and the earth stand by His command" contains, so this sentence is conjoined to it as an addition to clarify the meaning of His establishing the heaven and the earth.

The lam in His saying ﴿To Him belongs whoever is in the heavens and the earth﴾ is the lam of ownership (lam al-milk), and the lam in His saying ﴿all are devoutly obedient to Him﴾ is the lam of reinforcement (lam al-taqwiyah), meaning that it reinforces the transitivity of the governing verb to its object, because the verb is weak by virtue of being a derivative (far') in action, and by its being placed after its object.

On this basis, "man" (man) refers to rational beings, as is its most common usage.

The apparent meaning of qunut (devout obedience) is compliance with a command, so the meaning may be that they are submissive to His command. Since there are many disobedient among the rational beings, the interpretation of qunut must be restricted to compliance with the command of creation (amr al-takwin), or to testifying to Allah's oneness through the indication of the situation (dalalat al-hal). This is the intended meaning here, because this statement comes after the mention of the six signs, in the manner of a summation (fadhlakah) affirming Oneness. Therefore it should not be taken to mean their obedience to what Allah commands them by way of legal obligation (taklif), whether directly or through an intermediary, because created beings differ in their compliance with obligation. Iblis was commanded directly by Allah to prostrate to Adam and did not comply; Adam was commanded directly by Allah not to eat from the tree and he ate from it; but that was before the beginning of obligation.

The celestial created beings comply with His command, striving toward His pleasure. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And they act by His command﴾ [al-Anbiya: 27]. As for the earthly rational created beings, they were created for obedience. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And I did not create the jinn and mankind except to worship Me﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 56]. Thus the deviation of those who deviate from obedience to Allah, the Exalted, is a departure from them from the natural disposition (fitrah) upon which they were created, and in their departure they differ: the misguided who associated others with Allah and made for Him equals, and the disobedient who did not leave His Oneness but who perhaps opposed some of His commands, little or much, are in that taking a side of fleeing (ibaq), differing in it.

Thus the sentence ﴿To Him belongs whoever is in the heavens and the earth; all are devoutly obedient to Him﴾ is conjoined to the sentence ﴿And among His signs is that the heaven and the earth stand by His command﴾ [al-Rum: 25].

It is also possible that the sentence ﴿To Him belongs whoever is in the heavens and the earth; all are devoutly obedient to Him﴾ is a completion of the sentence ﴿Then when He calls you with a call from the earth, behold, you will come out﴾ [al-Rum: 25], in the sense: "To Him on that Day belongs whoever is in the heavens and the earth; all are devoutly obedient to Him." Then qunut carries the meaning of compliance occurring on that Day, which is compliance of submission, because compliance with obligation has ended with the ending of the world. That is, they have no recourse but submission in what Allah commands regarding their affairs, ﴿on the Day when their tongues, their hands and their feet will testify against them concerning what they used to do﴾ [al-Nur: 24]. In that case the sentence is conjoined to the sentence ﴿Then when He calls you with a call from the earth, behold, you will come out﴾ [al-Rum: 25].

Qunut was discussed previously in His saying ﴿devoutly obedient to Allah, upright﴾ [al-Nahl: 120] in Surah al-Nahl.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 30, verse 27:

﴿And He it is who originates creation, then repeats it, and it is most easy for Him. To Him belongs the highest likeness in the heavens and the earth, and He is the Mighty, the Wise.﴾ The beginning of this verse has a counterpart that was mentioned earlier in this surah, and it is repeated here so that His saying ﴿and it is most easy for Him﴾ can be built upon it, as a completion of the proof, since this completion was not mentioned there.

This is the start of addressing the discourse to the polytheists, because it refers back to its counterpart that was directed at them. This is closer to the dialectical concession (al-taslim al-jadali, the tactical acceptance of the opponent's premise) in debate. That is because when they acknowledged that God is the originator of the creation of man, but denied His restoring it after death, and the proof against them there was by the analogy of equality (qiyas al-musawat, an argument from equal cases), and since their denial of restoration after death implied limiting the scope of divine power, the concession in the argument came: if limiting the scope of power were granted to them, it would still require the possibility of resurrection by the analogy of the more fitting (qiyas al-awla, an argument a fortiori). For restoring a made thing a second time is easier for the maker than his first making, and it is brought under the influence of His power in what people commonly understand regarding their own capabilities.

So His saying (﴿most easy﴾) is a superlative, and its position is the position of the directed discourse. Its apparent meaning is that (﴿most easy﴾) is used in the sense of comparison, in the manner of granting latitude and dialectical concession, meaning: the second creation is easier than the first creation. This has the same sense as His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Were We fatigued by the first creation? Rather, they are in doubt about a new creation﴾ [Qaf: 15]. Its intent is: repeating the creation a second time is equal to beginning it in terms of the connection of divine power. Thus the form of the superlative carries the sense of the strength of the verb from which it is derived, as in His saying ﴿He said, "My Lord, the prison is dearer to me than what they invite me to"﴾ [Yusuf: 33].

Page 84

To indicate that His saying ﴿and it is most easy for Him﴾ is merely an approximation to their understanding, He followed it with His saying ﴿To Him belongs the highest likeness in the heavens and the earth﴾, meaning: it is established for Him, and He deserves the most perfect state that cannot be measured by the commonly known affairs of people, and this is only for the purpose of bringing it closer to your understanding.

Al-a'la (the highest) means the greatest, reaching the ultimate reality of greatness and power. Hujjat al-Islam said in al-Ihya': "No human has the capacity to penetrate the depth of wisdom, just as they have no capacity to take in the light of the sun with their eyes, but they receive from it what keeps their eyes alive. Some have been meticulous in expressing the subtlety of conveying the meanings of the glorious speech to human understanding, because of the high rank of the glorious speech and the limited level of human understanding. When people want to make animals understand what they want of them, such as moving forward or backward and the like, and they see them falling short of understanding speech issuing from minds, however fine and well-arranged it is, they descend to the level of distinguishing animals and convey their aims to them with sounds they set that are suitable for them, such as whistling and similar sounds close to their own cries." End of quotation.

And His saying ﴿in the heavens and the earth﴾ [Rum: 26] is an attribute of "the likeness" or a circumstantial qualifier of it, meaning: His deserving the highest likeness is firmly established in the heavens and the earth, that is, in the beings of the heavens and the earth. So what is meant is their inhabitants, in the manner of ﴿and ask the town﴾. That is, He is described with the noblest attributes and the greatest affairs on the tongues of the rational beings, who are the angels and the humans whose minds are counted, with no regard for those among them who are deprived of reason because of their feeble minds. And it is in the indications of the proofs that exist in the heavens and in the earth, for all those proofs bear witness that God has the highest likeness.

Among the highest likeness are His might and His wisdom, exalted is He. They were singled out for mention here because they are the two attributes whose effects appear in the subject being discussed, which is the origination of creation and its repetition. Might requires absolute self-sufficiency, so it requires complete power. Wisdom requires comprehensive knowledge. And among the effects of power and wisdom is that He restores creation by His power, and that the purpose of that is recompense, which is part of His wisdom.

[Page 85]

﴿He has coined for you a parable from yourselves: Do you have, among those whom your right hands possess, any partners in what We have provided you, so that you are equal in it, fearing them as you fear one another? Thus do We detail the signs for a people who reason.﴾

The coining of the parable (ḍarb al-mathal) is placed right after the proof of origination, in order to show that re-creation is possible. It follows the two earlier proofs in His words ﴿He brings the living out of the dead﴾ [al-Rum: 19] and ﴿and revives the earth after its death﴾ [al-Rum: 19]. This is so that the argument is ordered around these two fundamental principles: the principle of divine unity (tawhid) and the principle of resurrection (ba'th). The matter is made clear through illustration and comparison, after the rational proof has been established. The address is to the polytheists.

The phrase ḍarb al-mathal means setting up and presenting the parable. On this reading, mathalan is in the accusative as the direct object. Alternatively, "striking" it means making it a striking example, that is, a parable and a likeness. On this reading, mathalan is in the absolute accusative (al-mafʿul al-muṭlaq), since mathalan then carries the same meaning as ḍarban, the verbal noun of ḍaraba in this sense. What was discussed on this point at His words ﴿Indeed Allah is not ashamed to present an example﴾ [al-Baqarah: 26] is found in the commentary on Surat al-Baqarah.

The lam in His words lakum ("for you") is the lam of causation (lam al-taʿlil). That is, He coined the parable for your sake, that is, for the sake of your understanding.

The min in His words ﴿from yourselves﴾ is the min of origin (ibtidaʾiyyah) and is connected to ḍaraba. That is, He made for you a parable drawn from yourselves. Here "yourselves" (al-anfus) refers to the category of people, as in His words ﴿greet one another﴾ [al-Nur: 61]. That is, a parable drawn from the conditions of your community, since no community is free of people who have slaves and who know the conditions of slaves with their masters, whether they themselves own slaves or not. The address is therefore to the whole nation, on account of the existence within it of a group to whom this parable applies.

The interrogative is used for denial (inkar), and the basis of the denial is His words ﴿in what We have provided you﴾ and what follows, that is, "partners who have this status."

The min in His words ﴿of what your right hands possess﴾ [al-Nur: 33] is partitive (tabʿiḍiyyah). The min in His words ﴿among partners﴾ is superfluous (zaʾidah) and serves to reinforce the sense of negation derived from the denying interrogative. The combination of these particles within a single utterance is of the type known as perfect paronomy (al-jinas al-tamm).

The word shurakaʾ ("partners") is the plural of sharik, meaning one who shares in property, as in His words ﴿in what We have provided you﴾. The fa' in ﴿so that you are equal﴾ marks a consequence of partnership. That is, you would be equal in what you share as partners.

The clause ﴿fearing them﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥal) from the pronoun of the subject in "equal" (sawaʾ).

Fear (khawf) is a psychological state arising from anticipating the occurrence of a harm that remains. Here it means guarding against falling short in their shares of provisions. It does not mean terror, as the context of His words ﴿as you fear your own selves﴾ indicates. That is, just as you guard against neglecting your own rights with them.

The second "selves" means the selves of those who have partners among what their right hands possess, from among the addressees, since they are part of the addressees.

This parable is a comparison of a compound state (hay'ah murakkabah) with another compound state. The state drawn from the claim of the polytheists, that the idols are partners of God in disposing of affairs and in defending their devotees against whatever God wills of punishment or the like, was compared to this image. They claimed that the idols are their intercessors before God, while at the same time they acknowledge that the idols are created by God. In their talbiyah (the chant of pilgrimage) they say: "Here I am, O God, You have no partner, except a partner who is Yours, You possess him and what he owns." This state is compared to the state of people who have slaves who become partners in their masters' provisions on an equal footing, so that their masters, when they wish to dispose of those provisions, fear that their disposal will be displeasing to their slaves. This comparison, though it applies to the compound as a whole from the two states, has reached the utmost perfection among its kind. It is also capable of being divided into its component parts, by comparing the owner of all creation to those who own slaves, comparing the idols, which are created by God the Exalted, to human slaves, comparing the idols' sharing in disposal together with the Creator in His dominion to the slaves' sharing in disposing of their masters' provisions, and comparing their claim that God deviates from some of what He wills concerning creation for the sake of those idols, and their intercession, to the fear of owners of provisions about disposing of the shares of their partner slaves in a way that they would refuse. This comparative state is a hideous and deformed one, with no counterpart in their customs. The state being compared is therefore one that is denied and rejected. For this reason the interrogative of denial and repudiation has been applied to it, so that the result is that the imagined form of the idols is a false form, by way of depiction and modeling, displaying that false belief in a perceptible, deformed, and false image.

[Page 86]

For this reason He follows it with the clause ﴿Thus do We detail the signs for a people who reason﴾. That is, We detail the proofs for correct belief in a detail like this detail, with clear explicitness. The clause ﴿Indeed in that are signs for a people who reason﴾ [al-Rum: 24] is an independent resumptive sentence (istiʾnaf ibtidaʾi).

The people who reason are those who are free from obstinacy and aversion, and who seek the truth and realities because of the abundance of their intellect. Thus believers increase in certainty, and the heedless are guided, as are those whose minds have been led astray by the misguidance of the polytheists and who are then uncovered by clear proofs of this kind.

The mention of the word "people" (qawm) and attaching the attribute to it hints that these signs benefit only one whose reason is among the constituents of his peoplehood, as was said earlier at His words ﴿Indeed in that are signs for a people who reason﴾ [al-Baqarah: 164] in Surat al-Baqarah. Many similar instances have already passed.

What was said about choosing the attribute of reason here, rather than other attributes of reflection and thought, is like what was said earlier at His words ﴿And among His signs is that He shows you the lightning, as fear and as hope﴾ [al-Rum: 24], down to His words "who reason".

In this there is an indirect reproach to those who are obstinate in their polytheism, that they are not people of reason and are not among those who benefit, as in His words ﴿None understands them except those who have knowledge﴾ [al-ʿAnkabut: 43], and His words ﴿The example of those who disbelieve is like one who shouts to that which hears nothing but a call and a cry: deaf, dumb, blind, so they do not reason﴾ [al-Baqarah: 171].

As for His words "thus" (kadhalika), a parallel to it has already passed at His words ﴿Thus We made you a midmost community﴾ [al-Baqarah: 143].

﴿Nay, those who did wrong followed their desires without knowledge. So who can guide those whom Allah has led astray? And they have no helpers.﴾ This is an *idrab ibtali* (a transition that cancels what precedes it), returning to what was implied by the allusive statement in His words ﴿Thus do We detail the signs for a people who reason﴾ [al-Rum: 28]. That statement implied that the proper course was for people to benefit from such an example, so that the polytheists among them would give up their polytheism and enter the fold of faith. But they followed their desires and what their souls embellished for them, did not seek the truth, and did not reflect on its proofs. Thus they are far removed from knowledge. The sense is: "The detailed signs did not benefit them; rather, they followed their desires."

﴿Those who did wrong﴾: the polytheists, for indeed polytheism is a great wrong. Restricting the following of desire by the phrase "without knowledge" is a censure of this following, for it is the following of appetite together with ignorance. A person of knowledge who follows his desire is cautious about plunging deeply into it, because he knows its corruption. What is here is not similar to His words ﴿And who is more astray than one who follows his desire without guidance from Allah?﴾ [al-Qasas: 50], in that the latter is a clarifying qualifier, since desire is never found except mixed with something contrary to the guidance of Allah.

The *fa'* (ف) in ﴿fa-man yahdi﴾ is *li-l-tafri'* (consequential), meaning: from their following their desires without knowledge there necessarily follows the permanent absence of guidance from them.

﴿Man﴾ is an interrogative of denial (*ism istifham inkari*), meaning negation. It therefore expresses the generality of the negation of any guide for them. The sense is: no one guides those whom Allah has led astray, neither others nor themselves, for they are included in the generality of those who could be a guide.

The meaning of ﴿whom Allah has led astray﴾ is: whom He has decreed to be astray and whose heart He has sealed. Attributing misguidance to Allah is attributing it to His creative decree, not to His command to it, and this is clear. The meaning of the negation of their guide is that whoever attempts to guide them finds no path into their souls.

Then another statement about their condition is conjoined to the clause negating their guidance, namely ﴿and they have no helpers﴾, as a rebuttal of the polytheists who claimed that when they committed a sin before Allah, the idols would intercede for them before Allah.

**Commentary of Ibn ʿAshur (al-Taḥrīr wa'l-Tanwīr) on Surah 30, verse 30 (part 1 of 2):**

﴿So set your face toward the religion, inclining to truth, the nature (fiṭra) of God upon which He created mankind. There is no altering of God's creation. That is the upright religion, but most people do not know.﴾

The *fāʾ* in ﴿فَأقِمْ﴾ is *faṣīḥa* (an "eloquent" *fāʾ*, which signals an implied condition). The sense is: "When you have come to know the state of those who turn away from the proofs of truth, then set your face toward the religion."

The imperative here is used to request continuity (*ṭalab al-dawām*). The purpose is that you should not be concerned with their turning away. This is like His saying, ﴿So if they dispute with you, say: I have submitted my face to God, and so have those who follow me﴾ [Āl ʿImrān 3:20], and His saying, ﴿So be steadfast as you were commanded, and those who turned with you [in repentance]﴾ [Hūd 11:112],

that is, those who believed, and His saying, ﴿I call to God upon insight, I and those who follow me﴾ [Yūsuf 12:108].

So the meaning is: "So set your face toward the religion, and let the believers be with you," as His saying afterward indicates, ﴿turning back to Him and fearing Him﴾ [al-Rūm 30:31], in the plural form.

*Iqāmat al-wajh* (setting the face) means straightening and aligning it, orienting it directly toward what is in front of one's gaze, without turning right or left. It is a figurative depiction (*tamthīl*) of the state of devoting oneself entirely to something and being wholly occupied with it, with the gaze fixed on the direction in front, not turning to the right or left. This is like His saying, ﴿And set your faces [upright] at every place of worship and call upon Him, sincere in devotion to Him﴾ [al-Aʿrāf 7:29], and His saying, quoting Abraham, ﴿Indeed, I have turned my face toward He who created the heavens and the earth﴾ [al-Anʿām 6:79], and His saying, ﴿Say: I have submitted my face to God﴾ [Āl ʿImrān 3:20], meaning: "I have given it to God." This is the meaning of being wholly devoted to the worship of God and not turning toward any other object of worship.

The definite article in ﴿الدِّينِ﴾ is *lil-ʿahd* (referring to a known thing), and it refers to their religion, which they follow, namely the religion of Islam.

﴿حَنِيفًا﴾ (*ḥanīfan*, inclining to truth) may be a circumstantial state (*ḥāl*) of the implied pronoun in the verb ﴿أقِمْ﴾, so that it is a state of the Prophet (ﷺ), just as it was a description of Abraham (peace be upon him) in His saying, ﴿Indeed, Abraham was a nation, devoutly obedient to God, inclining to truth﴾ [al-Naḥl 16:120]. This is the more apparent reading in its interpretation.

It may also be a state of ﴿الدِّينِ﴾ according to what al-Zajjāj explained, in which case it is a metaphor (*istiʿāra*) by likening the religion to a man who is *ḥanīf*, being free of the stains of polytheism. Thus *al-ḥanīf* is an allegorical metaphor (*tamthīliyya*), and attributing it to the religion is an explicit metaphor (*istiʿāra taṣrīḥiyya*).

*Ḥanīf* is an intensive form (*ṣīghat mubālagha*) of being characterized by *ḥanaf*, which means inclination. This description came to be used predominantly for turning away from falsehood, that is, deviating from it by turning toward truth. So it means "upright and cut off from polytheism," as in His saying, ﴿Say: Rather, [follow] the religion of Abraham, inclining to truth, and he was not of those who associate others with God﴾ [al-Baqara 2:135]. This has already been discussed in Surat al-Baqara.

﴿فِطْرَةَ اللَّهِ﴾ (*fiṭrata Allāh*, the nature of God) is a substitute (*badal*) for ﴿حَنِيفًا﴾, a *badal al-ishtimāl* (comprehensive apposition). So it has the meaning of a state of ﴿الدِّينِ﴾ as well, and it is a second state. This is because, according to the grammarians, a state is like a predicate in that several of them may occur without a conjunction, by verification. This reading is better, because it more clearly conveys that this religion is distinguished by two qualities: being free of associating partners with God, and conforming to the *fiṭra*. This conveys that it is a tolerant, easy religion, without hardship. A parallel is His saying, ﴿and has not made in it any crookedness, but [made it] upright﴾ [al-Kahf 18:1], meaning that the religion is the *fiṭra* of God, because

monotheism is the *fiṭra*, and polytheism is an alteration of the *fiṭra*.

The word *fiṭra* originally is a noun of state (*ism hayʾa*) from *al-faṭr*, which means creating, like *al-khilqa* (creation/form). This is shown by His saying, ﴿upon which He created mankind﴾, meaning He instilled in mankind and created them upon it, that is, they are firmly established in it.

The preposition ﴿عَلى﴾ (*ʿalā*, upon) is used figuratively (*mustaʿār*) for the firm connection of an attribute to the one described, a firmness resembling the firmness of one who is elevated above something. A parallel of this was mentioned earlier in His saying, ﴿Those are upon guidance from their Lord﴾ [al-Baqara 2:5], in Surat al-Baqara. The literal meaning is: "the nature upon which He created mankind," that is, by which He created them.

The meaning of God having created mankind upon the upright religion is that God created people capable of accepting the rulings of this religion, and He made its teachings suitable to their natural constitution, not alien to it, not distant from it, and not rejecting it. An example is affirming the oneness of God, because monotheism is what accords with reason and sound reflection. Even if a person is left to his own thinking and is not indoctrinated with a false belief, he would be guided to monotheism by his *fiṭra*. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "What is relied upon in interpreting this term (i.e., *fiṭra*) is that it is the natural constitution and disposition that is within a human being, which is prepared and equipped so that he can distinguish God's creations, derive evidence through them about his Lord, and know His laws." End of quote.

Although I have not seen anyone who fully clarified the meaning of Islam being the *fiṭra*, I shall explain it: the *fiṭra* is the system that God established in every created thing. The *fiṭra* that is specific to the human species is what God created in them, both physically and intellectually. Thus, a human walking on his two legs is a physical *fiṭra*, and his attempt to take things with his feet is contrary to the physical *fiṭra*. Inferring causes from their effects and conclusions from premises is an intellectual *fiṭra*, and attempting to infer a matter without its cause is contrary to the intellectual *fiṭra*, which in the science of reasoning is called *fasād al-waḍʿ* (a defect in the formulation). Our conviction that what we perceive among things are established realities in existence and reality itself is an intellectual *fiṭra*, while the denial by the sophists (*sūfisṭāʾiyya*) of the reality of sensible things is contrary to the intellectual *fiṭra*.

Abū ʿAlī Ibn Sīnā (Avicenna) has clarified the reality of the *fiṭra* in his book *al-Najāt*, where he said: "The meaning of *fiṭra* is that a person imagines himself to have come into the world all at once, rational, but without having heard any opinion, adopted any doctrine, lived among any community, or learned any politics. Yet he has observed sensible things and drawn from them

the states. Then he presents to his mind something and doubts it. If doubt is possible for him, then the *fiṭra* does not testify to it. If doubt is not possible for him, then it is what the *fiṭra* requires. Not everything that the human *fiṭra* requires is true; what is true is the *fiṭra* of the faculty called intellect. As for the *fiṭra* of the mind in general, it may be false. This falsehood occurs in matters that are not sensible in themselves but are principles for sensible things. Thus the true *fiṭra* consists of premises and widely accepted opinions which necessitate assent to them: either the testimony of all, such as that justice is beautiful; or the testimony of the majority; or the testimony of scholars or of their excellent ones. Commonly accepted opinions, insofar as they are commonly accepted, are not among those things to which assent arises from the *fiṭra*. What is commonly accepted is not a self-evident intellectual or imaginative truth, for it is not natural. Yet it is firmly established in souls, because custom has continued upon it since childhood, and perhaps it is motivated by love of harmony and the mutual accommodation that people need, or by some human moral trait such as modesty and sociability, or by much induction, or by the statement having a subtle condition that would make it purely true, so that this condition is not noticed and it is taken as absolute." So describing Islam as the *fiṭra* of God means that the basis of its belief proceeds in accordance with the intellectual *fiṭra*. As for its legislation and its branches, they are either also natural matters, that is, proceeding in harmony with what reason perceives and testifies to, or they are for its benefit, in a way that does not contradict the *fiṭra*.

The laws of its transactions are traced back to what the *fiṭra* testifies to, because the pursuit of benefits comes from the *fiṭra*. The details of this are not the place for them here, and I have explained them in my book entitled *Maqāṣid al-Sharīʿa al-Islāmiyya* (The Objectives of Islamic Law).

Know that the evidences of the *fiṭra* may be clear and manifest, or they may be hidden, as Shaykh Ibn Sīnā's statement indicates. So when the natural meanings are obscured or mixed with other things, those who are qualified to distinguish and uncover them are the wise scholars who have become

Human society has suffered for long ages from illusions, customs, and habits that were introduced into it by people of misguidance. These became mixed with sound knowledge, so people repeated them and became accustomed to accepting them, and they stuck to their minds the way a spider's web sticks to its house. It is feared that these will be received with acceptance throughout the ages, making it difficult for people to abandon them and to recognize the distortion from the truth that they contain. Its original form is *fa'la*, in the pattern indicating a single occurrence, because it is one instance of *al-nawb*, which is one person standing in for another; from it comes *al-niyaba* (deputyship).
