Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 30, verses 33–34:

﴿When harm touches people, they call upon their Lord, turning to Him in repentance. Then when He lets them taste mercy from Him, behold, a group of them associate others with their Lord.﴾ ﴿So that they may deny what We have given them. Then enjoy yourselves; you will soon know.﴾

This is a continuation of the sentence ﴿They divided their religion and became sects﴾ [Ar-Rum: 32]. That is, they divided their religion and became sects. When harm touched them, they called upon God alone, and when He had mercy on them, they returned to their polytheism and disbelief, ungrateful for the blessing of the One who had shown them mercy. The purpose of the verse is His words ﴿then when He lets them taste mercy from Him, behold, a group of them associate others with their Lord.﴾ Its place within the censure of the polytheists is that they revert to disbelief, unlike the believers, whom God caused to taste mercy after harm, and who thanked their Lord for His blessing, which is part of their turning back to God.

The discourse is woven in this manner so that it serves as a concluding statement (tadhyil), and as an incorporation (idmaj) that honours the believers who do not deny the blessing of the Merciful. The definite article in "al-nas" (the people) is for comprehensiveness (al-istighraq).

Al-durr, with a dammah on the dad, is a bad state in the body, in one's livelihood, or in wealth. This is like what befell the Quraysh of hardship and famine, to the point that they saw something like smoke in the sky from the severity of the drought, and to the point that they ate bones and carrion. This affected both their polytheists and their believers, but its severity fell more heavily on the polytheists, because they had been living in luxury, so the hardship was harder on them. They sent to the Prophet ﷺ seeking his intercession, asking him to pray to God to remove the harm from them. He prayed, and they were given rain, and they returned to their comfortable life. God said: ﴿So watch for the day when the sky brings a visible smoke﴾ [Ad-Dukhan: 10], and so on. Thus their calling upon their Lord includes their request that the Messenger ﷺ pray for them.

Munibin (turning in repentance) is a state (hal) of all people; that is, they are equal in turning back to Him, returning to Him after that. The polytheists, however, were distracted from Him by calling upon the idols. God said: ﴿We will remove the punishment a little; indeed you will return﴾ [Ad-Dukhan: 15]. Munibin has already been mentioned just above.

Al-massu (touching) is used metaphorically for affliction. Its literal meaning is placing the hand on something to know its existence or to test its condition. It was discussed earlier in His words ﴿a painful punishment will touch those of them who disbelieve﴾ [Al-Ma'idah: 73], in the chapter of al-'Uqud.

It is chosen here because of what it implies of lightness of affliction; that is, they call upon God when a slight harm touches them, let alone severe harm.

Al-idhaqah (causing to taste) is also used metaphorically for affliction. Its literal meaning is the touching of food by the tip of the tongue, which is the weakest contact the body's organs have with food, being less than chewing and swallowing. It was mentioned earlier in His words ﴿that he may taste the consequence of his action﴾ [Al-Ma'idah: 95] in the chapter of al-'Uqud, and in ﴿And if We let people taste mercy after a hardship that had touched them﴾ [Yunus: 21] in the chapter of Yunus.

The verb "idhaqah" was chosen for what it indicates of their haste to associate partners with God at the very beginning of receiving mercy.

Al-rahmah (mercy) is their deliverance from hardship.

Thumma (then) is for a rank-based delay (al-tarakhi al-rutbi), because their associating others with God after supplication, repentance, and receiving His mercy is more astonishing than their earlier association. So in this rank-based delay there is a sense of wonder at the renewal of their polytheism. The particle of surprise "idha" also indicates that this group hastened back to polytheism immediately upon tasting mercy, because disbelief was deeply rooted in them and hidden within their souls.

The pronoun in "minhu" (from Him) refers to God, Exalted. "Min" is for the beginning of a point (ibtida'iyyah) and is connected to "asabahum" (touched them). "Rahmah" is the subject of "asabahum," and the verb is not feminine because the feminine marking of the named mercy is not real, and because of the intervening prepositional phrase. Placing the prepositional phrase before the subject serves to emphasise it, to show that what touched them is from God's favour and decree and nothing else.

The lam in His words "li-yakfuru" (so that they may deny) is the lam of causation. It is used metaphorically to mean causation in the sense that should properly be expressed with "fa" (so). For when they associated partners with God, they did not intend their polytheism to be the cause of their denial of God's blessing. Rather, they associated partners out of love for polytheism, so polytheism led them to deny God's blessing as a consequence and an inevitable result. This is causation by a final cause, similar to His words ﴿Then the family of Pharaoh picked him up, so that he might become for them an enemy and a grief﴾ [Al-Qasas: 8]. The pronoun in "li-yakfuru" refers to the group, taking into account its meaning.

Al-itaʼ (giving) means giving something beneficial, that is, with what We have bestowed upon them of blessings, namely the blessing of existence, provision, and the removal of harm from them.

Then the discourse shifts from the third person to the second person with His words "fa-tamatta'u" (then enjoy yourselves), as a rebuke and a warning. The particle "fa" of consequence is used in "fa-tamatta'u" because the warning and rebuke follow from the preceding discourse.

The imperative in "tamatta'u" is used to mean threat and rebuke.

Al-tamattu' (enjoyment) is benefiting from what is agreeable and from blessings for a limited period that will end.

The "fa" in "fa-sawfa ta'lamun" (then you will soon know) is a consequence, drawing the warning from the rebuke, and it is elegant.

"Sawfa ta'lamun" (you will soon know) is a warning that they will come to know something great in the future. Knowledge here is a metaphor (kinayah) for the occurrence of the matter that is known, that is, the arrival of calamities upon them whose true nature they do not now know. It implies the greatness of those calamities and that they were not something they expected. This points to what they would be struck by on the day of Badr, of annihilation and disgrace. They had been seeking hastily a punishment of the same kind as that with which the earlier nations had been punished, such as 'Ad and Thamud, and the end was the same. Their being struck by the punishment of the swords of the Muslims is more eloquent in showing that their annihilation came directly at the hands of the believers, and more manifest in saving the believers from a punishment that would not strike only those who did wrong. This is what is meant by His words ﴿We will remove the punishment a little; indeed you will return. On the day We seize with the greatest seizure, indeed We will take retribution﴾ [Ad-Dukhan: 15–16]. The greatest seizure is the seizure of the day of Badr.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 30, verses 33–34:

﴿When harm touches people, they call upon their Lord, turning to Him in repentance. Then when He lets them taste mercy from Him, behold, a group of them associate others with their Lord.﴾ ﴿So that they may deny what We have given them. Then enjoy yourselves; you will soon know.﴾

This is a continuation of the sentence ﴿They divided their religion and became sects﴾ [Ar-Rum: 32]. That is, they divided their religion and became sects. When harm touched them, they called upon God alone, and when He had mercy on them, they returned to their polytheism and disbelief, ungrateful for the blessing of the One who had shown them mercy. The purpose of the verse is His words ﴿then when He lets them taste mercy from Him, behold, a group of them associate others with their Lord.﴾ Its place within the censure of the polytheists is that they revert to disbelief, unlike the believers, whom God caused to taste mercy after harm, and who thanked their Lord for His blessing, which is part of their turning back to God.

The discourse is woven in this manner so that it serves as a concluding statement (tadhyil), and as an incorporation (idmaj) that honours the believers who do not deny the blessing of the Merciful. The definite article in "al-nas" (the people) is for comprehensiveness (al-istighraq).

Al-durr, with a dammah on the dad, is a bad state in the body, in one's livelihood, or in wealth. This is like what befell the Quraysh of hardship and famine, to the point that they saw something like smoke in the sky from the severity of the drought, and to the point that they ate bones and carrion. This affected both their polytheists and their believers, but its severity fell more heavily on the polytheists, because they had been living in luxury, so the hardship was harder on them. They sent to the Prophet ﷺ seeking his intercession, asking him to pray to God to remove the harm from them. He prayed, and they were given rain, and they returned to their comfortable life. God said: ﴿So watch for the day when the sky brings a visible smoke﴾ [Ad-Dukhan: 10], and so on. Thus their calling upon their Lord includes their request that the Messenger ﷺ pray for them.

Munibin (turning in repentance) is a state (hal) of all people; that is, they are equal in turning back to Him, returning to Him after that. The polytheists, however, were distracted from Him by calling upon the idols. God said: ﴿We will remove the punishment a little; indeed you will return﴾ [Ad-Dukhan: 15]. Munibin has already been mentioned just above.

Al-massu (touching) is used metaphorically for affliction. Its literal meaning is placing the hand on something to know its existence or to test its condition. It was discussed earlier in His words ﴿a painful punishment will touch those of them who disbelieve﴾ [Al-Ma'idah: 73], in the chapter of al-'Uqud.

It is chosen here because of what it implies of lightness of affliction; that is, they call upon God when a slight harm touches them, let alone severe harm.

Al-idhaqah (causing to taste) is also used metaphorically for affliction. Its literal meaning is the touching of food by the tip of the tongue, which is the weakest contact the body's organs have with food, being less than chewing and swallowing. It was mentioned earlier in His words ﴿that he may taste the consequence of his action﴾ [Al-Ma'idah: 95] in the chapter of al-'Uqud, and in ﴿And if We let people taste mercy after a hardship that had touched them﴾ [Yunus: 21] in the chapter of Yunus.

The verb "idhaqah" was chosen for what it indicates of their haste to associate partners with God at the very beginning of receiving mercy.

Al-rahmah (mercy) is their deliverance from hardship.

Thumma (then) is for a rank-based delay (al-tarakhi al-rutbi), because their associating others with God after supplication, repentance, and receiving His mercy is more astonishing than their earlier association. So in this rank-based delay there is a sense of wonder at the renewal of their polytheism. The particle of surprise "idha" also indicates that this group hastened back to polytheism immediately upon tasting mercy, because disbelief was deeply rooted in them and hidden within their souls.

The pronoun in "minhu" (from Him) refers to God, Exalted. "Min" is for the beginning of a point (ibtida'iyyah) and is connected to "asabahum" (touched them). "Rahmah" is the subject of "asabahum," and the verb is not feminine because the feminine marking of the named mercy is not real, and because of the intervening prepositional phrase. Placing the prepositional phrase before the subject serves to emphasise it, to show that what touched them is from God's favour and decree and nothing else.

The lam in His words "li-yakfuru" (so that they may deny) is the lam of causation. It is used metaphorically to mean causation in the sense that should properly be expressed with "fa" (so). For when they associated partners with God, they did not intend their polytheism to be the cause of their denial of God's blessing. Rather, they associated partners out of love for polytheism, so polytheism led them to deny God's blessing as a consequence and an inevitable result. This is causation by a final cause, similar to His words ﴿Then the family of Pharaoh picked him up, so that he might become for them an enemy and a grief﴾ [Al-Qasas: 8]. The pronoun in "li-yakfuru" refers to the group, taking into account its meaning.

Al-itaʼ (giving) means giving something beneficial, that is, with what We have bestowed upon them of blessings, namely the blessing of existence, provision, and the removal of harm from them.

Then the discourse shifts from the third person to the second person with His words "fa-tamatta'u" (then enjoy yourselves), as a rebuke and a warning. The particle "fa" of consequence is used in "fa-tamatta'u" because the warning and rebuke follow from the preceding discourse.

The imperative in "tamatta'u" is used to mean threat and rebuke.

Al-tamattu' (enjoyment) is benefiting from what is agreeable and from blessings for a limited period that will end.

The "fa" in "fa-sawfa ta'lamun" (then you will soon know) is a consequence, drawing the warning from the rebuke, and it is elegant.

"Sawfa ta'lamun" (you will soon know) is a warning that they will come to know something great in the future. Knowledge here is a metaphor (kinayah) for the occurrence of the matter that is known, that is, the arrival of calamities upon them whose true nature they do not now know. It implies the greatness of those calamities and that they were not something they expected. This points to what they would be struck by on the day of Badr, of annihilation and disgrace. They had been seeking hastily a punishment of the same kind as that with which the earlier nations had been punished, such as 'Ad and Thamud, and the end was the same. Their being struck by the punishment of the swords of the Muslims is more eloquent in showing that their annihilation came directly at the hands of the believers, and more manifest in saving the believers from a punishment that would not strike only those who did wrong. This is what is meant by His words ﴿We will remove the punishment a little; indeed you will return. On the day We seize with the greatest seizure, indeed We will take retribution﴾ [Ad-Dukhan: 15–16]. The greatest seizure is the seizure of the day of Badr.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 30, verse 35:

﴿Or have We sent down to them an authority, so that it speaks of what they used to associate with Him?﴾

"Am" (أم) here is disconnective (munqati'a), so it is like "bal" (بل) for turning away (al-idrab), and it is a transitional turning away (idrab intiqali). Since the particle "am" is a particle of conjunction, what follows it may be a turning away from the previous speech, so that it is the conjunction of one narrative upon another as if it were a new beginning. The speech is a rebuke and reproach connected to the rebuke conveyed by His words ﴿So enjoy yourselves, for you will soon know﴾ [al-Rum: 34].

In it there is an iltifat (shift) from address (al-khitab) to the third person (al-ghayba), turning away from addressing you to addressing the Muslims, expressing wonder at the state of the people of polytheism. It is also permissible that what follows it be connected to His words ﴿Rather, those who did wrong follow their desires without knowledge﴾ [al-Rum: 29], so it is the conjunction of one censure upon another, and what lies between them is a parenthetical interjection (i'tiraD).

Wherever "am" occurs, the interrogative is implied after it, because it is inseparable from the meaning of interrogation. The estimated reading is: "Rather, did We send down to them an authority?" and this is a denying interrogative (istifham inkari), meaning: We did not send down to them an authority. The meaning of the denying interrogative is that it is an affirmation of denial, as if the questioner asks the one questioned so that he may acknowledge the negation of what is asked about.

"Sultan" means proof (al-hujjah). Since "sultan" is made the object of the sending down from God, it is determined that what is meant by it is a book, as they said: ﴿until you send down to us a book that we may read﴾ [al-Isra: 93]. It is also determined that what is meant by speaking (al-takallum) is indication through writing, as in His words, exalted is He: ﴿This Our Book speaks against you with the truth﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 29], meaning its writing indicates, that is, it was written in it by the pen of power that polytheism is true, as in His words, exalted is He: ﴿Or have We given them a book before this, so that they hold fast to it?﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 21].

He placed "bihi" (به) before "mushrikun" (مشركون) for emphasis, drawing attention to the cause of their associating partners, which falls within the scope of the denial, for the sake of observing the fasilah (verse-ending rhyme).

The discourse about the polytheists' conditions is repeated to elaborate on the state in which they receive mercy and its opposite, a manner of receiving that is alike for them. Earlier, the polytheists' reception of mercy was identified as ingratitude (*kufran*), which implies that believers do not receive it with ingratitude. Here the aim is to warn them about their reception of the opposite of mercy, which is despair (*qunut*), so that they may avoid it, train themselves to hope for relief, turn to Allah in supplication about it, and take up the means of removing it. "Mercy" (*rahmah*) is used here for its effect, which is benefits and pleasant, agreeable conditions, as the contrast with "evil" (*sayyi'ah*) indicates. Evil is what afflicts its owner and grieves him. The purpose of this verse is therefore the cultivation of the complete character among Muslims. "People" (*an-nas*) refers specifically to the polytheists, as shown by the verse ending with ﴿Indeed in that are signs for a people who believe﴾.

In this verse, the befalling of mercy is placed before the befalling of evil, the reverse of the preceding verse, in order to give attention to the state that is made the starting point of the lesson and the basis of the inference. The phrase "they rejoice in it" (*fariḥū bihā*) describes the condition of people when mercy befalls them, so that its opposite may be built upon it in the words ﴿behold, they despair﴾, since despair entails complaint and anger. There is therefore no implicit disapproval of joy in the statement, so that we would be compelled to interpret joy as insolence (*bataran*) or the like, for that would be a departure from the apparent meaning without a reason. The meaning is: just as they rejoice when mercy comes, not thinking of its end and not grieving over the fear of losing it, so too they should be patient when harm touches them and not despair of its removal. Their despair of its removal does not follow the analogy of their condition when mercy befalls them, when they do not expect it to end. Thus despair is the object of the reproach against them. This is like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Man does not tire of asking for good, but if evil touches him, he is despairing and hopeless﴾ [Fussilat: 49], in that the object of wonder is despair and hopelessness. The mention of "tasting" (*idhāqah*) has already preceded.

*Qunut* means despair. It was mentioned earlier in Surat al-Hijr at His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So do not be of those who despair﴾ [al-Hijr: 55].

Woven into the reproach against them is His saying ﴿because of what their hands have sent forth﴾, to alert them that the evil condition that befalls them in this world is caused by their own actions, which Allah has made into causes for effects that are influential, and of whose secrets and fine details none encompasses knowledge except Allah, Exalted is He. Therefore, people should do nothing but take account of themselves and examine the causes of the befalling of evils, and make amends for what has passed. That is more effective in saving them from evils and more fitting than despair. This is a noble etiquette (*adab*) of the revelation. Allah, Exalted is He, said: ﴿Whatever good befalls you is from Allah, and whatever evil befalls you is from yourself﴾ [an-Nisa': 79].

The majority of reciters (*al-jumhur*) read *yaqnatūna* with a *fatḥah* on the *nūn*, as the imperfect of *qanita*, of the pattern *ḥasiba*. Abu 'Amr and al-Kisa'i read it with a *kasrah* on the *nūn*, as the imperfect of *qanata*, of the pattern *ḍaraba*. Both are dialectal forms of the same verb.

Then He reproached them for neglecting to reflect on the widespread custom (*sunnah*) of Allah among people: the touching of harm and its removal, and the apportioning of shares of provision between expansion and restriction. This occurs very frequently at all times. Just as they did not despair of the expansion of provision upon them in times of its restriction, and they strove to seek provision through means and supplication, so too it was their duty to meet rare misfortune with the same response they give to narrowness of provision. They should strive to remove evil through repentance, supplication to Allah, and pursuing the means of its removal among the means that Allah, Exalted is He, has established. Accordingly, the clause ﴿Have they not seen that Allah extends provision﴾, and so on, is coordinated (*'atf*) with the clause ﴿And when We let people taste mercy, they rejoice in it﴾.

The interrogative is rhetorical (*istifham inkari*), carrying the sense of negation. He reproached them for not seeing, treating their seeing of this as though it were not seeing, since they neglected its effects as lessons. The sense is: when they despair, how is it that they have not seen Allah's extending and restricting of provision, as if they had not seen it?

The seeing here is visual (*basariyyah*). The clause ﴿Indeed in that are signs for a people who believe﴾ is a concluding statement (*tadhyil*), meaning that in all that has been mentioned there are many signs. Their multiplicity arises from the fact that each of these conditions contains causes, hidden and apparent, and their effects likewise, and from the variety of people's conditions, in terms of the lessons drawn from them and the benefit taken from them, each according to his readiness.

The believing people were singled out for this because they have the deepest insight, owing to what their souls have been trained in from the etiquette of faith, and from their directing themselves to seek knowledge and wisdom from the sciences of religion and the wisdom of prophethood.

The conjunctive *fa'* (*fa' al-tafri'*, indicating that what follows is a consequence of what precedes) shows that the statement after it follows from the statement before it. The preceding discourse covered the reach of God's mercy to people, the affliction of harm that befalls them, the fact that the harm they suffer is due to what human hands have earned, and the mention of the expansion and restriction of provision. This implied that rejoicing distracts people from gratitude, and that despair distracts them from examining the causes (of their situation). Therefore the command to give to the weak and the afflicted was guidance toward the means of thanking God for a blessing when it is received, by giving thanks of the same kind, and toward removing harm when it descends. It also points out that it is a right of the one who is constrained in provision to be given a measure of expansion, just as one loves to have one's own provision expanded. Thus the address with the command is to the Prophet ﷺ, taking into account those believers with him who are obliged to give, and who are those whose provision has been expanded. That is, "So give the near of kin his right," as indicated by His words ﴿That is better for those who desire the Face of God﴾, and so on. It is also possible that the address is to an unspecified group of believers.

*Al-iytā'* (giving) means bestowing. It implies that what is given is wealth, and this is reinforced by the verse coming directly after His words ﴿Do they not see that God extends provision to whom He wills?﴾ [al-Rum: 37]. The form of the imperative in *fa-ātī* is general. Its original sense is obligation, although the one to be given is described as having a "right" (*haqq*), and the original meaning of *haqq* is obligation. The apparent meaning of the verse requires that the intended right is a right in the wealth of the giver.

From Mujahid and Qatadah: maintaining ties of kinship (i.e., with wealth) is an obligation from God, the Mighty and Majestic; a person's charity is not accepted while his kin are in need. Al-Hasan said: the right of the near of kin is consolation in ease, and a kind word in hardship. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: the main purpose is the command to help with wealth, and from it is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ, "In wealth there is a right besides zakat," and the needy and the wayfarer have a right, and it is clear that the right of these two is in wealth. End of quote. I say: for this reason a large group said that this verse has been abrogated (*mansukh*, i.e., subject to *naskh*, abrogation) by the verse of inheritance. A group said: it has not been abrogated; rather, the near of kin have a right in piety in every situation. That is, there is no abrogation in all that it contains; rather, some of it was abrogated by the verse of inheritance and what remains other than that stands. I say: what remains unabrogated has rulings that differ, and it is a general (*mujmal*) statement, which other scattered evidences from the Shari'ah clarify.

*Al-qurbā*: nearness of lineage and kinship. It was mentioned earlier at His words ﴿and the neighbour who is near of kin﴾ [al-Nisa': 36] in Surat al-Nisa'.

*Al-miskīn* was mentioned earlier at His words ﴿for the poor and the needy﴾ [al-Tawbah: 60] in Surat al-Tawbah.

*Ibn al-sabīl*: the traveller passing through the town or the quarter.

The right was stated in general terms, and the reference for its explanation is to what is customary among people and to what the Prophet ﷺ explained. Charity before the Hijrah was obligatory in general terms, left to the eagerness of the believer. It was called *zakāh* in many Meccan verses and was paired with prayer; so what is meant by it in those verses is obligatory charity. It was not restricted by a *nisab* at first, then it was specified by categories, a *nisab* and fixed amounts to be paid. Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may God be pleased with him, said: "Indeed, zakat is the right of wealth." It was specified after the Hijrah, so that what other than it of charity became non-obligatory, and the name *zakāh* was restricted to the obligatory, while the name *ṣadaqah*, or *birr*, or the like, was applied to what else. Thus the sum of the right of these three is the consolation (*muwāsāh*) with wealth, which indicates that this is obligatory for them. This was in the early period of Islam, then it was abrogated by the imposition of zakat. Then, each of these three categories has its own right: the right of the near of kin differs according to his need; for the wealthy there is his right in giving gifts out of affection, and for the one in need there is a stronger right. The apparent meaning is that the intended one is the near of kin who is poor in wealth, whose poverty has not reached the level of destitution, by the indication of the expression "right" for him, and by the indication of contrasting him with His words ﴿so that it may increase in the wealth of people﴾ [al-Rum: 39], according to one of the possible interpretations of it. As for giving to a wealthy relative, it is perhaps not intended here, and it is not something covered by the word "his right"; rather, it enters into good dealing, which is encouraged.

The right of the needy: meeting his need. The right of the wayfarer: hospitality, as in the hadith, "His reward is a day and a night." The aim is to nullify the custom of the people of ignorance, who preferred the distant over the near in gifts and bequests out of love for praise, and gave their gifts to chiefs and people of reputation seeking closeness to them. So the Muslims were commanded to avoid this. He, may He be exalted, said ﴿It is prescribed for you, when death approaches one of you, if he leaves goods, that he make a bequest to parents and the near of kin in fairness﴾ [al-Baqarah: 180], as mentioned earlier in Surat al-Baqarah.

For this reason He followed with His words here, ﴿That is better for those who desire the Face of God﴾, meaning those who intend by their gifts to seek God's pleasure and to obtain His reward, and they are the believers.

The reference in His words "That is better" is to the giving derived from His words ﴿So give the near of kin his right﴾, and so on.

The mention of "the Face" here is a figure of speech (*tamthīl*), as if the giver gave the wealth in the sight of God, because the face is the place of regard. Also there is in it a *mushākalah taqdīriyyah* (an implicit correspondence), because this command was intended to contrast with what the people of ignorance did in giving for the sake of the faces of notable people of the tribe; so here giving is made for the Face of God, and what is meant is that it is for the sake of carrying out His command and obtaining His pleasure.

The demonstrative in His words "That is better" serves to draw attention to what is commanded. "Better" (*khayr*) may be a comparative, and the thing compared against is understood from the context: that this is better than the conduct of the people of ignorance who give to distant wealthy people for show and reputation; or what is meant is that this is better than spending wealth in usury, which is mentioned after it in His words ﴿and whatever you give in usury﴾ [al-Rum: 39], and so on.

It is also possible that "good" (*khayr*) is the opposite of evil, meaning that there is good in this for the believers, which is God's reward.

In His words "and those are the successful" there is a restrictive construction (*qaṣr*) by means of the pronoun of separation (*ḍamīr al-faṣl*), and it is a relative restriction (*qaṣr iḍāfī*), meaning: those are the ones uniquely attaining success, which is the success of their deed in giving mentioned for the sake of God, the Exalted, not for show and boasting. So whoever gives for show and boasting, there is no success for him from his giving.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 30, verse 39:**

﴿And whatever you give in usury so that it may increase within the wealth of people, it does not increase with Allah. And whatever you give in zakah (obligatory almsgiving), seeking the Face of Allah, those are the ones who receive multiplied reward.﴾

When the commentary had encouraged and commanded the spending of wealth on those in need and on maintaining ties of kinship, and on what success lies in that, it followed this with a warning against another kind of giving of wealth that Allah does not accept. Usury (ribā) was widespread in the time of jahiliyyah (the age of ignorance) and at the beginning of Islam, especially among the Thaqif and the Quraysh. When Allah guided the Muslims to comfort their wealthy toward their poor, He followed this by preparing their souls to refrain from dealing in usury with those among them who borrowed, for dealing in usury contradicts comforting others, since the state of the borrower is one of need, and the state of the lender is one of wealth. So dealing with the borrower through usury is preying on his need and exploiting his distress, and that is not fitting for the believers.

The "mā" (whatever) is conditional and conveys generality, so the sentence is parenthetical after the sentence ﴿So give the relative his right﴾ [al-Rum: 38], etc. The waw is parenthetical (i'tirādiyyah). The meaning of this sentence is equivalent to a qualification (istidrāk), to draw attention to giving wealth that is blameworthy. The sentence was put in conditional form because it is more suitable to the sense of istidrāk over the preceding speech. So the address is to the Muslims who seek the Face of Allah, who used to lend at interest before it was prohibited.

The meaning of "ātaytum" is: some of you gave to others, because giving (ītā') requires a giver and a taker.

His saying (﴿to increase within the wealth of people﴾) is addressed to the party that takes.

"Li-turbū" means: so that you may increase, that is, so that you acquire wealth for yourselves over your wealth. His saying ﴿within the wealth of people﴾: "fī" is for the figurative sense of place, with the meaning of "min" (from) of origin, that is, so that you obtain increase and profits that come to you from the wealth of people. So the particle "fī" here is like that in the verse of Sabra al-Faqa'si:

*"And we drink from their prices and gamble"*

That is: we drink and gamble from the prices of our camels. Its explanation was already mentioned at His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and provide for them therein and clothe them﴾ [al-Nisa': 5] in Surat al-Nisa'.

The "min" in His saying "min ribā" and His saying "min zakāh" is explanatory (bayāniyyah), clarifying the vagueness of the conditional "mā" in both places. Ribā was already discussed in Surat al-Baqarah.

His saying ﴿it does not increase with Allah﴾ is the response of the condition. The meaning of ﴿it does not increase with Allah﴾ is that it is a deed deficient with Allah, not that which is with Him, and deficiency is used as a metaphor for blame and belittlement.

This interpretation is the one that fits the literal and well-known meaning of the word ribā, and agrees with the meaning of His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Allah destroys usury and makes charities grow﴾ [al-Baqarah: 276], and with the appropriateness of mentioning multiplication in His saying here ﴿those are the ones who receive multiplied reward﴾ and His saying ﴿Do not consume usury, doubled and redoubled﴾ [Al 'Imran: 130] in Surat Al 'Imran. This meaning is narrated from al-Suddi and al-Hasan, and the meaning has been made sound by this explanation from the standpoint of Arabic grammar regarding the sense of "fī" in His saying ﴿within the wealth of people﴾.

It is also possible that the word "ribā" in the verse is applied to an increase in the wealth of another, that is, giving wealth to people of wealth intending to increase their wealth, drawing near to them, so it includes the gift for reward (hibat al-thawāb) and the gift for nearness and flattery. The purpose of the verse would be to draw attention to the fact that what they used to do of that kind does not avail them anything in gaining the pleasure of Allah, exalted is He; its benefit is only for themselves. A large multitude of exegetes followed this meaning, so the meaning becomes: "And whatever increase you give in order that you may increase within the wealth of people," and the phrase "li-turbū" becomes a verbal emphasis so that "within the wealth of people" may be connected to it.

His saying ﴿And whatever you give in zakah﴾ and so on refers back to His saying ﴿So give the relative his right﴾ [al-Rum: 38], the verse, because that right is what is named zakah.

The clause ﴿those are the ones who receive multiplied reward﴾ is the response to ﴿And whatever you give in zakah﴾, that is: those who give it are the ones who receive multiplication, that is, those for whom multiplication has occurred, which is the multiplication of reward. The separating pronoun (ḍamīr al-faṣl, "hum") designates those who multiply, specifically these, and it is a restriction of a claimed kind for emphasis, because the multiplication of others is not regarded, since their multiplication is a worldly, transient multiplication.

The demonstrative in His saying ﴿so those are the ones who receive multiplied reward﴾ is for honouring these people and indicating that they are deserving of success. The demonstrative is an explicit noun in the place where a pronoun would be expected, as required by the context that calls for the use of the demonstrative.

Al-Jumhur (the majority of reciters) read "ātaytum" with two hamzas, meaning "you gave." Ibn Kathir read "atītum" with one hamza, meaning "you intended," that is, "you did."

Al-Jumhur read "li-yarbuwa" with a yā' vowelled with fatha and a fatha of case-ending (i'rab) on the waw of "li-yarbuwa." It is written in the codices with an alif after the waw, and it is not the waw of the plural by consensus, and the orthography of the codex is a sunnah. Nafi' read "li-turbū" with the second-person taʾ vowelled with ḍamma and a silent waw, which is the waw of the plural.

This resumptive clause (*isti'naf*, a new sentence that picks up the argument) is the second of the four in which the proofs are set out that God alone acts over people, and it refutes their claim of associating partners in divinity, as his words **"Are there any of your associates who does any of that?"** indicate. It also incidentally serves as evidence for the occurrence of resurrection.

This clause follows the pattern of his words, **"God originates creation, then brings it back"** (Q. 30:11). The opening with a similar phrase recurs in the verses intended to establish the resurrection, as was noted earlier at his words, **"God originates creation, then brings it back"** (Q. 30:11). It will also come in the two verses after this one.

**Thumma** (ثُمَّ) is used with both meanings: temporal sequence (*al-tarakhi al-zamani*) and sequence of rank (*al-rutbi*).

**"Are there any of your associates who does any of that?"** is an interrogative of denial (*istifham inkari*), meaning negation. For this reason **min** (مِنْ) was added, which indicates the strengthening of the negation of the whole category in his words **"any"** (مِن شَيْءٍ). The meaning is: none of your associates does any of that.

The first **min** (مِنْ) in **"any of your associates"** is explanatory (*bayaniyya*), clarifying the vagueness in **man** (مَنْ, "who") in **"who does"**, so that **man yaf'alu** is the subject, and its predicate is omitted, indicated by the interrogative, with the estimate: "exists" or "is found". Or it is partitive (*tab'idiyya*), describing an omitted noun, meaning: "Is there anyone of your associates?"

The second **min** (مِنْ) in his words **"of that"** (مِن ذَلِكُم) is partitive, in the position of a circumstantial qualifier (*hal*) for **shay'** (شَيْءٍ). The third **min** (مِنْ) is superfluous, for the comprehensive negation.

The attribution of **"associates"** (شُرَكَاءَ) to the pronoun of the addressees, who are polytheists, is because the addressees are those who ascribed to the idols the description of "partners" of God. Thus they were partners according to the addressees' claim, but they were not partners in reality. This works as sarcasm (*tahakkum*), like the words of Khalid ibn al-Sa'q to 'Amr ibn Ma'dikarib in one of the Arab assemblies on the outskirts of Kufa, when 'Amr began to tell them about his raids. He claimed that he had raided the tribe of Nahd, so they went out against him, led by Khalid ibn al-Sa'q, and that he had killed him. Khalid ibn al-Sa'q said to him: "Gently, Abu Thawr, your slain man is listening," meaning the slain man according to your claim. The indicator is his words **"is listening"**, just as the indicator in this verse is the clause declaring God free of any partner.

The demonstrative **"that"** (ذَلِكُم) refers to creation, provision, causing death, and giving life, which are the verbal nouns of the verbs mentioned. The demonstrative was singular in form, in view of the interpretation of "what has been mentioned."

The clause **"Glory be to Him, and exalted is He above what they associate"** is a new sentence (*mustaanifa*) that establishes the declaration of God's transcendence above a partner in divinity. Its position after the two preceding clauses is that of a conclusion after a syllogism (*qiyas*). The sense of the first clause is that the true God, who is the referent of the Name of Majesty (Allah), is the one who creates, provides, causes death and gives life. This amounts to a premise, the minor premise (*sughra*) of a syllogism. The sense of the second clause is that none of the idols does any of that, and this amounts to the major premise (*kubra*) of the syllogism, which is of the second figure (*shakl*). The sense of the declaration of God's transcendence above a partner is that none of the idols is a god. This is the conclusion of a syllogism of the second figure.

The evidence for the minor premise is the opponent's acknowledgment, and the evidence for the major premise is reason.

The majority of readers read **"they associate"** (تُشْرِكُونَ) with the second person (ta), following the address in **"you have given"** (آتَيْتُمْ). Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read it with the third person (ya), as an iltifat (shift) from address to the third person.

﴿Corruption has appeared on land and sea by what the hands of people have earned, that He may let them taste part of what they have done, so that they may return.﴾

The placement and meaning of this verse admit of several aspects of admonition, and it is one of the comprehensive expressions of the Qur'an. Its purpose is to admonish through events, past and present, so that people refrain from associating partners with God and from denying the Messenger (ﷺ). As for its placement, it may be connected to His saying before it: ﴿Have they not traveled through the earth and seen how was the end of those before them?﴾ [Fatir: 44], and the verses that follow. When they were called upon to acknowledge what they had seen of the traces of the earlier nations, or when their failure to reflect upon those traces was rebuked, this was followed by what the path of admonition leads to, namely His saying: ﴿Allah originates creation, then repeats it﴾ [al-Rum: 11], and by mention of the warning of the punishment of the Hereafter, the reminder of the proofs of God's oneness and of His blessings, and the derivation from this of His right to be thanked, both for His essence and for His bestowals, a right whose recognition is firmly established in human nature. Between these, there was guidance and admonition. Then the discourse returned to reminding that the calamities that befell the earlier nations were only because of what their hands had earned, that is, because of their deeds. Thus it is near that the like of what befell them will befall those addressed, whose hands have earned the like of what those [earlier] hands earned.

Accordingly, the placement of this sentence on this aspect is that of a conclusion drawn from the whole argument, or that of an explanatory resumption (al-isti'naf al-bayani), assuming a question about the cause of what befell those nations.

It is also permissible for this verse to stand as a completion of His saying: ﴿And when harm touches people, they call upon their Lord﴾ [al-Rum: 33], and what follows. It is then a statement used to express regret over the harm that befell the deniers who are addressed, so that they may know that this is a punishment from God, and thus desist from it, out of fear that something even worse will overtake them, as His saying after it, ﴿so that they may return﴾, indicates. The use of the word "people" in His saying ﴿by what the hands of people have earned﴾ is an explicit noun in place of a pronoun, for the sake of further clarifying the intended meaning. The expected form would have been "by what their hands have earned." The verse points to calamities that befell the lands of the polytheists and disabled their benefits. Perhaps they arose from the war between the Romans and Persians, and the Arabs were divided between the supporters of these and the supporters of those. As a result, the routes of travel by land and sea were cut off, trade was disrupted, and the provisions became scarce in Makkah and the Hijaz, as the context of this admonition in this surah, which opens with ﴿The Romans have been defeated﴾ [al-Rum: 2], suggests.

[Page 110]

Accordingly, the placement of this sentence on this aspect is that of an explanatory resumption concerning the cause of the harm that touched them, to the point that they resorted to supplication to God. What lies between it and the sentence ﴿And when harm touches people﴾ [al-Rum: 33] to its end is a parenthetical insertion (i'tiradh) and digression (istitrad) that came between.

It is also possible that its placement is that of a parenthetical insertion between the mention of people's supplication to God when harm surrounds them, then their turning away from worshipping Him when He lets them taste mercy from Him, and the mention of what befell the earlier nations. This insertion indicates that the corruption that appears in the world is only the result of people's earning, and that if they had been upright, their condition would have been one of goodness.

Corruption (al-fasad) is bad condition, the opposite of goodness (al-salah). His saying ﴿on land and sea﴾ indicates that it is bad condition in what people benefit from among the bounties of the earth, on its land and its sea.

Then the definiteness in "corruption" (al-fasad) is either the definiteness of anaphora (ta'rif al-'ahd), referring to a known corruption among those addressed, or the definiteness of the genus (ta'rif al-jins), encompassing every corruption that appeared on the earth, land and sea, as corruption in the conditions of land and sea, not in the deeds of people, as indicated by His saying ﴿that He may let them taste part of what they have done, so that they may return﴾.

The corruption of the land occurs through the loss of its benefits and the occurrence of its harms, such as the withholding of provisions from crops, fruits and pasture, the death of livestock that are useful, the migration of game animals that are hunted because of the drought of the land to other lands, and the occurrence of calamities such as locusts, insects and diseases.

The corruption of the sea likewise appears in the disabling of its benefits: the scarcity of fish, pearls and coral (and these two were among the greatest resources of the lands of the Arabs), the abundance of storms that prevent sea voyages, the drying up of rivers' waters, and the cessation of their floods by which people draw water. It has been said: by "land" is meant the desert dwellers and those in the deep interior, and by "sea" are meant cities and villages. This is from Mujahid and 'Ikrimah, who said: the Arabs call the cities "sea." It has been said that from this is the saying of Sa'd ibn 'Ubadah concerning 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul: "The people of this sea have agreed to crown him." [Page 111] By "the sea" (al-bahrah) he means the city of Yathrib, and this is far-fetched.

It seems that what prompted adopting this aspect in the application of "sea" is that he did not know that there had occurred a disruption in people's travel by sea and a scarcity of what comes out of it. The historians have mentioned that the Quraysh were struck by famine and ate carrion and bones, but they did not mention that their sea voyages were disabled, nor that the fish of the sea were cut off from them, especially since they were not known to subsist on fish.

On these three aspects, the bāʾ in His saying ﴿by what the hands of people have earned﴾ is for compensation (lil-'iwad), meaning as a recompense for them for their deeds, like the bāʾ in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And whatever affliction befalls you is because of what your hands have earned﴾, and the lām in His saying ﴿that He may let them taste﴾ is in its literal sense of causation (al-ta'lil).

It is also possible that the intended meaning of corruption is polytheism (al-shirk), as said by Qatadah and al-Suddi. Then this verse is connected to His saying ﴿Allah is the One who created you, then provided for you﴾ [al-Rum: 40], up to His saying ﴿Is there any of your partners who does anything of that?﴾ [al-Rum: 40]. The sentence then completes the argument for the oneness of God, exalted is He, drawing attention to the fact that God created the world sound, free from associating partners with Him, and that polytheism appeared through what the hands of people have earned of their own handiwork. This is the meaning of His saying in the sacred hadith in Sahih Muslim: "I created My servants as upright monotheists (hunafa'), all of them, and the devils came to them and turned them away from their religion and commanded them to associate others with Me." The hadith continues.

Thus, the mention of land and sea is for generalizing the directions, meaning: corruption appeared in all regions, those on the land and those on the islands and shores. The bāʾ in His saying ﴿by what the hands of people have earned﴾ is then causal (lil-sababiyyah), and the lām in His saying ﴿that He may let them taste part of what they have done﴾ is the lām of consequence (lam al-'aqibah), and the meaning is: "So We let them taste part of what they did." The lām of consequence is placed in the position of the fa' (so/then), as in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Then the people of Pharaoh picked him up, so that he might become for them an enemy and a grief﴾ [al-Qasas: 8], meaning: "So We let those who associated partners taste some of the punishment they deserved for their polytheism."

It is also possible that the meaning is that God, exalted is He, created the world in a firm, harmonious order suitable and good for people, and then human beings introduced into it evil and corrupting deeds, and these became seeds (wushuj) for their like:

"Does the spear-wood grow except from its own shaft?"

[Page 112]

Thus disorder began to penetrate the order of the world. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿We created man in the best of forms, then We returned him to the lowest of the low, except those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾ [al-Tin: 4]. On this aspect, the meaning of the bāʾ and of the lām is like their meaning on the fourth aspect.

The word "appeared" (zahara) has been used for the occurrence of an event that had not been, and that occurrence after non-existence was likened to the appearance of a thing that had been hidden.

The form of the verb "appeared" (zahara), if it is taken in its literal sense of the past tense, requires that the corruption has occurred and is not future. It is then an indication of a corruption that is witnessed or certain to occur by widely transmitted reports. The past form may also be understood as the expectation of the occurrence of corruption and a warning of it, so that it is as though it had already happened, in the manner of His saying ﴿The command of Allah has come﴾ [al-Nahl: 1].

Whether the corruption is the known one or the general one, the intended meaning is that its coming upon people is by the power of God, as His saying ﴿that He may let them taste part of what they have done﴾ indicates, and that God determines its causes with a particular determination, in order to requite those with whom He is angry for their evil deeds.

This is the intended meaning of "what their hands have earned," because the attribution of earning to the hands has become a proverbial expression for evil and bad deeds of all kinds, not specifically for what is done by the hands, since what people earn is by all the outward limbs and by the inner senses, including misguided beliefs and psychological ailments.

The "mā" is a relative pronoun (mawsulah), and the returning pronoun from the relative clause has been omitted. Its estimated form is: "by what the hands of people have earned [of it]," meaning: because of their deeds. The greatest of what the hands of people have earned of evil deeds is polytheism, and it is the one intended here, although the ruling is general. It is known that the degrees of the appearance of corruption are proportionate to what the hands of people have earned. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) was asked: "Which sin is greatest?" He said: "That you set up a rival to God while He created you." God, exalted is He, also said: ﴿And whatever affliction befalls you, it is because of what your hands have earned﴾ [al-Shura: 30], and He said: ﴿And that if they had remained upright on the way, We would have given them abundant water﴾ [al-Jinn: 16].

The ruling on the definiteness of "people" follows the same pattern as the definiteness of "corruption," whether of anaphora or generality. The known ones are the polytheists, and it has become widespread in the Qur'an that the term "people" is applied predominantly to them.

[Page 113]

The word "tasting" (al-idhaqah) is a implicit metaphor (isti'arah makniyyah): it likens the pains that befall them, which they feel, to food reaching the sense of taste.

Since what they did does not befall them in its very form, it is determined that "part of what they did" refers to the recompense for the deed. Accordingly, the partitive (al-ba'diyyah) is partitive of the recompense: the intended meaning is part of the recompense for the entire deed, not the recompense for part of the deed. That is, what He makes them taste of the punishment is part of what they deserve.

In this there is a threat, should they not desist from the evils of their deeds, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if Allah were to seize people for what they have earned, He would not leave upon its back a single creature﴾ [Fatir: 45]. Beyond that is the punishment of the Hereafter, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And the punishment of the Hereafter is more severe and more lasting﴾ [Ta-Ha: 127].

The shift from saying "some of their deeds" to ﴿part of what they did﴾ is to indicate, through the relative clause, the force of definiteness: that is, their deeds that are known to them, whose performance has been firmly established.

The hope conveyed by "la'alla" (so that perhaps) indicates that the corruption that has appeared is sufficient to make them desist from what they have earned, and that their condition is that of one whose return is hoped for. If they do not return, then their rebellion and the failure of admonition with them have become clear. This is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Do they not see that they are tested every year once or twice, and yet they do not repent, nor do they take heed?﴾ [al-Tawbah: 126].

The word "return" (al-ruju') is used metaphorically for desisting from sins, as though the one who disobeys his Lord were a slave who has run away from his master, or an animal that has strayed and then returned. In the hadith: "God is more delighted at the repentance of His servant than a man who stopped at a place where there was destruction, with his riding-beast carrying his food and drink. He placed his head and slept a sleep, then woke up and his riding-beast had gone. When the heat and thirst grew intense upon him, or as God willed, he said: 'I will return to my place.' He returned and slept a sleep, then raised his head, and there was his beast with him."

The majority of reciters read ﴿li-yudhiqahum﴾ with the yā' (third person), meaning "that God may let them taste." The referent of the pronoun is His saying ﴿Allah is the One who created you﴾ [al-Rum: 40]. Qunbul, from Ibn Kathir, and Rawh, from 'Asim, read it with the nun of majesty (nun al-'azamah), meaning "that We may let them taste."

[Page 114]

Say: "Travel through the earth and see how was the end of those before you, most of whom were polytheists." When He had admonished them with what had befallen them of corrupted conditions, and alerted them that this was only part of the requital for what their hands had earned, He turned to warning them of a greater corruption, one like which might befall them, namely what befell those before them because of their being in a state similar to that of these people in associating partners with God. So He commanded them to travel through the earth and reflect on the fate of the nations that associated partners with God and denied the truth, such as 'Ad, Thamud, the people of Lot, and others. This is because many of the polytheists had passed by the abodes of those nations during their journeys, as the Exalted said: ﴿And indeed you pass by them in the morning and at night. Will you not then reason?﴾ [al-Saffat: 137].

This is a repetition and emphasis of His earlier words: ﴿Have they not travelled through the earth and seen how was the end of those before them?﴾ [al-Rum: 9]. It was repeated out of concern for this lesson, together with the connection to His words: ﴿that He may make them taste some of what they did﴾ [al-Rum: 41]. The "end" (al-'aqibah) is the final outcome of a matter. The term "al-'aqibah" here denotes a genus, which takes multiple instances according to the multiplicity of "those before them," and each people has its own end.

The clause ﴿most of whom were polytheists﴾ stands in the position of a causal clause (ta'lil) for the clause ﴿how was the end of those before them﴾. That is, the cause of that observed end is the association of partners by most of them. In other words, most of those nations whose dreadful end was witnessed were among the people of association. So you know that the cause of that end befalling them was their polytheism. Yet some of those nations were not polytheists, but what befell them was due to their denial of their messengers, such as the people of Madyan. The Exalted said: ﴿Are your disbelievers better than those?﴾ [al-Qamar: 43].

[Page 115]

Following the warning and admonition against the consequences of polytheism comes the affirmation of the Messenger (ﷺ) in his law, and a promise that victory will come to him, like His saying ﴿And worship your Lord until certainty comes to you﴾ [al-Hijr: 99], with an allusion to guidance toward deliverance from polytheism by following the upright religion, i.e., the truth. This is an emphasis on the command to set one's face toward the religion in His saying ﴿So set your face toward the religion as a ḥanīf﴾ [al-Rum: 30]. When that was followed in His saying ﴿Have they not travelled in the land and seen how was the end of those before them?﴾ [al-Rum: 9], and with what was connected to the sequence of proofs and admonitions, this was likewise followed by its counterpart, upon His saying ﴿Say: Travel through the land and see how was the end of those before﴾ [al-Rum: 42]. The discussion of the counterpart of His saying ﴿So set your face toward the religion﴾, and of the meaning of setting the face, has already preceded at His saying ﴿So set your face toward the religion as a ḥanīf﴾ [al-Rum: 30].

"Al-qayyim" is on the pattern fayʻil, a form which indicates the intensity of what is derived from it, i.e., one whose standing is firm. Here "standing" (qiyām) is used metaphorically for correctness, since rightness is likened to standing upright, and its opposite is likened to crookedness. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and He did not make for it any crookedness, but made it straight (qayyim)﴾ [al-Kahf: 1] combines both. Thus Islam is described in the previous verse as ḥanīf and as the fiṭrah, and here it is described as al-qayyim. Between "aqim" and "al-qiyam" there is a paronomasia (jinās), a beautifying figure.

The address to the Prophet (ﷺ) with this command is a turning away from the explicit address to the polytheists. The intended meaning is an allusion that they have deprived themselves of following this great religion, in which lies salvation. This allusion is drawn from the command to the Prophet, upon him be blessings and peace, to persist in Islam, and from His saying after it ﴿On that day they will be divided﴾, and so on.

"Al-maradd" is a mimi verbal noun from "al-radd", which means repelling. "Lahu" is connected to it. "Min Allāh" is connected to "ya'tī", and "min" is inceptive (ibtidā'iyyah). The day intended is a day of punishment in this world, and that when it comes, no repeller will turn it back from those it is due upon, because it comes from God. The apparent meaning is that the day intended is the Day of Badr.

"Yaṣṣaddaʻūn" originally was "yataṣaddaʻūn", and the tā' was changed to ṣād because their points of articulation are close, so that assimilation (idghām) could produce lightening. "Al-tasaddu'" is the reflexive (muṭāwaʻ) of "al-ṣadʻ", and the literal sense of "al-ṣadʻ" is breaking and splitting, from which comes "tasaddaʻa al-qadah" (the cup cracked).

The day intended is the Day of Gathering. "Al-tasaddu'" means dispersal and separation. The plural pronoun may refer to all people, meaning: on that day the believers will be separated from the disbelievers, in the manner of His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And on the day the Hour is established, on that day they will be divided. As for those who believed and did righteous deeds, they will be in a meadow, made joyful. And as for those who disbelieved and denied Our signs and the meeting of the Hereafter, those will be in punishment, brought forth﴾ [al-Rum: 14].

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 30, verse 44–45:

[Page 116]
﴿Whoever disbelieves, upon him is his disbelief; and whoever does righteousness, for themselves they prepare [the way].﴾ ﴿That He may reward those who believed and did righteous deeds out of His bounty. Indeed, He does not love the disbelievers.﴾

This sentence serves as an explanation (bayan) of the general statement preceding it, which is ﴿So direct your face toward the upright religion﴾ [al-Rum: 43]. Since affirming upon the religion after mentioning the corruption that befell the polytheists because of their association (shirk) implies belittling their status before the Messenger (ﷺ) and the believers, He clarified that by saying that they harm no one by their disbelief except themselves. What reveals this meaning is the fronting of the predicate in His words ﴿upon him is his disbelief﴾, for it indicates restricting it to the subject, i.e., his disbelief is upon him and not upon you nor upon the believers. For this reason, the discussion begins with the state of whoever disbelieves, then mentions after it whoever does righteousness. The particle ʿalā (upon), a particle of elevation, implies that in disbelief there is consequence, severity, and harm upon the disbeliever, because ʿalā requires that in such a context, just as the lam in His words ﴿for themselves they prepare﴾ implies that its object (majrur) has benefit and gain. Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 30, verse 46:

﴿And among His signs is that He sends the winds as bearers of good news, and that He may let you taste of His mercy, and that the ships may sail by His command, and that you may seek of His bounty, and perhaps you will be grateful.﴾

This returns to the enumeration of the signs that indicate His singularity in divinity. It is a conjunction (ʿatf) to the preceding sentence, "And among His signs is that the heavens and the earth stand by His command," and to what lies between them of the various forms of argument for God's oneness and for resurrection, and of the methods of admonition, to refresh the attentiveness of the listeners to these clear and explicit proofs.

The "sending" (al-irsal) is used metaphorically for the arrangement of arrival, meaning that He determines the formation of the winds and their order, which directs them toward a land in need of rain.

Al-mubashshirat (the bearers of good news): those announcing good, which is rain. The root of bishara (good news) is a report that gladdens. The winds are likened to messengers dispatched with tidings of joy. The mention of bishara has already occurred in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And give good news to those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾ [al-Baqarah: 25] in Surat al-Baqarah, and His saying ﴿And when one of them is given good news of a female﴾ [al-Nahl: 58] in Surat al-Nahl, because the winds drive the rain-clouds to where they will rain.

The discussion of the winds has already preceded in many verses, among them His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and the turning of the winds﴾ [al-Baqarah: 164] in Surat al-Baqarah, and on their being fertilizing (lawaqih) in Surat al-Hijr.

His saying ﴿and that He may let you taste﴾ is conjoined (ʿatf) to "bearers of good news," because "bearers of good news" carries the sense of a reason (taʿlil) for the sending. The discussion of "taste" (al-idhaqa) has already preceded just above.

"Min rahmatihi" (of His mercy) is an adjective of an omitted noun indicated by the verb "liyudhiqakum," meaning: a thing tasted. The "min" is for origin (ibtida'iyya), and the mercy of God is the rain.

The sailing of ships by the winds is among the wisdom in the creation of the winds and among His blessings, and it has preceded in the verse of Surat al-Baqarah.

The restriction by His saying "by His command" serves as instruction for the believers and as affirmation of the favor: that is, were it not for God's decree of that and His making winds the causes of its occurrence, the ships would not sail. Beneath this are many meanings, gathered in God's inspiring humankind to build ships and to refine the means of their sailing. And He created the order of the wind and the sea to subject their course, as His saying "and perhaps you will be grateful" indicates. This has already preceded in Surat al-Hajj, and the meaning of "and that you may seek of His bounty" has already preceded there.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 30, verse 47:

﴿And We certainly sent before you messengers to their peoples, and they came to them with clear proofs. Then We took retribution against those who committed crime, and it was incumbent upon Us to help the believers.﴾

This is a parenthetical digression (jumlah i'tiradiyyah mustatradah), whose effect is the mention of the sailing of the ship (al-fulk) among the blessings. This is followed by what the sailing of the ship involved: a reminder of the punishment of the Flood upon the people of Noah, and of God's making the ship a means of salvation for Noah and his righteous people from the punishment of the Flood. Thus it is intended to warn the deniers from Quraysh that there might befall them what befell those who denied before them. In that punishment there was the victory of the believers, that is, the victory of the messengers and their followers. Do you not see the report of Noah's words, ﴿My Lord, help me, for they have denied me﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 26], in Surat al-Mu'minun, and His statement here, ﴿and it was incumbent upon Us to help the believers﴾?

The waw is parenthetical (i'tiradiyyah) and is not a conjunction (li-l-'atf).

Al-intiqam (retribution): it is of the form (ifti'al) from al-naqm, which is dislike and anger, and its verb is like daraba and 'alima. God said, ﴿And you do not resent us for anything﴾ [al-A'raf: 126]. In the proverb: "His example is like that of the black snake: if he is killed, he resents (yanqam, with a fatha on the qaf); and if he is left, he swallows (yalqam)." Al-intiqam is punishment for one who does what is displeasing, as if the form of ifti'al was formed from it to indicate the occurrence of the effect of resentment. It has already been discussed at His statement, ﴿And We took retribution against them﴾ [al-A'raf: 136], in Surat al-A'raf, and at His statement, ﴿and you do not resent us for anything﴾.

The phrase ﴿haqqan 'alayna﴾ is among the expressions of obligation. God said, quoting Moses, peace be upon him, (﴿It is incumbent upon me not to say about God except the truth﴾ [al-A'raf: 105]). One says "he is bound (mahquq) to such-and-such," meaning it is binding on him. Al-A'sha said:

Page 120

It is binding upon you (lamahquqatun) that you respond to his call, for the promise of the truthful is true.

God said, ﴿a promise upon Us; indeed We are ever doing it﴾ [al-Anbiya': 104].

The method of plainly expressing this purpose, namely the purpose of promising victory and threatening the opponent, has been abbreviated: the mention of victory includes the meaning of being victorious, and the mention of the two groups is incorporated, the group of those who affirm, who is promised, and the group of the deniers, who is threatened, though the speech was initially free of mention of both.

It is related from Abu Bakr Shu'bah, the narrator of 'Asim, that he would stop at His statement "haqqan," so that in "kana" there is a pronoun referring to retribution, meaning: "and the retribution against the criminals was just (haqqan), that is, fair," then he resumes with His statement ﴿'alayna nasr al-mu'minin﴾ [it is incumbent upon Us to help the believers]. It seems he intended to avoid the implication that servants have a right over God as an obligation, fleeing from the doctrine of the Mu'tazilah, though this is not necessary, as you know. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "This is a weak pause (waqf)," and al-Kawashi said likewise, citing Abu Hatim.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 30, verses 48–49:**

﴿It is Allah who sends the winds, so they stir up clouds, and He spreads them across the sky however He wills, and makes them into fragments, and you see the rain coming out from within them. Then when He causes it to reach whomever He wills of His servants, behold, they rejoice.﴾ ﴿And although they were, before it was sent down upon them, certainly in despair.﴾

This sentence comes in the same style as its counterparts, as was mentioned earlier in His words ﴿Allah originates creation, then repeats it﴾ [al-Rum: 11]. The context here is the argument from the sending of the winds in His words ﴿And among His signs is that He sends the winds as bearers of good news﴾ [al-Rum: 46]. It is an argument for His sole control over affairs and a depiction of wise craftsmanship that points to the breadth of His knowledge. Then the argument from the sending of the winds was followed by a bridge to mention the revival of the earth after its death, which is cited as evidence for the Resurrection. The restrictive form (al-hasr) in His words ﴿It is Allah who sends the winds﴾ conveys that He alone is the one who disposes of this wondrous matter, to the exclusion of anyone else. This suffices as a refutation of the divinity of idols, because they are unable to perform such an act, which is among the closest of acts to benefiting mankind.

The use of the present tense in "yursilu" (sends), "tuthiru" (stirs up), "yabsutuhu" (spreads it), and "yaj'aluhu" (makes it) serves to bring to mind the wondrous images of those acts, as though the listener were witnessing their formation, along with an indication that this recurs continually.

"al-Riyah" (the winds) is in the plural because of its common usage, where it is applied in the plural form to the wind that brings the good news of rain. The winds that stir up clouds are those blowing from different directions, among them the south wind, the north wind, the east wind and the west wind. This is unlike the singular "rih," which has come in usage to refer to a wind of force and intensity, because it arrives continuously from one direction and so keeps growing stronger. It is narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) used to say, when the wind blew: "O Allah, make it winds, not a wind." His words, may He be exalted, ﴿and the turning of the winds﴾ [al-Baqarah: 164] have already been mentioned in surah al-Baqarah.

"al-Ithara" (stirring up) means moving the dust so that it is set in motion away from its place. The stirring up of clouds means their creation by what the winds produce in the atmosphere of moisture, which arises from the interaction of heat and cold.

"al-Bast" (spreading) means dispersal. "al-sama'" (the sky) is the highest atmosphere, which is the atmosphere of clouds.

"Kayfa" (how) here is stripped of the meaning of interrogation, and its grammatical position is as an absolute object (al-maf'ul al-mutlaq) of "yabsutuhu," because it stands in place of the verbal noun. That is, He spreads it in a manner whose form Allah wills. This was mentioned in His words ﴿He is the One who forms you in the wombs however He wills﴾ [Al 'Imran: 6] in surah Al 'Imran. It was already noted that whoever claims that it is a conditional particle has not hit upon the correct view.

"Kisafan" (in fragments), read with a kasra then a fatha in the reading of the majority, is the plural of "kisf" (with a kasra then sukun), and it is said "kisfa" with the feminine ta', meaning a piece. It was mentioned in His words ﴿or cause the sky to fall upon us in fragments, as you claim﴾ [al-Isra: 92] in surah al-Isra, and "al-kisaf" was mentioned in His words ﴿so cause fragments of the sky to fall upon us, if you are of the truthful﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 187] in surah al-Shu'ara.

The meaning: because He spreads the clouds across the sky at one time, that is, He makes them extended and widespread in the atmosphere of the sky. This is the overcast cloud that darkens the atmosphere with it, and it is also called the closed cloud. And He makes them into fragments (that is, at another time), as the contrast indicates, that is, He makes them into scattered clouds, because the state of making them into fragments is other than the state of spreading them across the sky. Therefore it is necessary that the combination of the two in the mention be intended to convey the variation in the conditions of the clouds.

The purpose of this is that the variation in condition is a sign of the breadth of power.

The address in ﴿you see the rain﴾ is addressed to an unspecified person, namely everyone for whom it is possible to hear this and for whom it is possible to see the rain. "al-Wadq" is the rain.

The pronoun in "khilalihi" (from within it) refers to the clouds in their two mentioned states, namely the state of their being spread across the sky and the state of their being made into fragments, because the rain falls from between the closed cloud and the scattered clouds.

"al-Khilal" is the plural of "khalal" (with two fathas), which is the gap between two things. The likeness of this sentence was mentioned in surah al-Nur.

The mention of the variation in the conditions of the servants at the time the rain falls and at the time it is withheld, between rejoicing and despair, is an instance of "idmaj" (interweaving), serving as a reminder of Allah's mercy toward them and as a lesson regarding the variation in how their souls are affected in times of ease and hardship. In this there is an allusion to the great control of Allah over the creation of man, since He made him capable of varying in emotional response while his intellect and heart remain one, just as He made the clouds vary in their states, between spreading and fragmentation, while the act remains one, which is the emergence of the rain from within them.

In His words (wa in kanu) ("and although they were"), the "in" is the light (mukhaffafa) form of "inna," inactive in governing, and the "lam" in His words "lamubliseen" is the "lam al-fariqa" (the distinguishing lam) that separates the light "in" from the conditional "in."

"Al-iblas" is despair accompanied by brokenness. His words "min qablihi" (before it) are a repetition of His words ﴿before it was sent down upon them﴾, to emphasize the meaning of the prior occurrence of the rain's descent and to establish it in the minds of the listeners. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "The emphasis conveys the notice of how swiftly human hearts turn from despair to rejoicing." He means that the repetition of "min qablihi" is an added alert to the state that existed before the rain fell. And in al-Kashshaf he said: "In it is an indication that their experience of the rain had been prolonged, so their despair had become firmly established, and therefore their rejoicing was in proportion to their distress."

[p. 123]
He means that the benefit of repeating "min qablihi" is that the period before the rain fell was a long period, and its intensity is pointed out by the emphasis.

The pronoun in "qablihi" refers to the verbal noun derived from "an yunazzala 'alayhim" (that it be sent down upon them), that is, its sending down.
