In His words (wa in kanu) ("and although they were"), the "in" is the light (mukhaffafa) form of "inna," inactive in governing, and the "lam" in His words "lamubliseen" is the "lam al-fariqa" (the distinguishing lam) that separates the light "in" from the conditional "in."

"Al-iblas" is despair accompanied by brokenness. His words "min qablihi" (before it) are a repetition of His words ﴿before it was sent down upon them﴾, to emphasize the meaning of the prior occurrence of the rain's descent and to establish it in the minds of the listeners. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "The emphasis conveys the notice of how swiftly human hearts turn from despair to rejoicing." He means that the repetition of "min qablihi" is an added alert to the state that existed before the rain fell. And in al-Kashshaf he said: "In it is an indication that their experience of the rain had been prolonged, so their despair had become firmly established, and therefore their rejoicing was in proportion to their distress."

[p. 123]
He means that the benefit of repeating "min qablihi" is that the period before the rain fell was a long period, and its intensity is pointed out by the emphasis.

The pronoun in "qablihi" refers to the verbal noun derived from "an yunazzala 'alayhim" (that it be sent down upon them), that is, its sending down.

﴿So look at the traces of Allah's mercy, how He gives life to the earth after its death. Indeed, that is the One who gives life to the dead, and He is over all things Competent.﴾

This is placed as a consequence of what has been established concerning the imagining of the form of the formation of rain and the people's joy at its descent after their despair. It is introduced by the command to look at the trace of mercy and at Allah's relief of His servants when He gives life to the earth for them after its death through drought. The command to look is for taking a lesson (i'tibar) and for drawing inference (istidlal). Al-nazar (looking) means seeing with the eye.

He describes drought as death because the sustenance of life is moisture, and He describes its opposite as giving life. The address in "انظر" (look) is to an unspecified person, so that it includes everyone who is able to look, like His saying ﴿فترى الودق﴾ (you see the rain).

The mercy of Allah (rahmat Allah) is His attribute that relates to supplying His creatures who possess perception with what suits them and warding off from them what harms them, and that is bounty (in'am).

The trace (athar) of a thing is what arises from it and indicates it. Thus the mercy of Allah is indicated by the traces that point to His existence and His disposal in a way that contains mercy for creation. "كيف" (how) is either a substitute (badal) for "أثر" (trace) or an object of "انظر" (look), meaning: look at the condition of Allah's giving life to the earth after its death, that state which is one of the traces of His mercy. This is according to His saying ﴿أفلا ينظرون إلى الإبل كيف خلقت﴾ (Do they not look at the camels, how they were created?) [al-Ghashiyah: 17], where they made "كيف" a substitute for "الإبل" as a substitute of inclusion (badal al-ishtimal), although Ibn Hisham rejected this in Mughni al-Labib (a work on grammar). It has already passed at His saying ﴿ألم تر إلى ربك كيف مد الظل﴾ (Have you not seen how your Lord extended the shadow?) [al-Furqan: 45] in Surat al-Furqan, and it preceded just now in His saying ﴿فيبسطه في السماء كيف يشاء﴾ (and He spreads it in the sky however He wills) [al-Rum: 48]. The word "إحياء" (giving life) is applied to the earth's growth of vegetation, and "الموت" (death) to its barrenness, by way of metaphor (isti'arah).

The clause ﴿إن ذلك لمحيي الموتى﴾ (indeed, that is the One who gives life to the dead) is a resumptive new sentence (isti'naf), and it is an incorporation (idmaj) of the proof of resurrection right after the lesson drawn from the giving of life to the earth after its death. The emphatic particle, together with the affirmation of the statement, conveys an additional meaning of the "fa" of causation (fa' al-tasabbub), as in the saying of Bashshar:

بَكِّرا صاحِبَيَّ قَبْلَ الهَجِيرِ ... إنَّ ذاكَ النَّجاحَ في التَّبْكِيرِ

"Go early, my two companions, before the midday heat; indeed that success lies in early rising."

The implied sense is: "so success lies in early rising," as has been established more than once.

The demonstrative noun (ism al-isharah) refers back to the name of Allah, Exalted, with the report of His giving life to the earth after its death applied to Him, so that the demonstrative conveys the meaning that He is worthy of what follows after it of a statement about the one pointed to. The meaning is: the Allah who gives life to the earth after its death is indeed the One who gives life to the dead, bringing the concept of resurrection closer to the mind.

He turned away from the relative pronoun to the demonstrative for brevity, and because the demonstrative carries glorification. This is concluded with His saying ﴿وهو على كل شيء قدير﴾ (and He is over all things Competent), for it encompasses all things, and resurrection is among them, since it is nothing but bringing a creation into existence, which is within Allah's power, just as He originated creation the first time.

The resemblance is complete, because giving life to the earth is bringing into existence the like of what was on it of vegetation, and likewise giving life to the dead is bringing their like into existence.

Nafi', Ibn Kathir and Abu Bakr, from 'Asim, read ﴿إلى أثر﴾ (to the trace) in the singular. The rest read ﴿إلى آثار﴾ (to the traces) in the plural.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 30, verse 51:

﴿And if We send a wind and they see it turned yellow, they would surely continue to disbelieve after it.﴾

This is a conjunction (ʿatf) upon the clause ﴿And indeed, they were, before it was sent down to them, before that, utterly despairing﴾ [al-Rum: 49], and what lies between them is an interjection (i'tiraḍ) and a digression (istiṭrad) for a purpose you have already come to know. This clause is brought to alert that disbelief (kufran) is imprinted upon their souls, such that it returns to them by the slightest cause. So when blessing reaches them, they rejoice and do not give thanks; and when hardship reaches them, they hasten to disbelief. Thus their disbelief is depicted in the most striking image, namely their manifesting it right after the very thing they were rejoicing over, since the crop is green and the hope of sustenance from it is near; then a blight strikes it and it is burned, so they cry out because of that, and their state becomes the state of one who disbelieves in Allah, and expressions of wrath and despair flow from their tongues, as one of the rajaz poets of the Arabs said when a drought afflicted his people:

O Lord of the servants, what is between us and you?
You used to give us drink, but now what has become of you?
Send down upon us the rain, may you have no father!

Thus the pronoun in ﴿رَأَوْهُ﴾ (ra'awhu, "they see it") refers to "the trace of Allah's mercy" (athar raḥmat Allah), which is the crop, the herbage and the trees. Yellowing (al-ishfirar) in the crop and the like indicates its drying out, and "ṣufār" (with a ḍammah and a lightened fā') is called a blight that afflicts the crops.

Al-muṣfarr (ﷺ) is an active participle (ism fā'il) requiring the description with its meaning in the present, i.e., "they see it becoming yellow." The expression "muṣfarran" is used to portray the recent onset of yellowing upon it, rather than saying "ra'awhu aṣfar" (they see it yellow).

Ẓalla (ظَلَّ) means ṣāra (became). Bringing the verb of transformation (fi'l al-taṣyīr) together with the predicate in the imperfect (muḍāriʿ) portrays their haste toward disbelief and then their persistence in it. The summary is that the meaning is that disbelief overcomes their states.

Know that the three verbs are used in the past form because their occurrence within the context of a conditional (sharṭ) purifies them for the future; so the past form is preferred because it is lighter, and the speaker is free to bring either of the two forms with the conditional, like His saying ﴿Say: If mankind and the jinn gathered together to bring the like of this Qur'an, they would not bring its like﴾ [al-Isra': 88], in the imperfect form, because the context calls for negation with ﴿lā﴾, and it does not enter upon a past verb with a singular subject except in supplication.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 30, verses 52–53:

﴿So you cannot make the dead hear, nor can you make the deaf hear the call when they turn away, retreating.﴾ ﴿Nor can you guide the blind away from their error. You can make hear only those who believe in Our signs, and they are the ones who submit.﴾

The *fa'* (فاء) here indicates sequence following His words, ﴿they would certainly continue to disbelieve after it﴾ [al-Rum: 51]. It conveys that disbelief is the predominant state of these people, because they are between disbelief in God and turning away from thanking Him. Alternatively, the *fa'* is *fasihah* (فصيحة, an eloquent connective that implies an omitted clause). The meaning would then be: if their aversion weighs heavily on you and their persistence in disbelief distresses you, then indeed they are like the dead, and you cannot make the dead hear.

This is an excuse for the Prophet (ﷺ) and a reassurance that he has exerted full effort in conveying the message.

Apart from the *fa'*, the verse is similar to the one at the end of Surah al-Naml. Here we add the following: the enumeration of the comparisons (*tashbih*, simile) is considered in relation to the differing states of the groups of polytheists, so each group has its own comparison.

Some of them were so deeply immersed in polytheism that they do not believe what contradicts it and are not affected by the Qur'an or the call to truth. These are like the dead, forms without perception. These are their common people and the majority of them, and therefore the verse begins with them.

Some of them turn away from listening to the Qur'an. These are the ones who say ﴿There is a deafness in our ears﴾ [Fussilat: 5] and say ﴿Do not listen to this Qur'an, and make noise during it﴾ [Fussilat: 26]. These are their leaders and those who manage their affairs. They fear that if they listen to the Qur'an, it will take hold of their feelings, so they keep far from hearing it. For this reason, what they are compared to is restricted to the time of their turning away, retreating from the call. This is a *tashbih al-tamthil* (representational simile, a comparison of whole scenes).

Some of them followed the path of their leaders and walked in their footsteps, so their understanding deviated from what is correct. They hear the Qur'an but cannot act upon it. These are the ones accustomed to following their desires, and they are the ones who said ﴿Indeed, we found our fathers following a religion, and indeed we are guided by their footprints﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 22]. The overall result of all this is the comparison of their whole community to a group that gathers the dead, the deaf and the blind. This is not the multiplicity of comparisons for a single subject, such as in His words, ﴿or like a rainstorm from the sky﴾ [al-Baqarah: 19].

The majority (al-Jumhur) read ﴿وَلَا تُسْمِعُ الصُّمَّ﴾ with a *ta'* (ت) that is marked with a dammah above, and with the *mim* of *tusmi'* (تُسْمِعُ) kasrah, and *al-summa* (الصُّمَّ) in the accusative, treating it as addressed to the Prophet (ﷺ). Ibn Kathir read it as ﴿وَلَا يَسْمَعُ الصُّمُّ﴾ with a *ya'* (ي) that has a fatha above, and with the *mim* of *yasma'* (يَسْمَعُ) fathah, and he made *al-summu* (الصُّمُّ) nominative, as the subject (*fa'iliyyah*) of *yasma'*.

The majority read ﴿بِهَادِي﴾ with a *ba'* (ب) and with an *alif* after the *ha'* (ه), and with *hadi* (هادي) in construct with *al-'umy* (الْعُمْيِ). Hamzah alone read ﴿تَهْدِي﴾ with a *ta'* (ت) above, without an *alif* after the *ha'*, in the second person, and with *al-'umya* (الْعُمْيَ) in the accusative as the object.

**[Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur, al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir, on Surah 30, verse 54]**

﴿It is Allah who created you from weakness, then made after weakness strength, then made after strength weakness and grey hair. He creates what He wills, and He is the Knowing, the Competent.﴾

This is the fourth of the four preceding resumptions (*isti'naf*, a new sentence that begins a fresh topic). It returns to the argument from the vast power of God manifested in the various created things of the worlds, in order to establish the possibility of resurrection and to bring its occurrence closer to the minds of those who deny it. The variety of the forms and modes of God's creation, whether He originates things from non-existence or restores them after their annihilation, and whether they develop or not, increases the clarity of the possibility of resurrection for those who deny it. Thus the placement of this verse is like the placement of His saying: ﴿And of His signs is that He sends the winds, bringing clouds﴾ [al-Rum: 48], and its counterparts, as has already been explained. For this reason its opening came in the style of the openings of its counterparts, and this is what is indicated by its being followed by His saying: ﴿And on the day the Hour is established, the criminals will swear﴾ [al-Rum: 55], and so on.

Then His saying ﴿Allah, who created you﴾ is the subject (*mubtada'*) with a descriptive clause (*sifah*), and His saying ﴿He creates what He wills﴾ is the predicate (*khabar*). That is: He creates what He wills of what He has informed of, and you deny it.

The word *ḍu'f* (weakness) in the verse is pronounced with a *ḍamma* on the *ḍād*, and this is the more eloquent form; it is the dialect of Quraysh. It is also permissible to pronounce its *ḍād* with a *fatḥa*, which is the dialect of Tamim. Abu Dawud and al-Tirmidhi related from 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar, who said: "I recited it to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), *alladhi khalaqakum min ḍa'f* (with the *ḍād* pronounced with a *fatḥa*), and he corrected me to *min ḍu'f* (with the *ḍād* pronounced with a *ḍamma*)." The majority of reciters read all three instances of the word *ḍu'f* with a *ḍamma* on the *ḍād*. 'Asim and Hamzah read them with a *fatḥa* on the *ḍād*, and they have a chain of transmission that is undoubtedly sound, which contradicts the hadith of Ibn 'Umar. The reconciliation between this recitation and the hadith of Ibn 'Umar is that the Prophet (ﷺ) spoke in the dialect of the *ḍamma*, because it was the dialect of his people, and that the *fatḥa* is a concession for one who recites in the dialect of another tribe. And one who has no dialect of his own is free to choose between the two recitations. *Ḍu'f* means feebleness and softness.

The *min* (مِنَ) is for the starting point (*ibtida'iyyah*), meaning: the beginning of His creation is from weakness, that is, from a state of weakness, which is the state of being a fetus, then an infant, until he reaches his maturity (*ashudd*). This is like His saying: ﴿Man was created of haste﴾ [al-Anbiya: 37], which indicates that the attribute has taken firm hold of the one described, to the point that it is as if it were drawn out from him. He, exalted, said: ﴿And man was created weak﴾ [al-Nisa: 28].

The meaning is: just as He brought you into being in stages, beginning in feebleness and ending in it, so likewise He will bring you into being after death, for that is no more wondrous than the first creation and the stages that followed it. For this reason He informed of it by saying: ﴿He creates what He wills﴾.

He mentioned the attributes of knowledge and power because development is what wisdom requires, and wisdom is among the affairs of knowledge; and bringing it forth in the most perfect manner is among the effects of power.

The indefiniteness of (*ḍa'f* and *quwwah*) is for the category (*nau'iyyah*). Thus the *ḍu'f* mentioned the second time is the very same *ḍu'f* mentioned the first time, and the *quwwah* mentioned the second time is the very same *quwwah* mentioned the first time. As for their saying, "An indefinite noun, when repeated as indefinite, is other than the first," they mean by it an indefiniteness intended to denote an individual unit of the common kind, not an indefiniteness intended to denote the category.

The conjunction of *wa-shaybah* (and grey hair) serves to indicate that after this weakness there is no strength, and that after it comes non-existence, in accordance with what is widely held, that grey hair is a warning of death.

*Shaybah* is a noun of the verbal noun *shayb* (greyness). It has already been discussed in His saying: ﴿And the head has blazed with grey hair﴾ [Maryam: 4], in Surah Maryam.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 30, verse 55:

﴿And on the Day the Hour is established, the criminals will swear that they had not remained but an hour. Thus were they ever deluded.﴾

When he had mentioned that the polytheists derive no benefit from the signs of the Qur'an, and they were likened to the dead, the deaf and the blind, so that the monstrousness of their state in this world became evident, he followed this with a description of their state at the time the Hour is established, in continuation of their obstinacy which they lived by in the world. For when God restores their creation, brings into being for them bodies like their bodies, and returns to them their intellects, their thinking on that day will be in accordance with what they were upon in the world of sophistry, deception and delusion. So when they are raised from the graves and perceive the soundness of their bodies and their intellects, and they had known at the last moments of their lives that they were going to die, the creed of denying the Resurrection will cling to them at that time, and their sophistical argument is from their saying: ﴿Shall we show you a man who will inform you, when you have been completely torn apart, that you will indeed be in a new creation?﴾ [Saba': 7]. There, they wish to persuade themselves of the soundness of their old proof, and they seek a pretext for the non-fulfilment of the consequence, on the ground that their being resurrected to them shows that they were right in denying it in the world, since they had been told that the Resurrection would occur after the bodies had perished. So they wished to excuse their denial of the Resurrection when they had come to verify it, with what its upshot amounts to: that had they known the Resurrection would occur after an hour of lying in the grave, they would have acknowledged it.

This is indicated by the naming of their speech as an excuse in His saying after it: ﴿On that Day the excuse of those who did wrong will not benefit them﴾ [al-Rum: 57]. This is a trial which befell them at the time of the Resurrection; God made it for them so that they would be a mockery to the people of the Resurrection. Their error and their misunderstanding become clear, as indicated by His saying, exalted is He, after that: ﴿But those who were given knowledge and faith will say﴾ [al-Rum: 56], and the verse. He also hinted that this is the intended meaning of the verse when He said after it: ﴿Thus were they ever deluded﴾, that is, just as this error, they were in the world turned away from the truth by such nonsense. Some of this meaning was mentioned earlier at His saying: ﴿They will whisper among themselves, "You remained but ten"﴾ [Ta-Ha: 103], ﴿We are most knowing of what they say when their best in course says, "You remained but a day"﴾ [Ta-Ha: 104], in Surat Ta-Ha. Their going astray in this matter reached the point that they swear to it, and this comes after the disputation that takes place among them, from the saying of some of them: "You remained but ten," and the saying of another: "You remained but a day" [Ta-Ha: 104], and the saying of others: "We remained a day or part of a day" [al-Kahf: 19]. Part of a day is applied to an hour, as is related of them in this verse.

It is apparent that this oath is one they exchange among themselves, as the verse of Surat Ta-Ha implies, or it is another statement which they made public when the disagreement among them intensified, because resorting to oaths indicates contention and obstinacy in disagreement.

In His saying "al-sa'ah" (the Hour) and "sa'ah" (an hour) there is perfect paronomasia (jinas tam).

The clause ﴿Thus were they ever deluded﴾ is a explanatory resumptive clause (isti'naf bayani), because the strangeness of their state, from the corruption of their estimate of the duration and their swearing to it, while being a delusion, raises the question of a questioner about the source of this illusion in their souls. So His saying ﴿Thus were they ever deluded﴾ was an explanation of that. Its meaning: there is no wonder in such a thing proceeding from them, for they used to bring forth such illusions during their time in the world, so their illusions turned them away from certainty, and they used to swear to their beliefs, as in His saying: ﴿And they swore by God with their most emphatic oaths that God will not resurrect whoever dies﴾ [al-Nahl: 38], making light of oaths. Likewise, "thus" points to their turning away from the truth on the Day of Resurrection. The thing pointed to is the thing compared, and the thing compared is omitted, indicated by the particle of comparison (kaf), and the estimate is: "a delusion like this delusion of theirs, they were deluded by in their worldly life." The purpose of the comparison is similarity and equivalence.

Al-ifk, with a fatha on the hamza, means turning away, and it is of the pattern of "daraba," and it is transitive to the thing turned away from by the particle "'an" (from). It has already been discussed in the interpretation of His saying: ﴿They will surely say, "God." Say, "Praise be to God"﴾ [Luqman: 25], in Surat al-'Ankabut.

Their delusion is not attributed to a specific deluder, because some of their turning away comes from their allies and the leaders of their religion, and some of it is from God's sealing upon their hearts.

The insertion of the verb "kanu" (they were) indicates that the intended time is a period before that time, namely the time of the worldly life.

The meaning: that is a disposition they acquired and which became for them like a natural temperament during their worldly life, so that when God returns their spirits to them, there proceeds from them what they had acquired. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿He will say, "My Lord, why have You raised me blind, when I was seeing?"﴾ [Ta-Ha: 125] ﴿He will say, "Thus Our signs came to you, and you forgot them; and likewise today you are forgotten."﴾ [Ta-Ha: 126] and ﴿Thus do We recompense those who transgress﴾, the verse.

In this report there is a great lesson for the Muslims: that they should shun vices and major sins in the present life, lest they become a disposition for them and they be resurrected upon them.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 30, verse 56:

﴿Those who were given knowledge and faith will say: "You have indeed remained, according to the Book of Allah, until the Day of Resurrection. This is the Day of Resurrection, but you did not know."﴾

Allah made the deniers of the Resurrection a target for the arrows of confusion and exposure at the time of rising from the graves. When the believers, those who were given knowledge of the Qur'an, and whose minds were illuminated in the worldly life by sound beliefs and traces of wisdom, heard this, they could not restrain themselves from refuting their error with a refutation that would become for them a source of anguish, that they had not accepted the call to the truth as the believers had accepted it. This clause is parenthetical (mu'taridah).

He joined faith ('iman) to knowledge ('ilm) out of concern for it, because knowledge without faith does not guide to the correct beliefs by which success in the Hereafter is attained. The meaning is: the believers said to them, rebuking them and making them regretful.

The apparent sense is that the believers hear the disputing of the polytheists among themselves, and so they hasten to rebuke them, because changing wrongdoing (taghyir al-munkar) is their established disposition. In this there is an Islamic etiquette: whoever hears an error in religion and faith does not approve of it, even if he is not the one addressed by it.

Their saying ﴿You have indeed remained, according to the Book of Allah, until the Day of Resurrection﴾ is a turning of them away from that excuse, as though they were saying: leave this aside, for there is no benefit in it, and occupy yourselves with the purpose and with what you were promised of punishment on the Day of Resurrection.

The verb "labithtum" (you remained) is used in its literal sense, i.e., you stayed, that is, you settled in the graves. The statement is used for the purpose of causing grief and terror, in view of what follows it of the disclosure of the presence of the time of their punishment.

The "fi" (in) in His words ﴿in the Book of Allah﴾ is causal (lil-ta'lil), meaning: you remained until this day, and you were not punished before it, because of what came in the Book of Allah of threatening them with this day, like His words, exalted is He, ﴿And behind them is a barrier until the day they are resurrected﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 100]. That is: indeed, this reached you and you heard it, so the proper course was that you should have believed in it and not offered the excuse of saying "We remained only an hour."

The fa' (so) in "fa-hadha yawmu al-ba'th" is the fa' of explanation (fa' al-fasihah), which makes explicit a conditional clause that is implied, and it conveys the sense of suddenness, as was mentioned earlier at His words ﴿So they have indeed denied you in what you say﴾ [al-Furqan: 19] in Surat al-Furqan; that is: since it is so, then this is the Day of Resurrection, like the fa' in the verse of 'Abbas ibn al-Ahnaf:

They said: "Khurasan is the furthest that is intended for us; then the return." Indeed we have come to Khurasan.

This is a rebuke for them, a threat, and an hastening of their evil by what awaits them of punishment. Limiting the statement to ﴿This is the Day of Resurrection﴾ is so that they may expect every evil and punishment.

The istidrak (corrective exception) in ﴿but you did not know﴾ is a correction of what the clause ﴿You have indeed remained, according to the Book of Allah, until the Day of Resurrection﴾ contains; that is: indeed, this reached you, and it was the proper course that you prepare for it, but you did not know, that is, you did not take care to seek knowledge of what has benefit, rather your habit was turning away from affirming the Messenger (ﷺ).

In the expression of negating knowledge while intending to negate concern for it and care in receiving it, there is an indication that striving to learn is a means of acquiring it.

Ibn 'Ashur's commentary on surah 30, verse 57

﴿So on that Day, those who did wrong will not benefit from their excuse, nor will they be asked to make amends.﴾

This is a consequence (tafri') of the sentence "﴿Thus were they turned away﴾" [al-Rum: 55]. "Those who did wrong" (alladhina zalamu) are the polytheists who swore that they had not remained but an hour. The expression "those who did wrong" in place of a pronoun is an explicit mention in the position of a pronoun, for the purpose of recording upon them the description of wrongdoing, which is associating partners with God (shirk), because it encompasses all kinds of wrongdoing: it includes transgression against the right of God, the polytheist's wronging of himself by exposing himself to punishment, their wronging of the Messenger (ﷺ) through denial, and their wronging of the believers through aggression against their wealth and their persons.

Al-ma'dhira (excuse) is the verbal noun of i'tadhara, which means to present a pretext or argument in order to ward off blame for a sin or a shortcoming. It derives from the verb 'adhara, meaning to not hold someone to account for a sin or shortcoming because of the appearance of a cause that averts blame for what he did.

The annexation of ma'dhira to the pronoun of "those who did wrong" implies that the excuse proceeds from them. It may be that the annexation is for definiteness, referring to a known excuse, which would then be their statement "﴿We did not remain but an hour﴾" [al-Rum: 55], as mentioned earlier. It may also be that the definiteness is generic, as is the case with an annexed verbal noun; that is, no excuse by which they make excuse will benefit them, like their saying "﴿Our wretchedness overcame us﴾" [al-Mu'minun: 106] and their saying "﴿These are the ones who led us astray﴾" [al-A'raf: 38].

Know that this does not contradict His saying, "﴿nor are they permitted, so that they may make excuse﴾" [al-Mursalat: 36], which implies the negation of an excuse actually being offered by them, because the excuse that is negated is the excuse that is permitted, i.e., accepted. For if God had permitted them to make excuse, that would have been a preparation for accepting their excuse, similar to His saying, "Who is it that intercedes with Him except by His permission?"

What is affirmed here is an excuse that proceeds from their own selves, for which they were not granted permission, and so it does not benefit them, as God said: "﴿They say: Our Lord, our wretchedness overcame us, and we were a people astray﴾" [al-Mu'minun: 106], "﴿Our Lord, bring us out of it, and if we return, then we are wrongdoers﴾" [al-Mu'minun: 107], "﴿He said: Be silent in it, and do not speak to Me﴾" [al-Mu'minun: 108], and His saying, "﴿Do not cry out today; indeed, you will not be helped by Us﴾" [al-Mu'minun: 65].

The majority (al-Jumhur) read "tanfa'u" with a feminine (taa') prefix. Hamza, 'Asim, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read it with a yaa' prefix, and this is a permissible reading, because ma'dhira has a metaphorical feminine, and because a separation occurs between the verb and its subject by the object.

"Yusta'taboon" is in the passive voice, and its active form is is'ta'taba, meaning to ask for 'utba (reconciliation or the removal of displeasure), with a damma on the 'ayn and with the short vowel; it is a noun for i'tab, that is, the removal of 'atab (displeasure). Thus the hamza of i'tab is for removal, as God said: "﴿And if they ask for reconciliation, they will not be among those reconciled﴾" [Fussilat: 24]. So istu'tiba in the passive has come to follow ista'taba in the active. When it was said that ista'taba means "to seek 'utba," istu'tiba in the passive came to mean u'tibu (to be reconciled with). Thus the meaning of "wa la hum yusta'taboon" is: nor will the punishment be removed from them, similar to His saying, "﴿So they are not among those reconciled﴾" [Fussilat: 24].

This is a strange usage that runs through several derivations in eloquent speech, and some of its derivation is not analogical. Those who tried to subject it to analogy were compelled into forced meanings that sound nature does not accept, and it is surprising that these occur in the Kashshaf. In the Qamus he says: "wa-sta'tabahu: gave him 'utba, like a'tabahu; and talaba ilayhi al-'utba, is its opposite."

The meaning is: an excuse with a pretext will not benefit them, nor will an acknowledgment of sin and a request for pardon. The phrase "wa la hum yusta'taboon" has already been mentioned in Surat al-Naml.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 30, verses 58–59:

﴿And We have certainly presented to the people in this Qur'an every kind of example. And if you were to bring them a sign, those who disbelieve would surely say, "You are nothing but falsifiers."﴾ ﴿Thus does Allah seal the hearts of those who do not know.﴾

When the matter that this surah establishes, the proofs of God's oneness and the affirmation of resurrection, came to an end, it was followed by this, by the exalting of the Qur'an and its reaching the utmost degree of clarity in exposition and guidance.

The root meaning of *al-darb* is placing and attaching. It is used in verses such as this one to mean mentioning and clarifying, because it is like placing a signifier upon the thing signified by attaching it to it. It has already occurred in God's words ﴿Indeed, Allah is not ashamed to present an example, of anything﴾ [al-Baqarah: 26], and also just previously in His words ﴿He has presented to you an example from yourselves﴾ [al-Rum: 28]. This is like His words ﴿And We have certainly turned [the Qur'an] for the people in this Qur'an, of every kind of example﴾ [al-Isra': 89], which has passed in the surah of al-Isra'. The word *al-nas* (the people) is intended to mean the polytheists, because they are the ones at which the repetition of these examples is aimed. He joined to it His words ﴿And if you were to bring them a sign﴾, etc., so it is a description of how the polytheists receive the Qur'anic examples. When the Messenger ﷺ brings them a sign from the Qur'an containing guidance for them, they receive it with arbitrary dismissal and pure denial, and so they say ﴿You are nothing but falsifiers.﴾

The plural pronoun of address is directed at the Prophet ﷺ in order to honour him on the part of God, Exalted is He. What the disbelievers actually say is, "You are nothing but a falsifier," so their speech is reported in meaning in order to exalt the status of the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him. It has also been said that the address is to the Messenger ﷺ and the believers, so it is a report in its wording.

This is a consolation to the Messenger ﷺ regarding the lack of faith of his opponents, that is, the leaders of disbelief among them. For this reason, after the two conjoined sentences, there is interjected the sentence ﴿Thus does Allah seal the hearts of those who do not know﴾, as a preparation for the command to be patient with their obstinacy. That is, such is the custom regarding their like: just as you know, that sealing is what Allah places upon their hearts. This has already occurred in His words ﴿And thus We have made you a median nation﴾ [al-Baqarah: 143] in the surah of al-Baqarah, and in many other places in the Qur'an.

Sealing upon the heart (*al-tab'* ʿalā al-qalb) is rendering it unable to grasp religious matters, and it is the same as *al-khatm* (sealing). This has already occurred in His words ﴿Allah has sealed upon their hearts﴾ [al-Baqarah: 7] in the surah of al-Baqarah.

The phrase "those who do not know" is intended to mean those very people who disbelieved. He turned away from the pronoun to add the description of their lacking knowledge, after they had already been described as the criminals, those who did wrong, and those who disbelieved.

[p. 135]

﴿So be patient. Indeed, the promise of Allah is true, and let not those who have no certainty make you impatient.﴾

The command to the Prophet ﷺ to be patient follows from the previous statement, ﴿And even if you bring them every sign﴾ [al-Rum: 58], because that statement implies despair of their faith.

The object of the command to be patient is omitted, because the context indicates it. The meaning is: be patient with their obstinacy.

The clause ﴿indeed, the promise of Allah is true﴾ gives the reason for the command to be patient. It is a consolation to the Prophet ﷺ through the certainty of Allah's promise, both of retribution against the deniers and of victory for the Messenger ﷺ.

Al-haqq (the truth) is a verbal noun of ḥaqqa, yuḥiqqu, meaning "to be established." Thus al-ḥaqq is that which is established, about which there is no doubt and no exaggeration.

Al-istikhfāf (making light of, or being moved to lightness) is an intensification of making something light. The sīn and tā' serve to strengthen the meaning, like them in istajāba (he responded) and istamsaka (he held fast). It is the opposite of patience. The meaning is: do not let them move you to abandon patience.

Lightness (khiffa) is used figuratively for the state of impatience and the appearance of the signs of anger. It is like qalaq (agitation), used figuratively from the shaking of a thing, because the signs of impatience and anger resemble the trembling of a light object, which moves at the slightest stirring. Conversely, steadfastness and heaviness are used figuratively for its opposite. These figurative usages became so common that they equaled the literal usage.

The prohibition to the Messenger ﷺ against being made light by those who lack certainty is a prohibition against the lightness that naturally arises in a reasonable person when he sees the obstinacy of those he is guiding to righteousness. This is what stirs the anger of the forbearing. Thus istikhfāf here means that they influence his soul against patience. The saying of the Exalted, ﴿So he made light his people, and they obeyed him﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 54], in Surat al-Zukhruf, comes as a complement to what is here, so refer to it.

The attribution of istikhfāf to them is by way of al-majāz al-ʿaqlī (metaphor of attribution, attributing an action to a cause rather than its agent), because they are its cause through what proceeds from their obstinacy.

Those who have no certainty are the polytheists, to whom the previously mentioned attributes apply:

[p. 136]

criminality, wrongdoing, disbelief, and lack of knowledge. Their description here is an explicit mention in place of a pronoun, to make their faults plain. It was said that al-Naḍr ibn al-Ḥārith was among them.

The meaning of "they have no certainty" is that they do not have certainty regarding the matters of certainty, that is, those matters indicated by decisive proofs. Thus they are obstinate deniers.

Sūrat Luqmān

This sūrah is named after its attribution to Luqmān, because it mentions Luqmān, his wisdom, and sayings from his wisdom with which he educated his son. It has no other name than this, and by this name it is known among the reciters and the exegetes. I have not found an explicit statement of this name transmitted from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ through a acceptable chain.

Al-Bayhaqī related in Dalāʾil al-Nubuwwa from Ibn ʿAbbās: "The Sūrat Luqmān was revealed in Makkah."

According to Ibn ʿAbbās, in the more well-known of his two statements, it is entirely Makkan, and the general statement of the majority of the exegetes is in accordance with this. From Ibn ʿAbbās, by the narration of al-Naḥḥās, three verses are excepted, from the saying of the Exalted, ﴿And if whatever trees are on the earth were pens﴾ [Luqmān: 27], to His saying ﴿...that which you do is All-Aware﴾ [Luqmān: 29]. From Qatāda, two verses are excepted, up to His saying ﴿Indeed, Allah is Hearing and Seeing﴾ [Luqmān: 28]. In the tafsīr of al-Kawāshī, there is a report of a statement that it is Makkan except for one verse revealed in Madīna, which is ﴿Those who establish prayer and give zakāt, and they are certain of the Hereafter﴾ [Luqmān: 4]. He said that this is because prayer and zakāt were obligated in Madīna. Al-Bayḍāwī refuted this, even granting it, by saying that their obligation in Madīna does not negate their legislation in Makkah without obligation. The careful scholars deny that prayer and zakāt were obligated in Madīna. As for prayer, there is no doubt that it was obligated in general in Makkah. As for zakāt, it was obligated in Makkah without specifying the shares and amounts, and then the shares and amounts were specified in Madīna.

From this it follows that the one who said that the verse ﴿Those who establish prayer and give zakāt﴾ [Luqmān: 4] through its end was revealed in Madīna said so from his own opinion, and he has no chain of transmission to rely upon, as his saying "because prayer and zakāt..." etc. indicates. Moreover, this view requires that the beginning of the sūrah, which was revealed in Makkah, be guidance and mercy for the good-doers, ﴿These are upon guidance from their Lord﴾ [Luqmān: 5], etc., and then that ﴿Those who establish prayer and give zakāt, and they are certain of the Hereafter﴾ [Luqmān: 4] was attached to it.

[p. 138]

As for the view that two or three verses are excepted, it rests upon what Ibn Jarīr related from Qatāda and from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, from Ibn ʿAbbās, that the saying of the Exalted, ﴿And if whatever trees are on the earth were pens﴾ [Luqmān: 27], through the end of the two or three verses, was revealed because of a dispute the Jews had. Their scholars said: "O Muḥammad, what do you think of His saying, ﴿And you have not been given of knowledge except a little﴾ [al-Isrāʾ: 85]? Do you mean us or your people?" The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "I meant all of you." They said: "Do you not recite in what came to you that we were given the Torah, in which is the clarification of everything?" The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "It is, in the knowledge of Allah, little." So Allah revealed to him ﴿And if whatever trees are on the earth were pens﴾ [Luqmān: 27] and the verses." This is related through weak chains. Even granting them, it has been answered that the Jews argued about this while the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was in Makkah, by instructing a delegation of Quraysh who visited them in Madīna to say it. This is closer to reconciling the statements. Although these reports are not established through a sound chain, a matter like this is satisfied by what is acceptable in general.

Abū Ḥayyān said: "The occasion of revelation of this sūrah is that Quraysh asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ about the story of Luqmān with his son," meaning they asked him as a challenge and a test. What Abū Ḥayyān mentioned supports beginning the sūrah with the saying of the Exalted, ﴿And of the people is he who buys idle speech﴾ [Luqmān: 6].

This sūrah is the fifty-seventh in the order of revelation of the sūrahs. It was revealed after Sūrat al-Ṣāffāt and before Sūrat Saba.

Its verses are counted as thirty-three by the people of Madīna and Makkah, and as thirty-four by the people of Syria, Basra, and Kufa.

The Purposes of This Sūrah

The purposes contained in this sūrah are connected to its occasion of revelation mentioned above, that the polytheists asked about the story of Luqmān and his son. If we combine this with what comes at the saying of the Exalted, ﴿And of the people is he who buys idle speech﴾ [Luqmān: 6], that it refers to al-Naḍr ibn al-Ḥārith, who used to travel to the lands of Persia and acquire books of the stories of Isfandiyār, Rustam, and Bahrām, and he would recite them to Quraysh and say: "Muḥammad tells you about ʿĀd and Thamūd, and I tell you about Rustam, Isfandiyār, and Bahrām," then this sūrah begins with praise of the guidance of the Qur'an, so that people know that it contains nothing but what has in it guidance and direction to goodness and the like of spiritual perfection. Therefore there is no attention in it to the reports of tyrants and the people of misguidance, except in the context of warning against what they are in and its consequences. So the beginning of this sūrah served as a preparation for the story of Luqmān. This was already alluded to in the saying of the Exalted at the beginning of Sūrat Yūsuf, ﴿We relate to you the best of stories﴾ [Yūsuf: 3], and I pointed it out in the seventh introduction to this tafsīr.

It then moves from that to the foolishness of al-Naḍr ibn al-Ḥārith and his false stories.

The mention of Luqmān begins with a notice that Allah gave him wisdom and commanded him to be grateful for the blessing. The discourse on Luqmān's counsels is extended, and what they contain: the warning against associating partners with Allah, the command to be dutiful to parents, observing Allah because He is All-Knowing of hidden matters, establishing prayer, enjoining good and forbidding evil, patience, warning against arrogance and conceit, and the command to adopt the characteristics of the humble in walking and speech.

The sūrah follows various methods, having connections with what Luqmān's counsel to his son contains, and it incorporates into this a reminder to the polytheists of the proofs of Allah's oneness, of His blessings upon them, and of how they turned away from His guidance and held fast to what they found their fathers upon.

It also mentions the excellence of the religion of Islam.

And it offers consolation to the Messenger ﷺ, that the Muslims hold fast to the firmest handhold, and that the disbelief of those who disbelieve should not grieve him.

This sūrah also includes a response to the opponents of the Qur'an in the saying of the Exalted, ﴿And if whatever trees are on the earth were pens﴾ [Luqmān: 27] and what follows it. It concludes with a warning against the call of Satan and an alert to the falsehood of the claim to knowledge of the unseen.
